recon.greekSource: Both readers worked from the same primary Greek: the TLG text of Athanasius, Epistula ad Marcellinum (TLG 2035.059 = Migne PG 27.12-45), posted by Documenta Catholica Omnia (http://www.documentacatholicaomnia.eu/02g/0295-0373,_Athanasius,_Epistula_ad_Marcellinum_de_interpretatione_Psalmorum,_MGR.pdf). I re-read the disputed passages myself in reader A's working copies (scratchpad/greek/marc-greek2.txt, the TLG text one sentence per line; scratchpad/greek/pg27.txt, the archive.org OCR of Migne PG 27, which has both the Greek and the Latin columns). I also checked the C.S.M.V. text in its original Septuagint numbering (scratchpad/fe.txt, the fisheaters.com copy). Reader B's third witness was the modern Greek EPE translation (Athanasiou Apanta 5, 1975). In the digital TLG text, stigma (6) and koppa (90) both print as 'ς'. A lone 'ς' in front of a units letter is koppa (ςβ = 92); after a tens letter it is stigma (κς = 26). How I settled the disputes: (1) §12, trust and prayer: the TLG reads ιαʹ, ιςʹ, and I found the same in the Migne Greek ('τα’ καὶ τὸν ις’', where 'τα' is an OCR error for ια). That gives LXX 11 and 16 = English 12 and 17. The C.S.M.V. read 10 and 11; no Greek witness supports that. (2) §17: the TLG has ις for 'saved from your enemies' and πς in the prayer list. Four witnesses read 17 and 87 instead: the Migne Greek (ιζ’, πζ'), the Migne Latin ('decimum septimum'; '16, 85, 87 et 140'), the EPE translation and the C.S.M.V. So the answer is English 18 and 88. (3) §25, 'sing to the Lord': the TLG, the Migne Greek, the Migne Latin and EPE all give 92 and 97 (English 93 and 98). Only the C.S.M.V. reads 95. (4) The fear, sadness and failure lines belong to Migne §28, not §29: the Greek marker κη' comes just before them and κθ' just after, and λ' (30) opens the next part. Psalm 118/119 is in §33 (marker λγ'). SCOPE: reader B also listed the §14 genre catalogue (psalms that narrate, pray, give thanks, accuse and so on) and the §§3-8 survey of which psalms retell Genesis, the Exodus, the Judges, the kings and exile, or foretell Christ. Reader A left these out on purpose. I left them out too, because they describe what a psalm contains or its genre; they are not Athanasius's advice about which psalm to use in a given situation. I did check them against the Greek (lines 237-261 and 21-63 of marc-greek2.txt), and one error in the English copy surfaced there. In §4 the Joshua and Judges psalm ('they cried unto the Lord in their trouble') is 'the hundred and sixth' in the Greek, i.e. LXX 106 = English 107, not the copy's 105. The §14 catalogue is also where the C.S.M.V. wrongly renders ἐξομολόγησις as 'confessions' and adds Psalm 51. Neither the Gregg (Paulist, 1980) translation nor the Savvidis-Wyrwa critical edition was consulted.

entries.situation: Singing a psalm while thinking about your own troubles, so its words feel like your own
entries.greek: τὸν τρίτον ψάλλει τις εἰς τὰς ἰδίας θλίψεις συνορῶν
entries.evidence: Greek ordinal τρίτον in TLG and Migne; Eng 3 superscription: when David fled from Absalom; 3:1 'how many are my foes'

entries.situation: Putting your own trust in God and your own prayer into words
entries.greek: τὸν ιαʹ καὶ τὸν ιςʹ ὡς εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν πεποίθησιν καὶ προσευχήν
entries.evidence: ιαʹ, ιϛʹ in the TLG and in the Migne Greek (OCR 'τα’ καὶ τὸν ις’'). Eng 17 superscription 'A prayer of David'; §14 of the same letter also lists LXX 16 first among the psalms 'as prayer'. The C.S.M.V. read LXX 10 and 11, which its copy converted to 11 and 12
entries.settledBy: Reader A: Eng 12, 17, high confidence. Reader B: low confidence, with the C.S.M.V.'s LXX 10, 11 (Eng 11, 12) as the alternative. I read the numerals in both the TLG and the Migne Greek myself; both read ια, ις. No Greek witness reads 10, 11, so I followed the Greek

entries.situation: Singing Psalm 51 as though you yourself were speaking your own words of repentance
entries.greek: τὸν μὲν νʹ ψαλμὸν ὡς αὐτός ἐστι τὰ ἴδια τῆς μετανοίας ἑαυτοῦ λέγων ῥήματα
entries.evidence: νʹ in both Greek witnesses; Eng 51 superscription: Nathan, after Bathsheba
entries.settledBy: Reader B put this pairing first in §12 and described it as repentance stirred in the singer and the hearers, following the C.S.M.V., which moves 'Psalm 50' up to the earlier conscience clause. In the Greek the numeral νʹ comes after the 3rd, 11th and 16th, and it attaches to 'his own words of repentance'; the conscience clause names no psalm. I kept the Greek order and wording

entries.situation: Being persecuted and singing these psalms as the one who is suffering, not as if about someone else
entries.greek: τὸν δὲ νγʹ, καὶ τὸν νεʹ, καὶ τὸν νςʹ, καὶ τὸν ρμαʹ ... ὡς ὢν ὁ πάσχων
entries.evidence: Greek numerals agree in TLG and Migne. Eng superscriptions: Ziphites (54), seized in Gath (56), in the cave (57, 142)

entries.situation: Wanting to call someone blessed: how to do it, on what grounds, and what to say
entries.greek: ἄν τε μακαρίσαι τινὰ θελήσῃς ... αʹ, λαʹ, μʹ, ριαʹ, ριηʹ, ρκζʹ
entries.evidence: Greek list agrees in both witnesses; each Eng psalm opens with or turns on 'Blessed is...'

entries.situation: Rebuking the plot of the Jewish leaders against the Saviour
entries.greek: μέμψασθαι τὴν Ἰουδαίων κατὰ τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἐπιβουλήν, ἔχεις τὴν δευτέραν ᾠδήν
entries.evidence: Greek ordinal δευτέραν; Ps 2:1-2, the rulers take counsel against the LORD and His Anointed

entries.situation: Being hounded by your own people, with many rising up against you
entries.greek: ἂν δὲ διώκῃ παρὰ τῶν ἰδίων, καὶ πολλοὺς ἔχῃς τοὺς ἐπαναστάντας ... τὸν γʹ
entries.evidence: γʹ in both witnesses; Eng 3:1 'How many rise up against me'; superscription names Absalom, David's own son

entries.situation: Having called on the Lord in distress and been heard, and now wanting to give thanks
entries.greek: θλιβόμενος ἐπεκαλέσω τὸν Κύριον, καὶ εἰσακουσθεὶς ... τὸν τέταρτον, καὶ οδʹ, καὶ ριδʹ
entries.evidence: τέταρτον, οδʹ, ριδʹ. LXX 114 is only Eng 116:1-9 ('He has heard my voice'); the copy's 116 is right but should be limited to those verses

entries.situation: Seeing wicked people waiting to trap you and wanting God to hear your prayer; rise early and pray
entries.greek: τοὺς πονηρευομένους βλέπων ἐνεδρεύειν θέλοντας ... ὀρθρίζων τὸ πρωῒ ψάλλε τὸν εʹ
entries.evidence: εʹ in both witnesses; Eng 5:3 'in the morning You hear my voice'

entries.situation: Sensing the Lord's displeasure against you and being shaken by it
entries.greek: αἰσθόμενος δὲ ἀπειλῆς τοῦ Κυρίου ... τὸν ϛʹ καὶ τὸν λζʹ
entries.evidence: ϛʹ and λζʹ; Migne Latin '6 et 37'. Both Eng psalms open 'O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger'

entries.situation: People scheming against you, as Ahithophel did against David, and someone telling you of it; trust God, Who rescues
entries.greek: βουλεύωνταί τινες κατὰ σοῦ, ὡς ὁ Ἀχιτόφελ κατὰ τοῦ Δαβίδ ... ψάλλε τὸν ζʹ
entries.evidence: ζʹ in both witnesses. The link runs through the LXX title, which names 'Chousi' (Hushai, who foiled Ahithophel); BSB reads 'Cush, a Benjamite'

entries.situation: Seeing the Saviour's grace spread everywhere and the human race saved, and wanting to address the Lord
entries.greek: βλέπων δὲ τὴν πανταχοῦ χάριν τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἐκτεταμένην ... ψάλλε τὸν ηʹ
entries.evidence: ηʹ in both witnesses; Eng 8:1 'how majestic is Your name in all the earth'

entries.situation: Singing a winepress (grape-harvest) song in thanks to the Lord
entries.greek: ᾆσαι θέλεις ἐπιλήνιον ... τὸν ηʹ καὶ τὸν πγʹ
entries.evidence: πγʹ in TLG, Migne Greek and Latin ('8 et 83'), and EPE. Both psalms carry the LXX title 'for the winepresses' (BSB 'According to Gittith'). The C.S.M.V. misread the numeral as 18, hence the copy's 19

entries.situation: When the enemy is overthrown and creation saved: not boasting in yourself but knowing the Son of God did it
entries.greek: ἐπὶ δὲ τῷ κατηργῆσθαι τὸν ἐχθρὸν ... λέγε τὸν εἰς αὐτὸν εἰρημένον θʹ ψαλμόν
entries.evidence: θʹ; LXX 9 is Eng 9 and 10 together, so the copy's 9 is right but incomplete

entries.situation: Someone trying hard to unsettle or frighten you; hold on to your trust in the Lord
entries.greek: ἐὰν λίαν σέ τις ταράσσειν ἐθέλῃ, ἔχε σὺ τὴν πεποίθησιν εἰς τὸν Κύριον ... τὸν ιʹ
entries.evidence: ιʹ in both witnesses; Eng 11:1 'In the LORD I take refuge; how can you say to my soul, Flee...'

entries.situation: Seeing widespread arrogance and evil overflowing until nothing holy seems left among people; take refuge in the Lord
entries.greek: τὴν τῶν πολλῶν ὑπερηφανίαν ἴδῃς ... κατάφυγε σὺ ἐπὶ τὸν Κύριον, καὶ λέγε τὸν ιαʹ
entries.evidence: ιαʹ in both witnesses; Eng 12:1 'the godly are no more'

entries.situation: Opposition that drags on and on, tempting you to lose heart as though God had forgotten you; keep calling on Him
entries.greek: ἐγχρονιζούσης δὲ τῆς παρὰ τῶν ἐχθρῶν ἐπιβουλῆς, μὴ ὀλιγώρει ὡς ἐπιλησθεὶς ... ᾄδων τὸν ιβʹ
entries.evidence: ιβʹ in TLG and the Migne Greek; Latin 'duodecimum'; EPE agrees. Eng 13:1 'How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?' The C.S.M.V. printed LXX 26, which the copy converted to 27

entries.situation: Hearing people speak against God's providence; do not join them, but pray
entries.greek: βλασφημούντων τινῶν κατὰ τῆς Προνοίας ἀκούσῃς ... λέγε τὸν ιγʹ καὶ νβʹ
entries.evidence: ιγʹ, νβʹ; both Eng psalms open 'The fool says in his heart, There is no God'

entries.situation: Wanting to learn what kind of person is a citizen of the kingdom of heaven
entries.greek: ὁποῖός ἐστι τῆς βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν ὁ πολίτης, ψάλλε τὸν ιδʹ
entries.evidence: ιδʹ; Latin '14'. Eng 15:1 'LORD, who may dwell in Your tent?'

entries.situation: Needing to pray because of people who oppose you and hem your soul in
entries.greek: προσευχῆς σοι χρεία διὰ τοὺς ἀνθεστηκότας σοι καὶ περιέχοντάς σου τὴν ψυχήν ... ιςʹ, πεʹ, πζʹ, ρμʹ
entries.evidence: Migne Greek 'τις’ (= ις), πε', πζ', ρμ'; Migne Latin '16, 85, 87 et 140'; EPE and the C.S.M.V. (LXX '16, 85, 87') agree on 87. Only the TLG reads πς (86 = Eng 87, a Zion hymn that does not fit a prayer). ρμʹ = Eng 141 in every witness, so the copy's 140 is wrong (the C.S.M.V. read 139)
entries.settledBy: Both readers chose 87 but marked it medium because the TLG reads πς. I checked the Migne Greek and Latin myself (pg27.txt lines 1880-1891): both read 87, and so do EPE and the C.S.M.V. With four witnesses against one, and a better fit with the psalm, I raised it to high

entries.situation: Wanting to learn how Moses prayed
entries.greek: θέλεις μαθεῖν, πῶς Μωϋσῆς προσηύξατο, ἔχεις τὸν πθʹ
entries.evidence: πθʹ; Eng 90 superscription 'A prayer of Moses, the man of God'

entries.situation: Having been saved from your enemies and rescued from those hunting you
entries.greek: ἐσώθης ἀπὸ τῶν ἐχθρῶν σου, καὶ ἐῤῥύσθης ἀπὸ τῶν διωκόντων σε ... τὸν ιζʹ ψαλμόν
entries.evidence: Migne Greek 'ιζ’ ψαλμόν', Migne Latin 'decimum septimum', EPE 17 and the C.S.M.V. 17. The TLG reads ις (16). Eng 18 superscription: the day the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from Saul
entries.settledBy: Reader A: medium; reader B: high; both chose LXX 17. I read the Migne Greek (ιζ') and Latin ('decimum septimum') myself. Four witnesses agree against the TLG's ις, and the superscription fits exactly, so high

entries.situation: Marvelling at the order of creation, God's providence in it, and the holy commands of His law
entries.greek: θαυμάζεις τὴν τῆς κτίσεως τάξιν ... τοῦ τε νόμου τὰ ἱερὰ προστάγματα, ψάλλε τὸν ιηʹ καὶ τὸν κγʹ
entries.evidence: ιηʹ, κγʹ; Eng 19 is the heavens plus the law; Eng 24 'The earth is the LORD's'

entries.situation: Seeing others in distress and comforting them by praying over them
entries.greek: θλιβομένους δὲ ὁρῶν, παρακάλει τούτους ... τὰ ἐν τῷ ιθʹ ψαλμῷ ῥήματα
entries.evidence: ιθʹ; Latin 'decimi noni'. Eng 20:1 'May the LORD answer you in the day of distress'

entries.situation: Seeing yourself shepherded and guided on your way by the Lord, and rejoicing in it
entries.greek: ὁρᾷς σεαυτὸν ποιμαινόμενον καὶ εὐοδούμενον παρὰ τοῦ Κυρίου ... τὸν κβʹ
entries.evidence: κβʹ; Latin '22'. Eng 23 'The LORD is my shepherd'

entries.situation: Enemies all around you; lift your soul up to God
entries.greek: οἱ ἐχθροὶ περὶ σέ, ἀλλὰ σὺ τὴν ψυχὴν ἐπαίρων πρὸς Θεόν, λέγε τὸν κδʹ
entries.evidence: κδʹ; Latin '24'. Eng 25:1 'To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul'

entries.situation: Enemies who keep on, hands full of blood, trying to drag you down and ruin you; do not leave the verdict to people, but ask God, the only just One, to judge
entries.greek: μὴ δῷς ἀνθρώπῳ τὸ κρῖμα ... τὸν Θεὸν ἀξιῶν κριτὴν γενέσθαι ... κεʹ, λδʹ, μβʹ
entries.evidence: κεʹ, λδʹ, μβʹ; Latin '25, 34, 42'. All three Eng psalms open with a plea for God to vindicate or judge

entries.situation: The attack growing fiercer, the enemy massing like an army and scorning you as not yet anointed; do not cower
entries.greek: πλῆθος ὡς παρεμβολαὶ γένωνται ... ὡς μήπω σου χρισθέντος ... μὴ πτήξῃς, ἀλλ' ᾆδε τὸν κϛʹ
entries.evidence: κϛʹ; LXX title 'before he was anointed'; Eng 27:3 'Though an army encamps around me, my heart will not fear'

entries.situation: Schemers who are shameless: because human nature is weak, do not fix your attention on them but cry out to God
entries.greek: ἀσθενής ἐστιν ἡ φύσις τῶν ἀνθρώπων ... κράζε πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, λέγων τὰ ἐν τῷ κζʹ
entries.evidence: κζʹ; Eng 28:1 'To You, O LORD, I call'

entries.situation: Wanting to learn, with spiritual understanding, how to bring your thanks to the Lord
entries.greek: εὐχαριστῶν μαθεῖν πῶς δεῖ προσφέρειν τῷ Κυρίῳ, νοητῶς νοῶν ψάλλε τὸν κηʹ
entries.evidence: κηʹ; LXX 28:1 'Bring to the Lord' (Ἐνέγκατε τῷ κυρίῳ)

entries.situation: Dedicating your home, meaning both your soul that receives the Lord and the house you live in; give thanks
entries.greek: ἐγκαινίζων τὸν οἶκόν σου ... τόν τε κθʹ καὶ τὸν ἐν τοῖς ἀναβαθμοῖς ρκϛʹ
entries.csmv: 30 and 127 (with a bracket calling the Gradual Psalms 119-133)
entries.evidence: κθʹ, ρκϛʹ. Eng 30 superscription: for the dedication of the house/temple. Eng 127:1 'Unless the LORD builds the house'

entries.situation: Hated and hunted by all your friends and relatives for holding to the truth, with acquaintances turning away; do not shrink back, but look to what is coming
entries.greek: σαυτὸν διὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν μισούμενον καὶ διωκόμενον παρὰ πάντων τῶν τε φίλων καὶ συγγενῶν ... τὸν λʹ
entries.evidence: λʹ; Eng 31:11 'a dread to my acquaintances; those who see me flee'

entries.situation: Seeing people baptized and redeemed, wondering at God's love for people, and singing it over them
entries.greek: τοὺς βαπτιζομένους καὶ λυτρουμένους ... ᾆδε εἰς ἐκείνους τὸν λαʹ
entries.evidence: λαʹ; Eng 32:1 'Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven'

entries.situation: Wanting to sing together with a gathering of upright people
entries.greek: ψάλλειν μετὰ πολλῶν ... τοὺς δικαίους ἄνδρας ... τὸν λβʹ
entries.evidence: λβʹ; Eng 33:1 'Sing joyfully to the LORD, O righteous ones'

entries.situation: Having fallen among enemies but slipped away wisely from their scheme, and wanting to give thanks among gentle people
entries.greek: ἐμπεσὼν δὲ εἰς τοὺς ἐχθροὺς, καὶ σοφῶς αὐτοὺς διαφυγών ... τοὺς πραεῖς ἄνδρας ... τὸν λγʹ
entries.evidence: λγʹ; Eng 34 superscription: David feigning madness before Abimelech; 34:2 'the humble will hear and rejoice'

entries.situation: Seeing how eager lawbreakers are for evil, without concluding (as heretics say) that evil is in their nature: they are the cause of their own sin
entries.greek: μὴ νόμιζε ἐν αὐτοῖς κατὰ φύσιν τὴν κακίαν εἶναι, οἷα λέγουσιν οἱ αἱρετικοί ... τὸν λεʹ
entries.evidence: λεʹ; Eng 36:1-4 describes the wicked man's own plotting

entries.situation: Seeing the wicked do much wrong and lord it over the lowly, and warning yourself and others not to envy them, since they soon fade
entries.greek: μὴ προσέχειν τούτοις, μηδὲ παραζηλοῦν αὐτούς ... λέγε καὶ σαυτῷ καὶ τοῖς ἑτέροις τὸν λϛʹ
entries.evidence: λϛʹ; Eng 37:1-2 'Do not fret... do not envy... they will soon wither'

entries.situation: Having resolved to keep watch over yourself, then finding the enemy attacking all the harder, and wanting to steel yourself against him
entries.greek: προθέμενος προσέχειν σαυτῷ ... θέλῃς ἐπαλείφειν σαυτὸν κατ' αὐτοῦ, ᾆδε τὸν ληʹ
entries.evidence: ληʹ; Latin 'trigesimum octavum'; Eng 39:1 'I will watch my ways'

entries.situation: Enduring hardship while under attack and wanting to learn what patience gains
entries.greek: ὑπομένῃς τὰς θλίψεις, καὶ θέλῃς μαθεῖν τὴν ἐκ τῆς ὑπομονῆς ὠφέλειαν ... τὸν λθʹ
entries.evidence: λθʹ; Eng 40:1 'I waited patiently for the LORD'

entries.situation: Seeing many poor people and wanting them shown mercy: commend those who have helped and urge others to help
entries.greek: βλέπων δὲ πολλοὺς πένητας καὶ πτωχούς ... ἐν τῷ λέγειν τὸν μʹ
entries.evidence: μʹ; Latin 'quadragesimum'; Eng 41:1 'Blessed is he who cares for the poor'

entries.situation: Longing intensely for God while enemies taunt you; comfort your own soul with hope in God and soothe life's griefs
entries.greek: πάνυ τὸν πόθον ἔχων εἰς τὸν Θεόν ... παρακάλει σαυτοῦ τὴν ψυχὴν τῇ εἰς Θεὸν ἐλπίδι ... τὸν μαʹ
entries.evidence: μαʹ; Eng 42:1-3, 10: thirst for God, the 'Where is your God?' taunts, 'Hope in God'

entries.situation: Wanting to keep recalling God's kindness to the forefathers in the Exodus and the wilderness: how good He is and how ungrateful people are
entries.greek: ἀναμιμνήσκεσθαι θέλων τὰς εὐεργεσίας τοῦ Θεοῦ ... μγʹ, οζʹ, πηʹ, ρδʹ, ρεʹ, ρϛʹ, ριγʹ
entries.evidence: Greek list agrees in both witnesses; LXX 113 = Eng 114+115

entries.situation: Having fled to God and been saved from the troubles around you, and wanting to thank Him and tell how kind He was to you
entries.greek: καταφυγὼν δὲ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν καὶ διασωθεὶς ... ἔχεις τὸν μεʹ
entries.evidence: μεʹ; Eng 46:1 'God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble'

entries.situation: You have sinned, you are ashamed and turning back, and you are asking for mercy
entries.greek: ἀλλ' ἥμαρτες, καὶ ἐντραπεὶς μεταγινώσκεις καὶ ἐλεηθῆναι ἀξιοῖς ... ἐν τῷ νʹ
entries.evidence: νʹ; Latin 'quinquagesimum'; Eng 51 superscription: Nathan, after Bathsheba

entries.situation: Having been slandered to a wicked ruler and seeing the devil gloat over it; withdraw and pray
entries.greek: διεβλήθης πονηρῷ βασιλεῖ, καὶ ὁρᾷς τὸν διάβολον κατακαυχώμενον ... τὰ ἐν τῷ ναʹ
entries.evidence: ναʹ; Eng 52 superscription: Doeg informing Saul; 52:1 'Why do you boast of evil'

entries.situation: Being hunted and informed on by people who want to hand you over (as the Ziphites and Philistines did to David); do not lose heart
entries.greek: ὡς οἱ Ζιφαῖοι καὶ οἱ ἀλλόφυλοι τὸν Δαβίδ, μὴ ἀκηδιάσῃς ... τὰ ἐν τῷ νγʹ καὶ νεʹ
entries.evidence: TLG νγ, νε; Latin '53 et 55'. Eng 54 superscription: the Ziphites; Eng 56: seized by the Philistines in Gath

entries.situation: The pursuer coming, unknowing, into the very cave where you hide; still do not cower
entries.greek: εἰσέλθῃ εἰς τὸ σπήλαιον ἐν ᾧ καὶ σὺ κρύπτῃ ... τοὺς ἐν τῷ νϛʹ καὶ τοὺς ἐν τῷ ρμαʹ
entries.evidence: νϛʹ, ρμαʹ; Latin '56 et 141'; both Eng superscriptions: 'in the cave'

entries.situation: The one plotting against you has your house watched, yet you get away; give thanks and keep it as a memorial on your soul
entries.greek: φυλαχθῆναι τὴν οἰκίαν κελεύσῃ ὁ ἐπιβουλεύων, καὶ διαφύγῃς ... τὰ ἐν τῷ νηʹ ψαλμῷ
entries.evidence: νηʹ; Eng 59 superscription: Saul sent men to watch David's house

entries.situation: Enemies insult you and people you thought were friends gossip and slander, and you are grieved for a while; praise God and be comforted
entries.greek: φλυαροῦντες διαβάλλωσιν οἱ δοκοῦντες εἶναι φίλοι, καὶ λυπηθῇς ... τὰ ἐν τῷ νδʹ ῥήματα
entries.evidence: νδʹ; Latin '54'; Eng 55:12-14 'it is not an enemy who taunts me... but you, my companion'

entries.situation: Facing hypocrites who put on a show and boast; say this psalm to shame them
entries.greek: πρὸς μὲν ὑποκρινομένους καὶ ἐν προσώπῳ καυχωμένους ... τὸν νζʹ
entries.evidence: νζʹ; Eng 58:1-2 'Do you rulers indeed speak justly?... in your hearts you devise injustice'

entries.situation: People raging at you and out for your life; the fiercer they get, the more you submit to the Lord and take courage
entries.greek: πρὸς δὲ τοὺς ὁρμῶντας ἀγρίως κατὰ σοῦ ... ὑποτάσσου σὺ τῷ Κυρίῳ ... τὰ ἐν τῷ ξαʹ
entries.evidence: ξαʹ; Latin '61'; LXX 61:2 'Shall not my soul be subject (ὑποταγήσεται) to God'

entries.situation: Driven into a lonely wilderness by persecution; you are not alone there, so seek God at daybreak
entries.greek: διωκόμενος εἰς ἐρημίαν ἀπέλθῃς, μὴ φοβηθῇς ὡς μόνος ὤν ... ὀρθρίζων ψάλλε τὸν ξβʹ
entries.evidence: ξβʹ; Latin '62'; Eng 63 superscription: in the Wilderness of Judah; LXX 62:1 'I rise early to You'

entries.situation: Enemies who keep terrifying you, lying in wait and searching out everything against you, however many; do not give in, their blows are children's arrows
entries.greek: ἐκφοβούντων δὲ τῶν ἐχθρῶν ... βέλη γὰρ νηπίων ἔσονται ... τὸν ξγʹ, καὶ τὸν ξδʹ, καὶ ξθʹ, καὶ οʹ
entries.evidence: Greek list agrees in both witnesses; Latin '63, 64, 69, 70'; LXX 63:8 'the arrows of infants became their wounds' (Eng 64:7)

entries.situation: Wanting to sing a hymn to the Lord
entries.greek: ὅταν μὲν ὑμνῆσαι βούλῃ τὸν Κύριον, ᾆδε τὰ ἐν τῷ ξδʹ

entries.settledBy: Same psalm and verses in both readers, but different framing. A: soul (being a stranger, brought low). B: teaching (whoever cares for sufferers). In the Greek (marc-greek2.txt lines 598-605) the instruction is addressed to whoever cares for sufferers, and the psalm is cited as the psalmist's own proof. So I call it teaching, with the psalmist's affliction kept in the paraphrase

verdicts.reason: All three witnesses I checked read LXX 11 and 16. The TLG copy (marc-greek2.txt, line 00222) has ιαʹ and ιςʹ. The Migne Greek (pg27.txt, line 1350) has 'τα’ ... ις’', where τα is an OCR error for ια. The Migne Latin OCR gives 'undecimum vero et decimum sextum', read under the garbling. LXX 11 is English 12, and LXX 16 is English 17 ('A prayer of David'). The one point against it: English 11 ('In the LORD I take refuge', LXX 10) would fit 'trust' better. But no witness reads ιʹ, and in §16 Athanasius himself gives LXX 10 for trust and LXX 11 for 'no holy thing remains' (English 12). So the Greek stands. The copy's '11 and 12' matches no Greek reading.

νʹ appears in the TLG copy (00225) and in the Migne Greek. The Migne Latin OCR reads quinquagesimum. In both, the numeral comes after τὸν τρίτον and the 11th and 16th, and it goes with 'his own words of repentance'. The conscience clause in 00220 names no psalm, so the Greek order is right and the C.S.M.V. moved the number. LXX 50 is English 51, and the English 51 superscription (Nathan, after Bathsheba) fits.

The TLG copy (00334) and the Migne Greek (pg27 line 1782) both read ηʹ and πγʹ. The BSB superscriptions of English 8 and 84 both say 'According to Gittith', the Hebrew counterpart of the LXX title 'for the winepresses'. The only other Gittith psalm, English 81, is not the one named. Athanasius also uses πγʹ in §23 for longing for God's house, which is English 84:1 ('How lovely is Your dwelling place'), so he numbers it consistently. The copy's '19' is not supported.

ιβʹ appears in the TLG copy (00338) and the Migne Greek (pg27 line 1824). The Migne Latin OCR reads decimum secundum. It comes right after ιαʹ (English 12, 'no holy thing remains'), which the copy itself converts correctly to Psalm 12. English 13:1 is 'How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?', an exact match for ὡς ἐπιλησθείς. The copy's 27 is wrong.

The Migne Greek (pg27 lines 1832-1835) reads ις, πε, πζ, ρμ. The Migne Latin OCR clearly reads '16, 85, 87 et 140'. Only the TLG copy (00341) reads πςʹ. There is also internal evidence against πς here: in §23 (TLG 00422, Migne line 2296) Athanasius gives πςʹ (LXX 86, English 87, the Zion psalm) for the Church against the schisms, which fits it. So LXX 86 already has its own use, and a Zion hymn does not fit a prayer against oppressors. English 88 ('day and night I cry out before You') does fit. ρμʹ is LXX 140, which is English 141 ('let my prayer be set before You'), so the copy's 140 is off by one.

The Migne Greek (line 1839) reads 'ιζ’ ψαλμόν', and the Migne Latin OCR reads decimum septimum. The TLG copy (00347) reads ιςʹ, most likely a slip, since ις was named just before. The BSB superscription of English 18 (LXX 17) describes the day the LORD delivered David from all his enemies and from Saul, which matches the Greek clause exactly.

The TLG copy (00405) and the Migne Greek (line 2178) agree. The Migne OCR has '[α'' for ϙα and 'οζ'' for ρζ, and the TLG prints koppa as ς ('ςαʹ'), just as its 'πʹ καὶ ςδʹ' gives LXX 80 and 94, which the copy renders as 81 and 95. The §15 classification of psalms 'in exomologesis' gives the same eleven numerals in the Migne Greek (line 1578), and its Latin reads '9, 74, 91, 104, 105, 106, 107, 110, 117, 135, 137'. That is an independent check. The copy's extra 71 and 126 appear in no witness. One small correction to the evidence line: in the BSB, English 92 and 108 say 'praise', not 'give thanks', though the LXX uses ἐξομολογ- in both. English 9 is where LXX 9's thanks opening sits, and English 10 is its second half.

The TLG copy (00421) and the Migne Greek (pg27 lines 2290-2292) both read πδʹ and ρκεʹ, which are LXX 84 and 125, English 85 and 126. In the BSB, English 85:1 is 'You restored Jacob from captivity' and English 126:1 is 'When the LORD restored the captives of Zion', which matches the Greek's 'captivity loosed'. The copy's 116 has no support.

Greek copy (greek/marc-greek2.txt, sentences 428-429) reads 'Ψάλαι θέλεις τῷ Σαββάτῳ; ἔχεις τὸν ςαʹ', where the lone ς before a units letter stands for koppa. That makes it 91, and this is consistent within the passage: ςβʹ is used for the Friday psalm (LXX 92) and ςγʹ for the Wednesday psalm (LXX 93). The number also fits the LXX title of Ps 91 (for the Sabbath day). LXX 91 = Eng 92, and the BSB superscription of Eng 92 is 'A Psalm. A song for the Sabbath day.' The English copy does drop this pairing: it goes from the fearless-soul psalm (91) straight to the Lord's Day (24).

The Greek (sentences 434-435) reads 'λέγε τὰ ἐν τῷ μζʹ' = LXX 47, and the LXX title of Ps 47 names the second day of the week. LXX 47 = Eng 48. The copy's '95' fits neither the Greek nor the LXX titles. The copy's neighbouring day psalms (24, 93, 94) are correct English conversions, so 95 is an isolated error.

The Greek (sentences 464-465) lists ρδʹ, ρςʹ, ρλδʹ, ρμεʹ, ρμςʹ, ρμζʹ, ρμηʹ, ρνʹ = LXX 104, 106, 134, 145, 146, 147, 148, 150. Converted: Eng 105, 107, 135, 146, 147 (LXX 146 and 147 together make Eng 147), 148, 150. The copy's 113, 117 and 149 have no Greek basis. Ps 149 does appear later, but in the separate Alleluia list.

The Greek (sentences 472-474) reads 'τὰς ιεʹ τῶν ἀναβαθμῶν ᾠδάς' (the fifteen Songs of Ascents, with no numbers given). In the BSB, the superscription 'A song of ascents' appears on exactly Eng 120 through 134, fifteen psalms. The copy's '119-133' is the LXX range left unconverted.

The Greek (sentences 481-482) reads 'ψάλλε τὸν εʹ καὶ ρμβʹ' = LXX 5 and 142 = Eng 5 and 143. Both English psalms open as pleas: 5:1 'Give ear to my words, O LORD' and 143:1 'O LORD, hear my prayer'. The copy's 141, 142 and 146 are not in the Greek.

The Greek (sentence 485) ends 'λέγε τὰ τοῦ Δαβὶδ ῥήματα, ἅπερ καὶ αὐτὸς εἶπεν ἐν τῷ ρμδʹ ψαλμῷ' = LXX 144 = Eng 145. The fit is exact: the Greek verb εὐλογεῖν (to bless) matches Eng 145:1 'I will bless Your name', and 145:9 reads 'The LORD is good to all'. The superscription 'Of David' also matches 'David's words'. The copy's 105 is wrong.

The printed Greek (sentences 486-487, in both the TLG/DCO copy and marc-greek2) reads 'τὸν ςβʹ καὶ ςζʹ' = LXX 92 and 97 = Eng 93 and 98. The passage uses ς for koppa consistently, with ςβʹ as LXX 92 for Friday, so the reading is secure as printed. Nothing I found refutes it. I lowered confidence to medium for two reasons. First, the TLG, Migne Greek, Migne Latin and most likely EPE all descend from one edition (Montfaucon/Migne), so they are not four independent witnesses. Second, the content favours LXX 95: the question's verb ᾆσαι echoes 'ᾌσατε τῷ κυρίῳ ᾆσμα καινόν', which opens LXX 95 and 97, whereas LXX 92 (Eng 93) opens 'The LORD reigns'. Against emending to LXX 95: the same passage has already assigned it to the rebuilt house (ςεʹ, sentence 444). Keep Eng 93 and 98 as the text reads, and note the C.S.M.V.'s 96.

The Greek (sentence 494) lists ρδʹ, ρεʹ, ρςʹ, ριαʹ through ριηʹ, ρλδʹ, ρλεʹ, ρμεʹ through ρνʹ = LXX 104-106, 111-118, 134, 135, 145-150. Converted: 104-106 become Eng 105-107; 111-118 become Eng 112-119 (LXX 113 is Eng 114-115, and LXX 114-115 are Eng 116); 134-135 become Eng 135-136; 145-150 become Eng 146-150. The copy prints 111-118 unconverted.

Both Greek copies have βʹ and ρηʹ: marc-greek2.txt [00504], and the Migne scan pg27.txt line 2512 (β' ... ρη'). The passage sits under the Migne marker κς' (line 2505), so it is §26. LXX 2 is English 2 and LXX 108 is English 109. The C.S.M.V.'s '3' is a conversion error. It added one to a number where LXX and English numbering agree. The content fits too. English Psalm 2:1-2 has rulers plotting against the LORD and His Anointed, which Acts 4:25-27 applies to the Passion. English Psalm 3 is David fleeing his enemies, which does not fit this line. English Psalm 109:8 ('may another take his position') is the verse Acts 1:20 applies to Judas.

No numeral is printed. The Greek quote at marc-greek2.txt [00546] ('Ἵνα τί περίλυπος εἶ, ἡ ψυχή μου, καὶ ἵνα τί συνταράσσεις με;') is the LXX refrain of 41:6, 41:12 and 42:5. The BSB has the same refrain at English 42:5, 42:11 and 43:5. The section is confirmed in Migne pg27.txt: the marker κη' is at line 2706 before the passage and κθ' at line 2742 after it, so §28. The English copy's 'Why then art thou so heavy, O my soul' is the same verse.

The quote at marc-greek2.txt [00548] ('Ἐμοῦ δὲ παρὰ μικρὸν ἐσαλεύθησαν οἱ πόδες') is word for word LXX 72:2. Migne's commentary on that psalm has the same wording (pg27.txt line 75766). BSB 73:2 reads 'my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped'. LXX 93:18 ('my foot slipped') is worded differently, so it is not a rival. The passage falls between the Migne markers κη' and κθ', so §28.

The quote at marc-greek2.txt [00550] ('Κύριος ἐμοὶ βοηθὸς, καὶ οὐ φοβηθήσομαι τί ποιήσει μοι ἄνθρωπος') matches LXX 117:6, which is English 118:6. The added 'καὶ' matches its quotation in Hebrews 13:6 exactly. That does not change the source psalm. English 56:4 and 56:11 lack 'helper', so they are not a match. The passage is between κη' and κθ' in Migne, so §28.

Migne pg27.txt line 3164 reads 'ἔλεγεν ἐν τῷ ριη' Ψαλμῷ'. LXX 118 is English 119, so the C.S.M.V.'s 119 is correct here. The three quoted lines are LXX 118:16, 118:54 and 118:92. They match BSB 119:16 ('I will not forget Your word'), 119:54 ('songs to me in the house of my pilgrimage') and 119:92 ('I would have perished in my affliction'). The passage comes after the Migne marker λγ' (line 3102), so §33. Framing: the Greek addresses whoever cares for people who suffer ('εἴ τις κήδεται τῶν πασχόντων, ταῦτα λεγέτω'), so 'teaching' is right. One nuance for the wording: the following line has a plural participle (λέγοντες, 'they gained salvation, saying'). So the verse 92 line is put in the mouth of the saints generally, not only the psalmist.

needs.need: Anxiety, worry, stress, feeling overwhelmed
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete, US, queried 2026-09-23: 'psalm for anxiety' is 4th under 'psalm for ' and 3rd under 'psalms for '. The top completion under 'psalm when ' is 'psalm when feeling overwhelmed'. 'psalm to read when anxious' and 'psalm to read when worried' both appear, and 'psalm for stress', 'psalm for worry', 'psalm for overthinking' and 'psalm for panic attack' each have their own completions. Bing suggest lists 'psalm for anxiety' and 'psalms to read when anxious'. YouVersion's 2025 Verse of the Year release says 'the most searched terms included love, anxiety, and peace'. Crosswalk, The Navigators, Kevin Halloran and PrayerVest all publish 'psalms for anxiety' pages.
needs.athanasiusSituation: No pairing for anxiety as such. The closest are: when someone tries to frighten you (Ps 11, §16); strengthening yourself and others in how fearless a soul that hopes in God is (Ps 91, §22); and being downcast from the weakness of your nature and the strain of life (Ps 102, §24).
needs.note: Ps 102 ('strain of life') is the honest landing for 'overwhelmed and worn down'. Diffuse worry about the future has no pairing, so do not present Ps 11 or 91 as Athanasius's psalm 'for anxiety'.

needs.need: Fear of a person or a threatening situation
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm when i am afraid', 'psalm for when you are afraid', 'psalm for fear', 'psalm for fear and anxiety', 'psalm for overcoming fear', 'psalm for courage'. American Bible Society publishes '5 Psalms For When You Fear the Future'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Someone wants to alarm you (Ps 11, §16). Foes press harder and scorn you, and you are told to be unafraid (Ps 27, §17). The fear of foes and their plots follows you everywhere (Pss 64, 65, 70, 71, §20). The soul that hopes in God is fearless (Ps 91, §22).
needs.note: This honestly covers fear that has a human source. It does not cover fear of illness, death or the future. 'Fear of death' is a separate search ('psalm for fear of death') with no pairing in the letter.

needs.need: Feeling low, heavy-hearted, worn down (including searches for 'depression')
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for depression' has a full ten completions ('depression and anxiety', 'best psalm for depression', 'deep depression'...). Also 'psalm when sad', 'psalm for sadness', 'psalm for despair', 'psalm for hopelessness', 'psalm for when you feel hopeless', 'psalm when depressed'. American Bible Society publishes '6 Psalms for When You've Lost Hope in Life' and '7 Psalms for When You're Having a Bad Day'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Downcast and poor through the weakness of your nature and the strain of life, followed by Pss 103 and 104 to lift the heart (Ps 102, §24). The singing section also cites the refrain 'why art thou so heavy, O my soul' (Pss 42/43) as the words through which sadness is lightened (§29).
needs.note: This covers low mood and discouragement. Clinical depression is not in the letter, so the page must not imply a psalm treats it. Modern lists often send people to Ps 88 for depression, but Athanasius puts 88 among the prayers against enemies (§17). Do not reuse it here.

needs.need: Exhaustion, tiredness, burnout
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for when you're tired' (in the top ten under 'psalm for when'), 'psalm for tiredness', 'psalm for weakness', 'psalm for weariness', 'psalm for exhaustion'. 'psalm for burnout' returns only a thin list.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Downcast and poor through the weakness of your nature and the strain of life (Ps 102, §24). The BSB superscription of Ps 102 also names one who 'grows faint'.
needs.note: One of the best fits between modern search and the letter. Ps 102's own superscription is Scripture and can be quoted.

needs.need: Loneliness, feeling alone
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for loneliness', 'best psalm for loneliness', 'is there a psalm for loneliness', 'psalm for when you feel alone'. Bing suggest: 'psalms for when you feel alone'. Crosswalk, Billy Graham Evangelistic Association, The Daily Grace Co. and PrayerVest publish pages on it.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Persecution drives you into the desert, and you are not to fear as though you were alone, since God is with you, singing at daybreak (Ps 63, §20). Hated by friends and kin for your faith, go apart and look to the future (Ps 31, §18).
needs.note: Both are aloneness caused by being driven out or rejected, not ordinary loneliness. Ps 63 is honest only when a question shows the person has been pushed away or is in an empty stretch. Do not use it for plain loneliness.

needs.need: Grief, the death of someone you love
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for grief' (ten completions), 'psalm for when someone dies', 'psalm for loss of loved one', 'loss of a child', 'loss of mother', 'loss of father', 'psalms for funerals', 'psalm for comfort after death', 'psalm for someone grieving'. Bing lists 'psalm for funeral'. Bible Study Tools, iBelieve, Anglican Compass, CatholicMom and eCondolence publish grief-psalm pages.
needs.note: The letter never pairs a psalm with bereavement. The closing 'sad for any reason' (§30) is a summary, not a pairing, and does not honestly cover a death. This is the biggest gap between search demand and the letter.

needs.need: Betrayed by a friend or someone close
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for betrayal', 'psalm prayer for betrayal', 'psalm for feeling betrayed', 'psalm betrayed by a friend'. American Bible Society publishes '4 Psalms for when you feel betrayed', plus several church and devotional pages on Ps 55.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Not only enemies but those you thought were your friends reproach you, slander you and hurt you badly for a time (Ps 55, §20).
needs.note: A clean, strong pairing. The BSB heads Ps 41 'Victory over Betrayal', but Athanasius pairs 41 with showing pity to the poor (§19), so never use 41 for betrayal. Iscariot's betrayal (Pss 3, 109, §26) is prophecy about Christ, not a personal pairing.

needs.need: Family conflict, your own family against you
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for family problems', 'psalm for family healing', 'psalm for family unity', 'psalm for troubled marriage', 'psalm for troubled child', 'psalm for broken marriage', 'psalm for marriage restoration', 'psalm for reconciliation'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Persecuted by your own family and opposed by many (Ps 3, §15; the BSB superscription says David fled from his son Absalom). Hated and persecuted by all your friends and kin because of your faith in Christ (Ps 31, §18).
needs.note: This covers a family turned against you. It does NOT cover marriage trouble, a wayward child you are worried about, or wanting reconciliation. Those searches are about repair, and the letter has no pairing for them.

needs.need: Feeling far from God, God silent, unanswered prayer, 'how long?'
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for feeling far from god', 'psalm for feeling distant from god', 'psalms when god is silent', 'psalm for unanswered prayers', 'psalm how long o lord', 'psalm how long must i wait'. Crosswalk ('7 Scriptures for When God Feels Far Away'), Open the Bible and Desiring God publish on it.
needs.athanasiusSituation: When trouble drags on, do not lose heart as though God had forgotten you (§16; the online copy says Ps 27, but this is almost certainly LXX 12 = English Ps 13, 'How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?'). Also: feeling under the cloud of God's displeasure (Pss 6 and 38, §15).
needs.note: A strong pairing, but the number must be fixed to English 13 before anything is published. 'Under His displeasure' is a separate and recognisable state: the sense that God is disciplining you.

needs.need: Guilt, shame, needing forgiveness, repentance
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for forgiveness' (9th under 'psalm for '; its own ten completions include 'forgiveness of sin', 'forgiveness and mercy'), 'psalm for guilt and shame', 'psalm for feeling guilty', 'psalm for repentance' (ten completions). Bible Gateway's historical top keyword list includes 'forgiveness'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: You have sinned, are ashamed, and are repenting and asking forgiveness (Ps 51, §20). Also feeling under God's displeasure (Pss 6, 38, §15), and the letter's statement that the Psalms teach how to repent and in what words (§10).
needs.note: The letter's clearest and most emphatic pairing. It fits the quiz premise well because guilt can be drawn out with everyday questions without naming sin.

needs.need: Temptation, a habit you cannot break, addiction, lust
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for temptation', 'psalm for resisting temptation', 'psalm for addiction', 'psalm for addiction recovery', 'psalm for lust', 'psalm for overcoming lust'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: The enemy gets hold of you again and you want to be free (Ps 140, §25). Giving thanks once a test is safely past (Ps 139, §25). Realising you were led astray by other people's arguments, then stopping and weeping (Ps 137, §25).
needs.note: Ps 139 honestly covers 'I came through a temptation'. Ps 140's 'enemy' is ambiguous in the letter, so presenting it as an addiction psalm would be a stretch.

needs.need: Waiting, patience, something taking too long
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for waiting on the lord', 'psalms for waiting on god', 'psalm how long must i wait', 'psalm for patience' (with 'strength and patience'), 'psalm about waiting for love', 'psalm for endurance'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: You endure afflictions and want to learn the value of endurance (Ps 40, §19). Trouble long drawn out, as though forgotten (English Ps 13, §16).
needs.note: This covers waiting under hardship. Waiting for a spouse or a job ('waiting for love') is not in the letter.

needs.need: Anger, frustration, resentment, holding onto hurt
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for anger', 'psalm for anger and frustration', 'psalms for anger and resentment', 'psalm anger at god', 'psalm to read when angry', 'psalm for when you are angry'. Bing: 'psalms for when you are angry'. American Bible Society publishes '5 Psalms for When You're Holding Onto Hurt'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: When enemies keep on, give up human judgement and ask God alone to judge rightly (Pss 26, 35, 43, §17). As hostility grows fiercer, answer it with obedience and submission to God (Ps 62, §20). The letter quotes Ps 37's 'leave off from wrath' as an example of the Psalter laying down law (§9).
needs.note: Pss 26/35/43 honestly fit resentment toward someone who wronged you (entrust judgement to God). There is nothing for anger at God, or for a short temper in general.

needs.need: Injustice; the wicked prospering; envy of people who seem to have it easy
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm about the wicked prospering', 'psalm envy the wicked', 'psalm how long will the wicked prosper', 'psalm for jealousy and envy', 'psalm for injustice' (a thin list). Franciscan Media (Ps 73) and several devotional pages publish on it.
needs.athanasiusSituation: You see wicked people prospering and good people in trouble; do not be offended or shaken (Ps 73, §21). You see the wicked attacking the weak and want to warn their victims not to envy them, since they will soon come to nothing (Ps 37, §18). Pride everywhere, as if nothing holy is left (Ps 12, §16).
needs.note: A close, honest match. The search wording ('envy the wicked') is almost the letter's own situation.

needs.need: Slandered, falsely accused, gossiped about
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for false accusations', 'psalm against false accusations', 'psalm for court case', 'psalm for court'. 'psalm for slander' has a thin list. Ray Stedman, GotQuestions, Bible Hub and BibleTruths publish on it.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Slandered to a powerful person, while the slanderer boasts of it (Ps 52, §20). Persecuted and slandered as David was by the Ziphites (Pss 54, 56, §20). Friends slander you (Ps 55, §20). Someone plots against you and you are told of it (Ps 7, §15). Let human judgement go and ask God to judge (Pss 26, 35, 43, §17).
needs.note: Rich and honest. Ps 52 (the boasting slanderer, before someone with power over you) maps directly onto a workplace or a court.

needs.need: Enemies; people against you; hostility at work; being bullied
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for enemies' (ten completions including 'enemies at work'), 'psalm for protection from enemies', 'psalm when people are against you', 'psalm for bad neighbors', 'psalm for bullying' (thin). A 2022 blog list of search figures (source tool unnamed) gives Ps 35 at 135,000 monthly searches.
needs.athanasiusSituation: This is the letter's largest theme: family and many against you (Ps 3); the wicked trying to trap you (Ps 5); surrounded by enemies (Ps 25); enemies closing in (Pss 17, 86, 88, 140); a host that scorns you (Ps 27); being hunted (Pss 57, 59, 142); fear of their plots (Ps 64). §§15-20.
needs.note: Some searches want enemies harmed ('psalm for enemies to die'). Athanasius's steer is to hand judgement to God and answer rage with obedience (Pss 26/35/43, 62). Results should carry that, not curse-use.

needs.need: Protection (general, family, travel, night, 'spiritual warfare')
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for protection' is 3rd under 'psalm for ' and 1st under 'psalms for '; 'which psalm is for protection' and 'what psalm is for protection' both appear, alongside 'psalm for travel protection', 'psalm for family protection' and 'psalm for spiritual warfare' (ten completions). Bible Gateway said Ps 91 'continued its ascent' in 2025 (Christianity.com and Religion Unplugged reports). A 2022 blog figure (tool unnamed) gives Ps 91 at 1,220,000 monthly searches.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Strengthening yourself and others in the fear of God, showing how fearless the soul that hopes in Him is (Ps 91, §22). In the closing (§§31-32): whoever says the Psalms when tempted or persecuted will know the Lord's protection, and the devil and demons are put to flight by Scripture.
needs.note: Protection from hostile people is fully covered (see enemies). Travel, night, a family's safety and general safety have no pairing. Ps 91 is paired with courage in God, not a protective charm.

needs.need: A hard diagnosis, sickness, surgery, praying for healing
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for healing' is 2nd under 'psalm for ', with 'psalm for health and healing', 'psalm to read when sick', 'psalm for cancer diagnosis', 'psalm for surgery' (ten completions incl. 'before surgery'), 'psalm for a sick loved one', 'psalm for someone in hospital'. Bible Gateway's historical top keywords include 'healing'. A 2022 blog figure (tool unnamed) gives 'prayer for healing' 450,000/month.
needs.note: The letter pairs no psalm with illness, even though Marcellinus was recovering from an illness when he wrote (§1). Ps 102's 'weakness of your nature' is not sickness. Ps 6 is paired with God's displeasure, not illness. Ps 107's 'He sent His word and healed them' is read as prophecy of Christ (§6). Do not stretch any of these.

needs.need: Gratitude, thanksgiving, relief that something is over
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for gratitude' (ten completions), 'psalm for thanksgiving' (ten), 'psalm of gratitude for a new day', 'psalm for a good day', 'psalm for blessings'. Bing lists 'psalm for thanksgiving'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Thanks when your affliction ends (Pss 4, 75, 116, §15). After deliverance, fleeing to God to tell of His mercy to you (Ps 46, §19). Delivered from enemies (Ps 18, §17). Thanks once a test is safely past (Ps 139, §25). Thanks when the danger lifts and you are free again (Pss 85, 116, §22).
needs.note: Rich. The letter's thanksgiving is nearly always thanks AFTER something specific, which makes a strong 'it's finally over' result.

needs.need: Joy, wanting to praise
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for joy', 'psalm for joy and happiness', 'psalm joy comes in the morning', 'psalm shout for joy'. Bible Gateway's historical top keywords include 'joy'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Fed and guided by the Lord, seeing it and rejoicing (Ps 23, §17). Wanting to sing praise (Ps 65, §21; Pss 96, 98, §25). The Alleluia and praise psalms (Pss 105-107, 111-118, 146-150, §§24-25).
needs.note: Ps 23 as 'you see how you are provided for, and it makes you glad' is an honest and very searchable result.

needs.need: A new start, moving forward, a new home
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for new beginnings' (with 'best psalms for new beginnings'), 'psalm for new home', 'psalm for a new month', 'psalm for new job', 'psalm for new school year', 'psalm for renewal', 'psalm for restoration'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Pressing forward, forgetting what lies behind: the fifteen Gradual Psalms, one for each step (English Pss 120-134; the online copy's '119-133' are LXX numbers, §24). Dedicating your home, read as the soul (Pss 30, 127, §17).
needs.note: The Gradual Psalms honestly cover 'I am starting over and moving on'. The house pairing is allegorised to the soul, so it serves a new home only loosely. It is fifteen psalms, not one, so a single result would need a choice made and explained.

needs.need: Guidance, a decision, feeling lost, uncertainty
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for guidance' (ten completions), 'psalm for wisdom' (ten), 'psalm for clarity', 'psalm for discernment', 'psalm for uncertainty', 'psalm for god's direction'. American Bible Society publishes '4 Psalms For When You Feel Lost in Life'.
needs.note: No pairing for seeking direction. 'Led astray by others' arguments' (Ps 137) is about realising you were deceived, not about deciding, so do not use it for this.

needs.need: Peace of mind, calm, sleep, sleepless nights, nightmares
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for peace' (8th under 'psalm for '), 'psalm for peace of mind' (ten completions), 'psalm for sleep' (ten, incl. 'sleepless nights'), 'psalm for insomnia', 'psalm for nightmares', 'psalms for bedtime', 'psalm for calm'. Bing lists 'psalm for sleep' and 'psalm for peace'. YouVersion's 2025 top searches include 'peace'.
needs.note: No sleep pairing. Inner peace appears only in the letter's teaching that singing the Psalms brings a troubled mind into harmony, as David calmed Saul (§§27-29). That is a claim about the practice, not a pairing. Ps 97 is about public peace after war (§23).

needs.need: Strength and courage to face something bigger than you
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for strength' (6th under 'psalm for ', ten completions incl. 'strength during difficult times'), 'psalm for courage', 'psalm for encouragement', 'psalm for endurance'. A 2022 blog figure (tool unnamed): 'prayer for strength' 135,000/month.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Some Goliath has risen up against you and your people: fear not, trust God as David did (Ps 144, §25). Ignore your own weakness and their boldness and keep crying out to God (Ps 28, §17).
needs.note: 'A Goliath in front of you' is a vivid, honest result for facing an overwhelming challenge. The letter's Goliath is a human opponent, so it fits a person or problem that has to be faced, not general low energy.

needs.need: Everything going wrong, distress, needing help now
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for when everything is going wrong', 'psalm for troubled times', 'psalm to read when in distress', 'psalm for help in trouble', 'psalm for immediate help', 'psalm for urgent help', 'psalm for a troubled soul'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Singing while bearing your own afflictions in mind (Ps 3, §12). Your place of refuge is taken and you are hard pressed: pray, and give thanks when heard (Ps 77, §21). Enduring affliction (Ps 40, §19). The closing: help in trouble and temptation (§30).
needs.note: Ps 77's 'the place you ran to for safety is gone' is especially recognisable.

needs.need: Someone you love is going through something (praying for another person)
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete, 'psalm for someone ...': 'in jail', 'who is dying', 'who is sick', 'in hospital', 'having surgery', 'grieving', 'struggling', 'who lost a loved one'. Also 'psalm for my daughter' and 'psalm for our children'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Words to comfort and pray with others in distress (Ps 20, §17). Suffering with those who suffer and pleading for them (Ps 79, §21, a context of persecution). The closing: whoever cares for those who suffer should use these words (§33).
needs.note: Ps 20 ('May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble') honestly covers praying for someone else. It would make a good 'you are carrying someone else' result. It does not make any promise about healing.

needs.need: Longing for God, spiritual dryness, wanting to be closer to Him
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm longing for god', 'psalm 42 longing for god', 'psalm 63 longing for god', 'psalms to get closer to god'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Burning with longing for God while enemies mock you, comforted by hope (Ps 42, §19). Longing for God's house (Ps 84, §22). In the wilderness at daybreak (Ps 63, §20).
needs.note: Ps 42 in the letter comes with mockers ('where is your God?'). The quiz can draw out both the longing and the pressure from people around the person.

needs.need: Heartbreak, a breakup
needs.evidence: Google autocomplete: 'psalm for a broken heart', 'psalm for broken heart', 'psalm for heartbreak', 'psalm for breakup', 'psalm for broken relationship', 'psalm for the brokenhearted'.
needs.athanasiusSituation: Only when the breakup was a betrayal: those you thought your friends turn on you and hurt you (Ps 55, §20).
needs.note: Romantic loss as such has no pairing. Offer Ps 55 only if the person's answers show betrayal, not ordinary sadness at an ending.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: The people who should be on your side have turned on you, and others are joining in (Ps 3, §15: persecuted by your own family and opposed by many; the BSB superscription says David fled from his son Absalom).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: Few people would type 'psalm for my family turning on me', but it is common and painful. A disguised question can surface it (for example: 'the last time you felt outnumbered, who was on the other side?').

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: Everyone around you turned cold because of what you believe, so you went quiet and kept to yourself (Ps 31, §18: hated by friends and kin for your faith; go apart and look ahead).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: This names a quiet social cost many believers carry without calling it persecution.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: Someone is boasting about damaging your name to a person who has power over you (Ps 52, §20; the BSB superscription names Doeg reporting to Saul).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: The details (a boss or authority, and the slanderer pleased with himself) are specific enough to feel eerily exact.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: You have just been told someone is scheming against you (Ps 7, §15: a plot like Ahithophel's, reported to you).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: The moment of finding out is distinct from ongoing conflict, and the letter gives it its own psalm.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: You got out of trouble by refusing to go along with bad advice (Ps 34, §18: escaping enemies by wisely refusing their counsel, then gathering others to give thanks).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: It turns relief at having said no into gratitude, a positive state searches never ask for.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: It has dragged on so long that you feel God has forgotten you (English Ps 13, §16, printed as '27' in the online copy).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: People feel this but search for it only vaguely ('God is silent'). The letter's wording, 'do not lose heart as though forgotten', names it exactly.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: You feel you are under God's displeasure, as if He is correcting you (Pss 6 and 38, §15).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: This is different from guilt over one act. It is a mood of being disciplined that people rarely put into words.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: It seems no decent people are left and pride has won everywhere (Ps 12, §16).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: This fits the modern feeling of being fed up with the world and news-weary, which people would never search as a 'psalm'.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: People around you mock the idea that God is in charge, and part of you is tempted to join them (Pss 14 and 53, §16).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: The pull to agree with cynics is a jolt of self-recognition. The letter says intercede instead of joining in.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: You were talked into something by clever arguments and have just realised it (Ps 137, §25: stop, sit down and weep).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: This is the moment a person sees they were deceived, a common experience no one searches for.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: You came through a real temptation without falling (Ps 139, §25: thanking God once the test is safely past).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: It gives a thankful result to someone who resisted, a state no search list covers.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: The place you ran to for safety is gone (Ps 77, §21: the enemy takes your refuge; pray, and give thanks when heard).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: This names the loss of a safe place (a home, a church, a friendship) in words people would not think to search.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: Someone keeps watch on you, and you just managed to slip away (Ps 59, §20: a watch set on your house, and you escaped; keep it as a memorial).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: This covers being monitored or controlled and getting out. It resonates strongly with anyone who has left a controlling situation. Handle with care.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: You are cornered, and the danger is in the room with you, unaware (Pss 57 and 142, §20: the pursuer enters the very cave where you hide).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: A vivid picture of hiding in plain sight from someone who holds power over you.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: Someone's hostility keeps growing, and you choose to answer it with stillness and trust instead of fighting (Ps 62, §20).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: This names a posture rather than a feeling: choosing not to retaliate, which people may recognise as what they are trying to do.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: You have been given responsibility over others and feel too small for it (Ps 151, §25).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: A promotion or a new leadership role, with humility. CAUTION: Ps 151 is only in Orthodox Bibles (and in the Septuagint as a supernumerary psalm). It is not in the BSB file or Protestant Bibles and cannot be printed from the BSB.

unaskedButRecognisable.situation: You are longing for God while people around you ask where He is (Ps 42, §19).
unaskedButRecognisable.why: This combines the longing people do search for with a pressure from others they do not name.

modern.caveats:
1. Search volumes: I found no publicly quoted keyword-tool figure for any 'psalm for [need]' phrase. The only numbers I found are the 2022 figures from intimacywithgod.com. They cover psalm numbers and prayer phrases, not needs, and the post does not name the tool that produced them, so treat them as weak. Autocomplete shows a phrase is searched often enough to be suggested, not how often. As a rough relative signal, a stem that returns a full ten completions (anxiety, healing, protection, grief, depression, sleep, forgiveness, strength, guidance, financial) is deeper than one that returns two or three (slander, injustice, persecution, bullying, rejection, burnout). The owner's Bing Keyword Research figures should replace all of this.

2. The central finding: the letter is strongest where search is middling, and silent where search is heaviest. It thoroughly covers hostile people, slander, betrayal, family opposition, guilt, the wicked prospering, long waiting, feeling forgotten, exhaustion, gratitude after trouble, and praying for others. It has NO honest pairing for grief or bereavement, illness, diagnosis or surgery, sleep, guidance or decisions, money, jobs or exams, or marriage and children. It covers anxiety, loneliness, protection, anger and new starts only loosely. The closing summary's 'sad for any reason' (§30) is not a pairing and must not be used to fill these gaps. The quiz's result pages can still target 'psalm for anxiety' honestly only through Ps 102 ('strain of life') or Ps 11 (someone trying to frighten you), and each page should say what situation Athanasius named.

3. Section numbers: the online copy has no section numbers. I assigned §s by the standard 33-section division as best I can reconstruct it (§§14-26 hold the pairing list; §§27-29 cover singing; §30 is 'all human life is covered'). Check every § against Gregg's or the C.S.M.V. print edition before it appears on the site.

4. More numbering errors in the online copy, beyond those already flagged. (a) The weekday list gives 'Monday, the 95th'. The Septuagint heading 'for the second day of the week' belongs to LXX 47 = English Ps 48, so 95 is probably wrong; check before use. (b) The 'as though God had forgotten you' psalm printed as 27 should be English 13, which the BSB opening confirms ('How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?'). (c) The Gradual Psalms are English 120-134. (d) The refrain 'they cried unto the Lord in their trouble' is English 107. Spot-checks against BSB superscriptions and openings confirm the copy otherwise uses English numbering for Pss 3, 5, 6, 12, 25, 27 ('not yet anointed'), 30, 31, 34, 37-42, 52, 54-59, 62-64, 73, 77, 79, 102, 127, 137, 139, 140, 142, 144.

5. Traps of the 'do not stretch' kind. The BSB section heading for Ps 41 is 'Victory over Betrayal', but Athanasius pairs 41 with mercy to the poor. Ps 88 is widely used today for depression, but the letter lists it among prayers against enemies. Ps 6 contains 'heal me', but the letter pairs it with God's displeasure. Ps 107:20 'He sent His word and healed them' is read as prophecy of Christ. None of these may be used for the modern need their wording suggests.

6. Ps 151 (authority though weak) is not in the BSB file or Protestant Bibles, so it cannot be printed in full from the site's text source.

7. The autocomplete lists include a cluster of magical, talismanic searches: 'psalm for luck in gambling', 'love spell', 'return to sender', 'uncrossing', 'road opening', 'evil eye', 'enemies to die', 'urgent money'. The quiz should not court these. The letter itself rebukes using sacred words as incantation apart from faith (§§32-33).

8. Several searches are occasion-based rather than feeling-based ('psalm for today', 'morning prayer', 'birthday', 'funeral', 'wedding', 'baptism'). The quiz premise ('which psalm are you living right now') naturally answers 'what psalm should I read today', which appears in autocomplete, and that is a useful angle for the landing page.

9. The Google data is the US locale only. The 'Sounds Like Scripture'-type verification of verbatim text does not apply here: all letter content above is paraphrased, with no more than a few words quoted.

# How "Which Psalm are you living right now?" would fit into the site's code

The short answer is that the engine can't take this quiz as it stands. Every piece of it assumes five-point agree/disagree statements, and every result must be one of two shapes: poles (the Compass, the figure quiz) or a ranking (gifts, sins). This quiz needs multiple-choice questions and a new shape whose result is one of Athanasius's own pairings. The engine was built to allow a third shape; `types.ts` says so in a comment. It is a real piece of work, though, not a new data file.

## 1. How a quiz is defined today

**`site/src/lib/engine/types.ts`**
- A question is `QuizItem { n, text, group, direction: 1 | -1 }`. An answer is `Answer = -2|-1|0|1|2`, and a set of answers is `Sheet = Array<Answer | null>`. Only agree/disagree answers exist.
- `QuizGroup` is either an axis with two poles or a single category.
- `Outcome { name, slug, position?, mask?, who?, note? }`.
- `ResultView = BipolarView | UnipolarView`, told apart by `shape`. Both views carry `quizSlug, code, named[], headline, headlineParts[], summary, ranked[]`.
- `ScoringStrategy { id, shape, score(quiz, sheet) → number[], result(quiz, values) → ResultView, encode, decode, shareText }`.
- `Quiz` has `slug, title, tagline, description, intro?, icon, minutes, status, items, groups, outcomes, strategy, config, shareTitle, codePrefix?`, plus optional words and notes: `outcomeNoun*`, `outcomePathBase`, `hideOutcomeScore`, `groupNoun*`, `notes: QuizNotes`, `groupNote`, `unipolarCopy`, `uniformSheet`.
- Helpers: `notesFor`, `resultNotes`, `groupNoteFor`, `isUniformSheet`, `outcomePathBase`, `rankWord`.

**`site/src/lib/engine/registry.ts`**
- `QUIZZES = [theologyCompass, sevenDeadlySins, bibleFigure, spiritualGifts]`. Adding a quiz means one import and one entry in this list.
- Wrappers: `scoreQuiz`, `resultFor`, `encodeFor`, `decodeFor`, `shareTextFor`. URLs are re-exported from `urls.ts` and `compare.ts`.
- Checks that run when the file loads:
  - `validate()` requires every group to have questions keyed both ways, and checks `config.radix === itemsPerGroup*4+1`. **A multiple-choice quiz fails this at load time.**
  - `validateOutcomeSlugs()` stops two quizzes sharing a page address.
  - `validateCodePrefixes()` requires unique prefixes, and only the Compass may go without one.
  - `validateOutcomePositions()` and `validateOutcomeMasks()` apply to pole quizzes only.

**`site/src/lib/engine/codec.ts`**
- `makeCodec(radix, slots, prefix)` stores one 0..100 value per group, with a body of at least 6 base-36 characters. It switches to `makeWideCodec` (BigInt) when the numbers get too large.
- A value is stored as `round(v*steps/100)`. That loses information once there are more than 101 steps, so **it cannot safely hold an item number above about 100.** It is also clumsy for a single number.

**`site/src/lib/engine/urls.ts`**
- `quizHref` → `/q/<slug>/`, `groupHref` → `/axis/…`, `resultHref` → `/r/<slug>/<code>/`, and `outcomeHref` → `/${outcomePathBase}/<slug>/`.

**`site/src/lib/engine/compare.ts`**
- `compare()` handles the pole shape and otherwise **assumes** a ranking (`va as UnipolarView`). `parseCodes`, `compareHref` and `inviteHref` (`/q/<slug>/?with=<code>`) serve the two-person page.

**The strategies**
- `strategies/bipolar.ts` (`bipolar`): each axis gets a 0..100 score. Results are named by nearest distance, using `nearest()` and `nearestState()` with the states near/tie/loose/central, plus bands and `lean()`.
- `strategies/category.ts` (`category`): each category gets a 0..100 score and they are ranked. It has `pull()`, `tieMargin()` (via `config.tieSteps`), `namingFloor()`, up to four level categories named, and the states clear/tie/flat.

**The quiz files**
- `quizzes/theology-compass.ts` maps `data/compass.json` (no code prefix).
- `quizzes/bible-figure.ts` is a pole quiz. It uses `outcomePathBase: 'figure'`, `hideOutcomeScore`, masks, and its own `FigureOutcome` with `evidence`. Prefix `BF`.
- `quizzes/spiritual-gifts.ts` is a ranking with 19 categories and uses the wide codec. Prefix `SG`.
- `quizzes/seven-deadly-sins.ts` is a ranking. Prefix `S`.

**Important: quiz files end up in the browser.** The quiz runner's script imports the registry (`q/[quiz].astro`), and so does the script on `/me/`. That pulls every quiz file into the page's JavaScript. Psalm text and long explanations must therefore **not** live in the quiz file.

## 2. Does it fit an existing strategy?

No. I compared four designs.

| Design | How it works | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Ranking** (`category`) | Each Athanasius situation is a category, with at least two statements each keyed both ways | Rejected. 30–60 situations would need 60–120 statements. The result page would rank every feeling (`CategoryStack` shows all rows), and ties are settled by the spelling of the names. |
| **B. Poles** (`bipolar`) | Invent 5–6 dimensions (source, duration, what the person wants…), give each psalm coordinates, pick the nearest | Rejected. The coordinates would be made up: Athanasius describes situations, not points in a space. The distance between "repenting" and "slandered before a king" means nothing, and a nearby psalm can be handed out even though the thing that defines it was never said. The figure quiz's mask machinery shows how hard it is to keep this honest. |
| **C. Weighted votes** | Each answer adds points to situations; highest total wins | Rejected. The weights are our own judgement. It can hand out Psalm 51 (repentance) to someone who never said anything about their own wrongdoing, which in effect invents a pairing. It also produces many ties. |
| **D. Sieve** (recommended) | Below | Every result is a situation Athanasius named, and every part of it was matched by the person's own answer. |

### D. The sieve: a new `strategies/reading.ts` with shape `'reading'`

**The data**
- One entry per situation Athanasius wrote about: `{ id, psalm, lxx, section, also?: number[], facets: {feel?, source?, who?, howLong?, want?}, line, why }`.
  - `id` is permanent and never reused.
  - `psalm` is the English number; `lxx` is his number.
  - `also` holds the other psalms he names for the same situation. When he lists several ("17, 86, 88 and 140"), his first is the result and the rest are listed after it.
  - `facets` holds **only the parts his own sentence states**, each traceable to the section it came from.
- The five questions (what it feels like, where it comes from, who is involved, how long it has lasted, what the person most wants to say) are multiple choice. Each option sets one value of one facet, in everyday words that don't point to Scripture.

**Scoring**
1. A situation is **eligible** only if every facet it states matches the person's answer. Facets it doesn't state match anything.
2. Among eligible situations, the **most specific wins**: the one where the most stated facets matched, meaning the fullest description of this person that Athanasius gave.
3. **Ties are settled by the person, never by the arithmetic.** If two or three situations are still level, the last screen shows each one as a single plain-language line (no psalm numbers) and asks which is closer. This is the same kind of screen as the existing `#uniform` box in the runner.
4. **The questions adapt.** A question is skipped when every remaining candidate either agrees on that facet or doesn't state it. Most people answer four or five questions, not all of them.
5. **No path may end with no answer.** The test file enumerates every possible set of answers (5 questions × 4–6 options is a few thousand paths). It asserts that every path gives at least one and at most three candidates, and that every situation can be reached. That makes the set of situations complete by construction and removes any need for a fallback reading nobody wrote.

**Result code**
- Write a dedicated codec with prefix `PS` plus the situation `id` in base 36, padded to 2 characters (for example `/r/<slug>/PS1F/`). It is exact-length, uppercase, and anything else is refused.
- **Store the situation, not the psalm.** Athanasius pairs some psalms with more than one situation, so the psalm number alone would lose the reason.
- An unknown id gets a 404. A situation that is later retired keeps its id so old links still resolve.
- The code checks `^[0-9A-Z.]{1,96}$` in `account/schema.sql` and the shelf both accept this.
- The code should **not** carry the person's answers, because the link is what gets shared and it would reveal their feelings. The finisher's "because you said…" lines can come from the tab-scoped `sessionStorage` the runner already writes (`ww:took:<slug>`), so only the finisher's own tab would see them.

**Changes the engine needs** (all additions; nothing existing changes behaviour)
- `types.ts`:
  - `QuizItem` gains `kind?: 'scale' | 'choice'`, `options?: {key, text}[]`, `facet?`.
  - `Sheet` widens to `Array<number | null>`. Today it is only used in `registry.ts` and the strategies.
  - Add `ReadingView { shape: 'reading'; state: 'clear'; reading; psalm; rows: []; ranked: [] }` to `ResultView`.
  - `ScoringStrategy` gains optional `validate?(quiz)`, `next?(quiz, sheet)` (which question comes next) and `candidates?(quiz, sheet)` (the tie screen).
- `registry.ts`: `validate()` must hand off to `strategy.validate` for choice quizzes (skip the both-ways and radix checks).
- `compare.ts`: refuse this shape so `/c/` gives a 404. The share block and runner need a flag (for example `Quiz.comparable?: false`) to hide "See where you land next to them" and ignore `?with=`. Comparing two people's psalms makes no sense and would expose feelings.

**Numbering: put a check in code, not just in data.** Add `lxxToHebrew(n)`, which maps his numbering to English Bibles: 1–8 stay the same, 9 becomes 9–10, 10–112 become 11–113, 113 becomes 114–115, 114 and 115 both become 116, 116–145 become 117–146, 146 and 147 both become 147, and 148–150 stay the same. A test asserts that every situation's `psalm` is inside `lxxToHebrew(lxx)`. That catches the online copy's mistakes (its 27 for his 12, which is English 13; the Gradual Psalms as 120–134; the "cried unto the Lord in their trouble" refrain as English 107). Wherever one of his numbers covers two English psalms, the data must say which one is meant.

## 3. Pages for each psalm

**What exists now**
- `pages/figure/[slug].astro` is written for one quiz only: it imports `bibleFigure` directly, builds its pages from `outcomes` in `getStaticPaths`, and uses the figure's plate from `artForOutcome()`, `Hero`, `CompassWheel` and `RailStack`, `TraditionNeighbours`, `CorrectionNote`, and the quiz card at the foot.
- `pages/tradition/[slug].astro` does the same for the Compass.
- Gift and sin pages come from the generic `pages/axis/[quiz]/[axis].astro`, one page per group that has a `summary`.

**What a psalm needs**
- A new `pages/psalm/[slug].astro`, with `outcomePathBase: 'psalm'` and outcomes `{ name: 'Psalm 42', slug: '42' }`. The slug check accepts plain digits, and `validateOutcomeSlugs` will guard collisions.
- Each page is built once (not on request) and can be indexed. It would show:
  - every situation Athanasius paired with that psalm, reworded in our own words and cited by section of the Letter to Marcellinus;
  - the psalm in full from the Berean Standard Bible, with its superscription marked as Scripture and the BSB's own section headings marked as the translators' (or left out);
  - the other psalms he named alongside it;
  - a way into the quiz.
- `lib/seo.ts`: `ogImageFor()` needs a `/psalm/<n>/` branch. Without it these pages fall back to the home page's social card. Page titles and descriptions must pass `seo-test.mjs`: title 65 characters or fewer, description 50–160 characters and not cut mid-word, exactly one `<h1>`, a canonical link, `og:image`, and alt text on every image.
- On the quiz's intro page, `OutcomeIndex.astro` lists the outcomes automatically (e.g. "N psalms, one page each").

## 4. Bible text: how it is fetched now, and what whole psalms would cost

**How it works now**
- `scripts/fetch-passages.mjs` is run by hand and needs the network. It reads `data/compass.json`, fetches `https://bible.helloao.org/api/BSB/<BOOK>/<ch>.json`, keeps only the **first 5 verses** of each reference, and writes `data/passages.json` with a licence block (BSB, public domain since 30 April 2023). The file is generated but committed.
- Right now: 50 references, 34.7 KB.
- It is read only by `components/PassagePills.astro`, which runs on the server, so the text sits in the HTML and never in a script.

**Whole psalms, measured from `psalms-bsb.json` in the scratchpad**
- All 150 psalms: about 265 KB as compact JSON, 39,479 words.
- A typical psalm: about 1.4 KB (Psalm 32, 11 verses). The largest are 119 (15.6 KB, 176 verses), 78 (7.4 KB), 18 (5.4 KB) and 89 (5.3 KB).
- 116 psalms have a superscription.
- Only the psalms the situations use would ship: **roughly 70–120 KB for 40–60 psalms**, more if 119 or 78 are among them.

**Build steps**
- Add a new `scripts/fetch-psalms.mjs` modelled on `fetch-passages.mjs`. It reads the situation list and writes `src/data/psalms.json`, also committed.
- Unlike the scratch fetcher, it should **keep the order of headings and verses** and tell the superscription apart from the BSB's editorial headings. The scratch version collapses all headings into one list and loses where they sat, including in Psalm 119.
- Where the text is read:
  - The per-psalm pages are built once, so there is no runtime cost.
  - The result page is rendered on request (`export const prerender = false`), so importing `psalms.json` there adds about 100–265 KB to the server function. That is negligible.
- **Never import it from the quiz file**, or it lands in every quiz page's JavaScript.

## 5. The surfaces a new quiz touches

**Quiz page, `pages/q/[quiz].astro`**
- The runner is built for agree/disagree only:
  - the `SCALE` array and its five buttons;
  - "Statement N of M" and the progress pips;
  - keys 1–5;
  - `finish()` → `isUniformSheet` → `goToResult(scoreQuiz(...))`.
- It needs a choice renderer that follows `strategy.next()`, a Back button that steps back along the adaptive path, and the tie screen.
- Intro text assumes statements: the stat tiles ("Statements" and the Axes label), the scale icon in the how-to list, and the heading "`{n} statements, about {m} minutes`". `QuizPreview.astro` only has pole and ranking versions, so it needs a third version or must be hidden for this quiz.
- `goToResult` already saves to the shelf (`addResult`), fires the `ww:finished` event for accounts, and redirects. Both work as they are.

**Result page, `pages/r/[quiz]/[code].astro`**
- It branches on `bipolar` versus everything else, and everything else gets `CategoryStack`. It needs a `'reading'` branch with a new component (for example `PsalmReading.astro`) showing:
  - Athanasius's situation in our words, with its section;
  - the full psalm;
  - the other psalms he named;
  - a link to `/psalm/<n>/`.
- With `ranked: []` the outcomes section doesn't render, and the depth panels only render for pole quizzes. The title comes from `view.headline`; the description comes from `view.summary`. The page is not indexed.
- `EmailCapture.astro` assumes the ranking rows (`r.rank`). It needs a branch, and there is a privacy question: the form sends `quiz` and `code` to the mail provider, and that code would name the person's emotional situation.

**Share block, `components/ShareBlock.astro`**
- The share card is drawn on a 1080×1350 canvas, and only pole results get a picture (`drawWheel`). A ranking draws the headline, summary and notes only. A reading could draw the headline plus one exact verse.
- Fixed wording that needs changing:
  - `data-mine="Share your compass"` (wrong for every quiz except the Compass);
  - "`N statements, about M minutes`";
  - the compare-invite row, which must be hidden when the quiz can't be compared.
- `shareText` must be written by the new strategy. Test 7 expects its first line to be `shareTitle` and the text to contain `/r/<slug>/`.

**Social cards**
- `design/og/cards.mjs` lists them and `design/og/render.mjs site` draws them. It needs headless Chrome at `C:/Program Files/…` and Python with PIL, so it runs **locally, not on Vercel**.
- The output goes to `site/public/og/*.jpg` (about 140 KB each; 56 cards is 7.8 MB now) and the list to `site/src/data/og-cards.json`, which `seo.ts` reads.
- Add `quiz-<slug>`, and optionally `psalm-<n>` for each psalm. 40–60 more cards is about 6–8 MB committed.

**The `/me/` shelf and accounts**
- `lib/shelf.ts` stores `{quiz, code, at}` in `ww.shelf.v1` and treats every quiz the same. It only keeps a result if its code decodes.
