- `/me/` draws one room per quiz from `QUIZZES`, using `resultFor(...).headline` and `.summary`, so it works as long as the new view provides those. It needs a room colour in `me.css` (`.mroom--<slug>`).
- Accounts: `lib/account/schema.sql` keeps `(quiz, code, taken_at)` in Supabase, so for signed-in users **the psalm situation is stored on the server**. `/method/` should say so.

**Quiz lists**
- `pages/index.astro` codes each quiz's panel by hand (`getQuiz('bible-figure')` and so on, with `.room--figures` style classes). It needs a new panel plus CSS in `styles/pages/home.css`.
- `pages/quizzes.astro` lists from the registry, but needs a colour entry and a `.qcard--<slug>` rule in `styles/pages/reference.css`.
- `components/NextUp.astro` needs a colour entry.
- `lib/art.ts` needs the quiz's picture via `ART[slug]`. There is no psalm or harp plate in `public/img/`, so a new public-domain image and a line in `CREDITS.md` would be needed.
- `layouts/Base.astro` has `FOOT_SHORT` for long footer titles, which this title needs.
- `lib/seo.ts` needs a `SEO['/q/<slug>/']` entry.
- Articles cross-link through the `quizzes: [...]` field in their front matter (`content.config.ts`).

**Tests**
- `scripts/engine-test.mjs` runs before every build and in `npm run test`. Several sections loop over every quiz and make up answer values per group:
  - §2 codec round-trips (uses the radix and `groups.length`);
  - §7 share text;
  - §10 both-ways keying (**would fail** a choice quiz);
  - the §12c loop that checks no foreign code decodes (`encodeFor(q, q.groups.map(()=>50))`);
  - the §14 notes loop.

  These must learn about the third shape.
- New sections to add:
  - add the quiz to the §1b publication-status list;
  - every situation reachable, every answer path giving 1–3 candidates;
  - `lxxToHebrew` consistency;
  - every psalm present in `psalms.json` with the right verse count;
  - ids unique, with a frozen id → psalm map so a live code never changes meaning;
  - junk and foreign codes refused.
- Other test scripts:
  - `seo-test.mjs` runs after the build and checks the built pages and sitemap, so the new `/q/` and `/psalm/` pages must pass it.
  - `seo-plumbing-test.mjs`, `account-test.mjs`, `auth-test.mjs` and `email-test.mjs` are not affected.
  - `switch-test.mjs` does 4 full builds, so it gets slower but needs no changes.
- There is no `astro check` in the scripts, so type mismatches in `.astro` files will **not** fail the build. The new shape's branches have to be found by reading, using the list above.
- `astro.config.mjs` imports the registry when it loads, to leave draft quizzes out of the sitemap. If the quiz ships as `draft`, its `/q/` and `/psalm/` addresses are left out of the sitemap automatically.

## 6. Files a build would touch or add, in order

1. `site/scripts/fetch-psalms.mjs` (new) → `site/src/data/psalms.json` (new, generated, committed).
2. The situation data: `site/src/lib/quizzes/psalm-readings.ts`, or a JSON file under `site/src/data/`. It holds `id, psalm, lxx, section, also, facets` and short copy only; the longer explanations go in a file the browser never loads.
3. `site/src/lib/engine/types.ts`: choice questions, the wider `Sheet`, `ReadingView`, the optional `validate/next/candidates` hooks, and `comparable?`.
4. `site/src/lib/engine/codec.ts`: the id codec (or put it in the strategy).
5. `site/src/lib/strategies/reading.ts` (new): the sieve, specificity, candidates, `lxxToHebrew`, encode/decode, and share text.
6. `site/src/lib/quizzes/<slug>.ts` (new) with `codePrefix: 'PS'`, `outcomePathBase: 'psalm'`, and `status: 'draft'` until the owner has seen it.
7. `site/src/lib/engine/registry.ts`: register it and hand validation to the strategy. `site/src/lib/engine/compare.ts`: refuse the new shape.
8. `site/scripts/engine-test.mjs`: make the generic loops aware of the shape and add the new sections.
9. `site/src/pages/q/[quiz].astro`: the choice runner, adaptive Back, the tie screen, and intro wording and stats. `site/src/components/QuizPreview.astro`: a third version or hidden.
10. `site/src/components/PsalmReading.astro` (new). `site/src/pages/r/[quiz]/[code].astro`: the new branch. `site/src/components/EmailCapture.astro`: branch, or off for this quiz.
11. `site/src/components/ShareBlock.astro`: fix "Share your compass" and the statements count, hide the compare row, and add the card branch.
12. `site/src/pages/psalm/[slug].astro` (new).
13. `site/src/lib/seo.ts`: `SEO` entries and the `/psalm/` branch in `ogImageFor`.
14. `site/src/lib/art.ts`, `site/public/img/<plate>.jpg`, and `site/public/img/CREDITS.md`.
15. `site/src/pages/index.astro` and `styles/pages/home.css`; `pages/quizzes.astro` and `styles/pages/reference.css`; `components/NextUp.astro`; `styles/pages/me.css`; `layouts/Base.astro` (`FOOT_SHORT`).
16. `design/og/cards.mjs`, then run `node design/og/render.mjs site` locally. This writes `site/public/og/*.jpg` and `site/src/data/og-cards.json`.
17. `site/src/pages/method.astro`: one line saying the psalm result is kept on the shelf and, for signed-in users, in the account.
18. The `quizzes:` front matter in related articles (worry, joy, forgiveness).
19. Run `npm run test` in `site/`, then a full build so `seo-test` runs.

## Decisions for the owner

- **Does the result page carry a safety line?** Some of Athanasius's situations are about despair or feeling abandoned by God. A plain line for someone in danger (for example 988 in the US) is his call, not a code choice.
- **Does the shared link carry only the situation, not the answers?** I recommend only the situation, since sharing is voluntary and the answers are personal.

psalms.superscription: A Psalm of David, when he fled from his son Absalom.
psalms.movement: It opens with David surrounded: foes multiplying and people saying God will not save him (vv.1-2). At v.3 it turns on a single 'But You', and from there it is trust: God answers, he sleeps and wakes safe, he will not fear the crowd (vv.4-6). It closes with a cry for God to act and a quiet line that salvation is the Lord's, with a blessing on His people.

namesIt.text: O LORD, how my foes have increased! How many rise up against me!

turn.text: But You, O LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the One who lifts my head.

lastLine.text: Salvation belongs to the LORD; may Your blessing be on Your people. Selah

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 3:7 asks God to strike the enemies on the jaw and break the teeth of the wicked, which is violent imagery for a modern reader. Psalm 3:2 (people saying God will not deliver him) may sting someone who hears that said about them.
psalms.fitNote: Fits well, with no sign of a numbering error. The superscription itself ties it to David fleeing his own son Absalom, which is exactly the §15 case of being hounded by your own people, and v.1 names the many rising up. The §12 use (singing a psalm while thinking of your own troubles, so the words feel like yours) is a general point Athanasius illustrates with this psalm; it fits any reader under pressure.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It starts as a call to be answered, but in the same breath it remembers that God has already relieved his distress (v.1). He then turns to the people who malign him, telling them the Lord hears and urging them to search their hearts and trust (vv.2-5). It ends in joy greater than a good harvest and in lying down to sleep in peace.

namesIt.text: Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have relieved my distress; show me grace and hear my prayer.

turn.text: Know that the LORD has set apart the godly for Himself; the LORD hears when I call to Him.

lastLine.text: I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.

psalms.hardParts: Little to trip on. Psalm 4:2 speaks of honour being maligned and people loving lies, and Psalm 4:4 ('Be angry, yet do not sin') could read as a rebuke to someone who is angry, though it is addressed to his detractors.
psalms.fitNote: Fits honestly. Athanasius read the Greek of v.1 as 'when I called, You heard me; in distress You set me at large', which the BSB renders 'You have relieved my distress'. The thanks is expressed as joy and peace (vv.7-8) rather than the word 'thank', so the result copy should present it as the gladness of someone already heard. No numbering error.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster, to be accompanied by flutes. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It begins as a groaning morning prayer, laid before God at daybreak with expectation (vv.1-3). It sets God's holiness against deceitful enemies and asks to be led straight because of them (vv.4-10), with a first 'But I' of trust at v.7. It rises at v.11 into joy for all who take refuge in God and ends with God surrounding the righteous like a shield.

namesIt.text: In the morning, O LORD, You hear my voice; at daybreak I lay my plea before You and wait in expectation.

turn.text: But let all who take refuge in You rejoice; let them ever shout for joy. May You shelter them, that those who love Your name may rejoice in You.

lastLine.text: For surely You, O LORD, bless the righteous; You surround them with the shield of Your favor.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 5:5 says God hates all workers of iniquity, which a reader who feels guilty may take personally. Psalm 5:9 (throats as open graves) and Psalm 5:10 (declare them guilty, let them fall, drive them out) are sharp words against enemies.
psalms.fitNote: Fits well. The morning prayer is explicit in v.3 (the Greek reads 'early'), the wish to be heard is vv.1-2, and the trapping enemies are vv.8-10. No numbering error.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments, according to Sheminith. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It opens afraid of God's anger and asks not to be disciplined in wrath, then pours out frailty, agony, sleepless weeping and a long 'how long' (vv.1-7). At v.8 it turns suddenly: the Lord has heard his weeping and accepts his prayer (vv.8-9). It closes with his enemies turned back in shame.

namesIt.text: O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath.

turn.text: Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard my weeping.

lastLine.text: All my enemies will be ashamed and dismayed; they will turn back in sudden disgrace.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 6:5 ('there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?') can sound bleak about death to a grieving or depressed reader. Psalm 6:6 (flooding the bed with tears) is raw. The last line, Psalm 6:10, ends on enemies' disgrace rather than on the person's own comfort, so the hope to lead with is vv.8-9.
psalms.fitNote: Fits exactly: the opening verse is a person shaken by the sense of God's displeasure. Athanasius pairs it with another psalm for the same state; this one is sound. No numbering error.

psalms.superscription: A Shiggaion of David, which he sang to the LORD concerning the words of Cush, a Benjamite.
psalms.movement: It starts by taking refuge in God from pursuers who would tear him apart, then protests his innocence with an oath (vv.1-5). He asks God to rise and judge, and at v.10 settles: his shield is with God, Who saves the upright; the schemer falls into the pit he dug himself (vv.10-16). It ends in thanks and praise to the Lord Most High.

namesIt.text: O LORD my God, I take refuge in You; save me and deliver me from all my pursuers,

turn.text: My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart.

lastLine.text: I will thank the LORD for His righteousness and sing praise to the name of the LORD Most High.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 7:3-5 is a self-curse ('may my enemy pursue me... trample me to the ground') if he is guilty, which a self-blaming reader may turn on themselves. Psalm 7:6 calls God to arise in anger; Psalm 7:11-13 pictures God sharpening His sword and shooting fiery arrows at the unrepentant. Psalm 7:2 (shredded like by a lion) is vivid.
psalms.fitNote: Fits, and the Ahithophel link comes from the superscription rather than the body. The Greek names the man 'Chousi', which Athanasius's tradition read as Hushai, the friend who warned David of Ahithophel's counsel (2 Samuel 15-17). The Hebrew calls him Cush a Benjamite, and Hushai was an Archite, so the identification is Athanasius's reading, not something the English text states. It is not a numbering error: plotting enemies (vv.14-16) and trust in the God Who rescues (vv.1, 10) are plainly there. If the site explains the Ahithophel reference, it should say it follows the ancient reading of the title.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “The Death of the Son.” A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It opens in wholehearted thanks and praise for God's wonders, because God has upheld his cause and the enemy has fallen (vv.1-6). It celebrates God as the just judge and a refuge for the oppressed, Who does not forget the cry of the afflicted (vv.7-12), then dips into a fresh plea for mercy at v.13 before holding on to the hope that the needy will not always be forgotten (v.18). It ends by asking God to rise and judge the nations.

namesIt.text: I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart; I will recount all Your wonders.

turn.text: For the needy will not always be forgotten; nor the hope of the oppressed forever dashed.

lastLine.text: Lay terror upon them, O LORD; let the nations know they are but men. Selah

psalms.hardParts: The final verse, Psalm 9:20 ('Lay terror upon them'), ends harshly, so the result should not leave the reader on it without the hope of v.18 or vv.9-10 highlighted. Psalm 9:5-6 (names erased, cities uprooted) and Psalm 9:17 (the wicked returning to Sheol) are stark. Psalm 9:12 ('the Avenger of bloodshed') may jar.
psalms.fitNote: Fits on its opening: the Greek begins 'I will confess/acknowledge You, O Lord, with my whole heart' (exomologesomai), which is thankful acknowledgement, and the English v.1 is thanks. One numbering caution: the Septuagint Psalm 9 that Athanasius used is English Psalms 9 and 10 joined as one poem, so his 'Psalm 9' also contains English Psalm 10 ('Why, O LORD, do You stand far off?'). Printing English Psalm 9 alone matches his reason for choosing it, but the site should know it is printing only the first half of his psalm.

psalms.movement: It opens by asking why God stands far off and hides, then spends most of its length (vv. 2-11) on a portrait of a proud predator who preys on the helpless and tells himself God has forgotten. At v. 12 the speaker cries for God to rise, and at v. 14 turns: God has in fact seen the trouble and is the helper of the fatherless. It ends in confidence that He is King, has heard the humble, and will defend the oppressed.

namesIt.text: You have heard, O LORD, the desire of the humble; You will strengthen their hearts. You will incline Your ear,

turn.text: But You have regarded trouble and grief; You see to repay it by Your hand. The victim entrusts himself to You; You are the helper of the fatherless.

lastLine.text: to vindicate the fatherless and oppressed, that the men of the earth may strike terror no more.

psalms.hardParts: v. 1 says God seems far off and hidden (honest, but can land hard on someone who already feels abandoned). vv. 7-10 describe ambush, killing the innocent and crushing the helpless. v. 2 asks that the wicked be caught in their own schemes; v. 15 asks God to break the arm of the wicked until none is left; v. 16 has the nations perishing from His land.
psalms.fitNote: MISFIT for thanksgiving. English Psalm 10 has no thanks or open acknowledgement of God anywhere in it; it is a lament about oppression. Athanasius used the Septuagint, where Psalm 9 is English Psalms 9 and 10 joined as one poem, and that psalm begins with the words of exomologesis: English Psalm 9:1, 'I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart' (both check it in the BSB). The online copy's '9' in section 21 is the Septuagint 9 left unconverted. The honest pairing for 'give thanks and acknowledge Him openly' is English Psalm 9 (or 9 and 10 printed together as the one psalm he knew). Handing a thankful reader English Psalm 10 alone would give them a complaint. Psalm 10 would honestly suit his other use of Septuagint 9 in section 16 only as the second half of that whole.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. Of David.
psalms.movement: It starts with a settled claim, 'In the LORD I take refuge', and then quotes the frightened advice of others: run for the hills, the wicked are aiming at you, the foundations are gone. At v. 4 it answers that fear by looking up: the LORD is on His throne and sees everything. It ends with the promise that the upright will see His face.

namesIt.text: In the LORD I take refuge. How then can you say to me: “Flee like a bird to your mountain!

turn.text: The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD is on His heavenly throne. His eyes are watching closely; they examine the sons of men.

lastLine.text: For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice. The upright will see His face.

psalms.hardParts: v. 5 says His soul hates the lover of violence; v. 6 has God raining fiery coals and sulfur on the wicked. vv. 2-3 (archers shooting from the shadows, foundations destroyed) are voiced by the fearful advisers, not the psalmist, which a reader could miss.
psalms.fitNote: Fits well. Athanasius (section 16) prescribes his Septuagint 10, which is English 11, for when someone tries to alarm you: hold to your trust in the Lord. That is exactly the psalm's situation: others urging panic and flight, the speaker refusing because the LORD is his refuge. The online copy's '11th' here is correctly converted.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Sheminith. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It opens with a cry for help because the faithful seem to have vanished and everyone lies and flatters. At v. 5 God Himself speaks and promises to rise for the oppressed, and the psalmist answers that His words are pure as refined silver and that He will keep His people. The last verse goes back to the plain fact that the wicked still roam and vileness is prized, so the hope is held in the middle of a situation that has not yet changed.

namesIt.text: Help, O LORD, for the godly are no more; the faithful have vanished from among men.

turn.text: “For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise,” says the LORD. “I will bring safety to him who yearns.”

lastLine.text: The wicked wander freely, and vileness is exalted among men.

psalms.hardParts: v. 3 asks the LORD to cut off all flattering lips and every boastful tongue (mild). The final verse (v. 8) ends on the bleak state of things rather than on the promise, so a hurting reader who stops at the end may feel it leaves them there; the hope sits in vv. 5-7 and a result page should point to it.
psalms.fitNote: Fits section 16 squarely: his Septuagint 11 (English 12) for seeing pride and evil everywhere until nothing holy seems left; v. 1 says almost exactly that. The section 12 use (voicing one's own trust and prayer) fits more loosely: the trust is in v. 7 ('You, O LORD, will keep us'). One caution on section 12: the online copy prints 'Psalms 11 and 12' there, and if those are Septuagint numbers they would be English 12 and 13; if English, 11 and 12. The pairing of English 12 with section 12 is defensible under either reading, but check it against the Greek before relying on it.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It begins with four 'How long?' questions: forgotten by God, His face hidden, sorrow every day, the enemy on top. It then asks God to look and answer before the speaker goes under. At v. 5 it turns, with nothing outwardly changed, to trust in His loving devotion, and it ends singing because He has been good.

namesIt.text: How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?

turn.text: But I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation.

lastLine.text: I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me.

psalms.hardParts: v. 3 'lest I sleep in death' could land hard on someone who is seriously ill or has thought about dying; it is a fear of death voiced in prayer, not a wish for it. v. 1 openly says God seems to have forgotten, which is the point of the psalm but may need a word that the psalm itself says this so the reader can too.
psalms.fitNote: Fits perfectly, and confirms the numbering error in the online copy. Section 16 prescribes, for trouble drawn out so long you feel God has forgotten you, his Septuagint 12, which is English 13; v. 1 is word for word that feeling. The online copy's 'Psalm 27' is wrong and should not be used.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens with the fool who says in his heart there is no God, and widens to God looking down on a humanity that has turned aside, corrupt and preying on His people. At v. 5 it turns: the scoffers are the ones in dread, because God is with the righteous and is the shelter of the oppressed. It ends with a longing prayer for salvation to come from Zion and for His people to rejoice.

namesIt.text: The fool says in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt; their acts are vile. There is no one who does good.

turn.text: There they are, overwhelmed with dread, for God is in the company of the righteous.

lastLine.text: Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion! When the LORD restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!

psalms.hardParts: v. 1 calls the one who denies God a 'fool' and 'corrupt'; a reader with unbelieving family, or with doubts of their own, could feel condemned. v. 3 says no one does good, not even one, which reads as total and can sting someone already down on themselves. v. 4 speaks of evildoers devouring God's people like bread.
psalms.fitNote: Fits. Section 16 prescribes his Septuagint 13 and 52 (English 14 and 53, near-twin psalms) for hearing people speak against God's providence: do not join them, but pray. The psalm names that talk directly (v. 1) and ends in prayer (v. 7). Worth saying honestly on the result: the instruction to intercede rather than join in is Athanasius's; the psalm itself does not tell you to pray for the scoffers, though its closing longing for salvation is the prayer he means. The online copy's '14th and 53rd' is correctly converted.

psalms.superscription: A prayer of David.
psalms.movement: It opens as a plea to be heard and cleared, from someone who has searched his own heart and kept to God's paths. From v. 6 it asks, with growing confidence that God will answer, to be kept as the apple of His eye and hidden under His wings from enemies who have surrounded him like a lion in ambush. After asking God to confront them, it ends quietly: the speaker will see His face and be satisfied in His presence when he wakes.

namesIt.text: from the wicked who assail me, from my mortal enemies who surround me.

turn.text: As for me, I will behold Your face in righteousness; when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence.

lastLine.text: As for me, I will behold Your face in righteousness; when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence.

psalms.hardParts: v. 13 asks God to bring enemies to their knees and deliver 'by Your sword'. v. 14 is obscure and could be misread either as a curse or as a blessing on the wicked. vv. 3-5 protest innocence ('You have tested me and found no evil'); a reader carrying guilt may feel the psalm is not for them, when it is a plea of innocence in this particular quarrel, not a claim to be sinless. vv. 11-12 (tracked down, a lion lurking in ambush) may be vivid for someone who feels hunted.
psalms.fitNote: Fits both uses. Section 17 lists it (his Septuagint 16, English 17; the online copy's '17' is correctly converted) for praying against enemies who hem you in, and vv. 9 and 11 say 'surround' twice. Section 12 (putting your own trust and prayer into words) fits too: its superscription is literally 'A prayer of David', and v. 6 voices confident prayer. The same numbering caution noted under Psalm 12 applies to the section 12 pairing: the online copy prints '11 and 12' there, so confirm against the Greek that Septuagint 16 (English 17) is what he named.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. Of David the servant of the LORD, who sang this song to the LORD on the day the LORD had delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. He said:
psalms.movement: It opens in love and praise for God as rock and fortress (vv. 1-3), then looks back on the cords of death and the cry for help (vv. 4-6). God comes down in storm and fire and draws the singer out of deep waters (vv. 7-19). It then reflects on God's faithfulness and strength given for the fight (vv. 20-45) and ends in praise for the God who rescues and keeps faith with His anointed forever (vv. 46-50).

namesIt.text: He rescued me from my powerful enemy, from foes too mighty for me.

turn.text: In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried to my God for help. From His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for His help reached His ears.

lastLine.text: Great salvation He brings to His king. He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 18:37-42 dwells on pursuing, crushing and grinding enemies like dust, and v. 41 says the foes cried to the LORD and He did not answer, which a reader who feels unheard could take personally. Vv. 20-24 claim a reward for the singer's righteousness and clean hands, which may sting someone weighed down by guilt. The storm scene with His anger (vv. 7-15) and v. 26 ("to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd") could also unsettle. It is long (50 verses) for a printed result.
psalms.fitNote: Exact fit. The letter sends the person who has been delivered from enemies and oppressors to this psalm, and the psalm's own superscription says David sang it on the day the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from Saul. Letter's LXX 17 = English 18; the online copy's number is correct here.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It begins with the skies speaking God's glory without words and the sun running its course (vv. 1-6). It moves to the Law of the LORD, perfect, reviving the soul and sweeter than honey (vv. 7-11). It ends inward and personal, asking to be cleansed of hidden faults and kept from willful sin, and praying that the words of the mouth and the heart please the LORD, 'my Rock and my Redeemer' (vv. 12-14).

namesIt.text: The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands.

lastLine.text: May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be pleasing in Your sight, O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer.

psalms.hardParts: Little to trip on. Vv. 12-13 (hidden faults, willful sins, 'great transgression') could stir anxiety in a scrupulous reader, though the psalm asks God to cleanse rather than condemn.
psalms.fitNote: Exact fit, and it covers all three things the letter names: the order of creation (vv. 1-6), God's providence in it (the sun's circuit, 'nothing is deprived of its warmth'), and the holy commands of His law (vv. 7-11). Letter's LXX 18 = English 19; numbering is correct.

psalms.superscription: A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It opens with the LORD as shepherd and nothing lacking, then green pastures, quiet waters and a restored soul (vv. 1-3). It passes through the valley of the shadow of death without fear because He is there (v. 4). It ends at a table spread in front of enemies, with goodness and mercy following all one's days and a home in the LORD's house forever (vv. 5-6).

namesIt.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.

lastLine.text: Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever.

psalms.fitNote: Exact fit. The letter's words for this one are being fed and guided by the Lord and rejoicing in it, which is the psalm's whole picture (vv. 1-3, 5). Letter's LXX 22 = English 23; numbering is correct. Note that v. 4, the valley of the shadow of death, is well known as a psalm for grief, but Athanasius prescribes it for grateful joy in being shepherded, not for grief.

psalms.superscription: A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It opens by claiming the whole earth and everyone in it for the LORD, Who founded it on the seas (vv. 1-2). It asks who may climb His holy hill and answers: clean hands and a pure heart, those who seek His face (vv. 3-6). It ends with the ancient gates called to lift up their heads for the King of Glory, the LORD of Hosts (vv. 7-10).

namesIt.text: The earth is the LORD’s, and the fullness thereof, the world and all who dwell therein.

lastLine.text: Who is He, this King of Glory? The LORD of Hosts— He is the King of Glory. Selah

psalms.hardParts: Vv. 3-4 make clean hands and a pure heart the condition for standing in His holy place; a reader who feels unworthy could hear that as shutting them out. 'Mighty in battle' (v. 8) is martial but mild.
psalms.fitNote: Partial but honest fit. Creation and God's ownership and founding of the world are explicit (vv. 1-2). The 'holy commands of His law' are present only indirectly, through the moral requirements of vv. 3-6 (clean hands, no idol, no false oath); the psalm's climax is the King of Glory entering, which the letter does not mention. The letter pairs it with 19, which carries the law theme fully. Letter's LXX 23 = English 24; numbering is correct, not a misfit.

psalms.superscription: Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens by lifting the soul to God in trust and asking not to be shamed before enemies (vv. 1-3). It moves back and forth between asking to be taught His ways, asking forgiveness for the sins of youth, and quiet confidence that the LORD is good and guides the humble (vv. 4-15). Near the end the pain comes out openly: loneliness, a troubled heart, many enemies who hate (vv. 16-19). It closes by taking refuge and waiting on God and praying for all Israel (vv. 20-22).

namesIt.text: Consider my enemies, for they are many, and they hate me with vicious hatred.

turn.text: Surely none who wait for You will be put to shame; but those who engage in treachery without cause will be disgraced.

lastLine.text: Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress.

psalms.hardParts: The enemies' 'vicious hatred' (v. 19) is named bluntly. The repeated focus on sin (vv. 7, 11, 18) may weigh on a guilty reader, though each time it asks for mercy. V. 13 promises prosperity and land to those who fear the LORD, which could jar someone suffering. The hope does not arrive at the end: the hardest lines (vv. 16-19) come late, and the psalm closes on a plea rather than a resolution.
psalms.fitNote: Good fit. The letter says: when enemies surround you, lift up your heart to God and say this psalm. V. 1 is exactly that act ('To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul'), and enemies appear at vv. 2 and 19. The letter's promise that the sinners will be routed matches v. 3. Letter's LXX 24 = English 25; numbering is correct.

psalms.superscription: Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens by asking the LORD to vindicate the singer and to test and examine heart and mind (vv. 1-3). The singer declares he stays apart from deceitful and wicked people and loves God's house (vv. 4-8). He then prays not to be swept away with men of bloodshed and bribery (vv. 9-10), promises to keep walking with integrity, and ends on level ground, blessing the LORD among His people (vv. 11-12).

namesIt.text: Vindicate me, O LORD! For I have walked with integrity; I have trusted in the LORD without wavering.

turn.text: My feet stand on level ground; in the congregations I will bless the LORD.

lastLine.text: My feet stand on level ground; in the congregations I will bless the LORD.

psalms.hardParts: Vv. 1-6 protest the singer's own innocence ('I wash my hands in innocence') and v. 5 says 'I hate the mob of evildoers'; a reader carrying guilt may feel shut out, and others may hear it as self-righteous. V. 2 invites God to test heart and mind, which some will find frightening. There are no violent curses.
psalms.fitNote: Fair fit on the main point: it hands the verdict to God ('Vindicate me', 'Test me') rather than to people. The letter's 'hands full of blood' matches vv. 9-10 (men of bloodshed, right hands full of bribes). It is weaker on enemies pressing hard: the psalm presents the wicked as company to avoid and a fate to be spared, not as active attackers. The letter groups it with 35 and 43, which carry the attack. Letter's LXX 25 = English 26 ('Judge me, O Lord'); numbering is correct, no sign of a conversion error.

psalms.superscription: Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens in bold confidence (vv. 1-6): the LORD is light and stronghold, and even an army encamped around the speaker cannot make him afraid. At v. 7 it drops into urgent pleading: do not hide Your face, do not forsake me, false witnesses are rising up (vv. 7-12). Then at v. 13 it steadies again into certainty of seeing the LORD's goodness 'in the land of the living', and it ends by telling the reader, twice, to wait for the LORD and be strong.

namesIt.text: Though an army encamps around me, my heart will not fear; though a war breaks out against me, I will keep my trust.

turn.text: Still I am certain to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living.

lastLine.text: Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 27:10 ('Though my father and mother forsake me') may hit hard for a reader who has actually been rejected by a parent, though the line itself is a comfort (the LORD will receive me). Psalm 27:2 and 27:6 speak of enemies stumbling and of the speaker's head held high above them, which could read as gloating. Psalm 27:12 ('false witnesses... breathing out violence') is vivid but not a curse. No imprecations.
psalms.fitNote: Fits well. The online copy's number is right here: English 27 = Septuagint 26, whose Greek title reads 'Of David, before he was anointed', which is exactly why Athanasius speaks of foes scorning you as not yet anointed. Note that this phrase is NOT in the Hebrew-based BSB superscription (which is only 'Of David.'), so the site must not present 'before he was anointed' as part of the printed psalm; attribute it to the Greek title Athanasius read. Verse 3 (an army encamped, a war breaking out, yet no fear) matches 'massing like an army' and 'do not cower' directly. (Separately: the same online copy's earlier use of '27' for 'as though God had forgotten you' in §15 is the misnumbered one, almost certainly English 13; that is a different prescription from this §17 one.)

psalms.superscription: Of David.
psalms.movement: It starts with a cry not to be met with silence, afraid of going down to the Pit (vv. 1-2), then asks not to be swept away with smooth-talking people whose hearts are full of malice, and asks God to repay them (vv. 3-5). At v. 6 it turns sharply: the LORD has heard. It ends in thanks, strength and a prayer for all God's people, that He would shepherd and carry them forever.

namesIt.text: Do not drag me away with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity, who speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts.

turn.text: Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard my cry for mercy.

lastLine.text: Save Your people and bless Your inheritance; shepherd them and carry them forever.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 28:4-5 is an imprecation ('Repay them according to their deeds... bring back on them what they deserve'; 'He will tear them down and never rebuild them'). Psalm 28:1 ('like those descending to the Pit') may land heavily on a reader who feels near despair, though it is the fear the psalm moves out of.
psalms.fitNote: Fits. English 28 = Septuagint 27; the numbering is consistent with the rest of §17 in this copy. The two-faced schemers are in v. 3 (peace on the lips, malice in the heart), and the unceasing cry to God is vv. 1-2. One nuance for the copy: Athanasius's point is not to fix your attention on the weakness of your own humanity nor on the brazenness of their attack; the psalm itself says nothing about human weakness, so any wording about 'weak nature' should be attributed to him, not the psalm.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It opens pleading for refuge while already naming God as rock and fortress, and includes 'Into Your hands I commit my spirit' (vv. 1-8). From v. 9 it sinks into the deepest part: grief wasting body and years, scorned by neighbours, dreaded by friends who cross the street, forgotten like the dead, terror on every side (vv. 9-13). At v. 14 it turns ('But I trust in You'), puts its times in God's hands, and rises into praise of the goodness God has stored up for those who take refuge in Him, admitting honestly 'In my alarm I said, I am cut off' yet God heard (v. 22); it ends by telling everyone who hopes in the LORD to be strong.

namesIt.text: Among all my enemies I am a disgrace, and among my neighbors even more. I am dreaded by my friends— they flee when they see me on the street.

turn.text: But I trust in You, O LORD; I say, “You are my God.”

lastLine.text: Be strong and courageous, all you who hope in the LORD.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 31:6 ('I hate those who cling to worthless idols'). Psalm 31:17 ('Let the wicked be put to shame; let them lie silent in Sheol') and 31:18 are imprecations. Psalm 31:10 ('my iniquity has drained my strength') could make a hurting reader think their isolation is their own fault. Psalm 31:12 ('I am forgotten like a dead man... like a broken vessel') and 31:13 ('terror on every side... plot to take my life') are very heavy for a depressed or frightened reader, though the psalm does not leave them there.
psalms.fitNote: Fits well. English 31 = Septuagint 30, consistent with this copy's §18. Friends and neighbours turning away is v. 11, and 'looking to the future' matches vv. 19-24 (goodness laid up for those who fear Him; be strong, all who hope). The psalm does not say the hatred is 'because of faith in Christ' or 'for holding to the truth'; that is Athanasius's application (v. 18 speaks of the righteous, and v. 5 is the word Christ prays on the cross, Luke 23:46). Present that reason as his, not the psalm's.

psalms.superscription: Of David, when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, so that the king drove him away.
psalms.movement: It begins already rejoicing, calling the humble to hear and inviting others to magnify the LORD together, then tells its own story: I sought the LORD, He answered, this poor man called and was saved (vv. 1-7). From v. 8 ('Taste and see') it turns teacher, calling 'children' to learn the fear of the LORD, to guard their tongue and pursue peace (vv. 8-14). It closes on promises: the LORD hears the righteous, is near to the brokenhearted, delivers from many afflictions, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned.

namesIt.text: Magnify the LORD with me; let us exalt His name together.

lastLine.text: The LORD redeems His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 34:16 ('to wipe out all memory of them from the earth') and 34:21 ('Evil will slay the wicked') are judgment lines. Psalm 34:10 ('those who seek the LORD lack no good thing') and 34:20 ('not one of them will be broken') could read as broken promises to someone who is in need or physically hurt; v. 19 ('Many are the afflictions of the righteous') is the honest counterweight, and John 19:36 applies v. 20 to Christ. The superscription describes David escaping by feigning madness, which a reader may find odd.
psalms.fitNote: Fits closely. English 34 = Septuagint 33, consistent. The escape among enemies is the superscription itself (David getting away from a hostile king by his wits, 1 Samuel 21:10-15, where the king is named Achish; 'Abimelech' is the psalm title's name for him, so do not 'correct' the superscription). Gathering others to give thanks is v. 3, and 'gentle people' echoes v. 2, where the Greek Athanasius read has 'the meek' and the BSB has 'the oppressed'. Because it is thanks from the first line, there is no turn to point to: the hope is the whole psalm.

psalms.superscription: Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens by asking the LORD to take up arms and to say to the speaker's soul 'I am your salvation', then asks that those hunting his life be shamed and driven off (vv. 1-8), closing that section with a vow of joy (vv. 9-10). The middle tells the painful story of betrayal: people he fasted and grieved for when they were ill now repay him evil and mock his stumbling, and he cries 'How long, O Lord' (vv. 11-18). The last section begs God to wake and vindicate him and not let them gloat (vv. 19-26), and it ends with his friends shouting for joy and his own tongue praising God's righteousness all day long.

namesIt.text: Awake and rise to my defense, to my cause, my God and my Lord!

turn.text: Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD and exult in His salvation.

lastLine.text: Then my tongue will proclaim Your righteousness and Your praises all day long.

psalms.hardParts: Many imprecations: Psalm 35:4-6 ('May their path be dark and slick'), 35:8 ('May ruin befall them by surprise... may they fall into the hazard they created'), 35:26 ('clothed in shame and reproach'). Psalm 35:13 ('my prayers returned unanswered') may sting for someone whose prayers feel unanswered. Psalm 35:17 ('How long, O Lord, will You look on?') voices God's apparent inaction plainly.
psalms.fitNote: Fits. English 35 = Septuagint 34, consistent with this copy's §17 (Athanasius groups it with English 26 and 43 for asking God, the only just Judge, to judge). The Greek he read opens 'Judge, O Lord, those who wrong me' where the BSB has 'Contend with my opponents', so the judging theme is sharper in his text; in the BSB it is carried by vv. 23-24 ('Vindicate me by Your righteousness'). The persistence and murderous intent are in vv. 4, 7 and 17. Caution: 'hands full of blood' is not in Psalm 35; it is closer to Psalm 26:9-10 (one of the three he names), so do not attach that phrase to this psalm's result. The psalm turns to praise three times (vv. 9-10, 18, 27-28) rather than once.

psalms.superscription: A Psalm of David, for remembrance.
psalms.movement: It opens begging God not to rebuke in anger, and spends most of its length describing a body and heart crushed under sin and God's hand: festering wounds, burning pain, failing strength, friends keeping their distance, enemies setting snares (vv. 1-14). At v. 15 the speaker, silent before his accusers, rests his case with God ('You will answer'), confesses his iniquity openly (v. 18), and notes he is hated for pursuing the good (v. 20). It ends not with rescue but with a plea: do not forsake me, come quickly, O Lord my Savior; the hope is in whom he calls on, not in a resolved ending.

namesIt.text: O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath.

turn.text: I wait for You, O LORD; You will answer, O Lord my God.

lastLine.text: Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 38:2-3 ('Your arrows have pierced me deeply... no soundness in my body because of Your anger') and 38:5 ('My wounds are foul and festering because of my sinful folly') tie illness directly to sin and divine anger; a reader who is chronically ill or depressed could take this as a verdict on their own suffering, so the site should say this is one man's confession, not a rule that sickness means punishment (compare John 9:3). Psalm 38:11 (loved ones shun my disease) is painful for the isolated. No curses on enemies. The psalm ends without an answer received.
psalms.fitNote: Fits exactly. English 38 = Septuagint 37, and Athanasius pairs it with Psalm 6 for feeling under God's displeasure; both open with the same line (compare 6:1 and 38:1), which confirms the numbering. It is one of the seven traditional penitential psalms. The honest caution for a hurting reader is that it ends in waiting and plea, so the hope to point to is v. 15 and the closing address 'O Lord my Savior', not a rescue story.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. For Jeduthun. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It opens with a man who has resolved to guard his tongue while the wicked are near, holds it in until it burns, and then speaks out, but to God, asking to know how short his life is. Midway (v7) he says plainly that his hope is in God, then asks for deliverance from his sins and from God's chastening hand. It does not end in resolution: the last line asks God to look away so he can have some cheer before he dies.

namesIt.text: I said, “I will watch my ways so that I will not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle as long as the wicked are present.”

turn.text: And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in You.

lastLine.text: Turn Your gaze away from me, that I may again be cheered before I depart and am no more.”

psalms.hardParts: v10-11: the psalmist's suffering is God's own scourge and discipline for his iniquity, which a hurting reader may take as 'this is God punishing me'. v13 (the last line): asking God to turn His gaze away before 'I depart and am no more' ends on a note close to despair. v5-6, v11: every person is 'but a breath', 'a phantom', 'a vapor', bleak to someone already low. The only hope stated outright is v7; the result copy must point to it, because the ending will not.
psalms.fitNote: Partial but honest fit, no numbering error (LXX 38 = English 39, consistent with the neighbouring 40 and 41). Verse 1 matches the prescription exactly: a resolve to watch oneself while the wicked are present. But the enemy disappears after v1 (apart from 'the reproach of fools' in v8); the rest of the psalm is about how short life is and about God's discipline, not about holding out against an attacker. If the quiz uses it for 'I promised myself to do better and it is getting harder', the opening fits; do not sell it as a psalm about beating an enemy.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It begins at the end of a long wait: God heard, lifted him out of the pit and the miry clay, and gave him a new song (v1-3), which becomes praise and open testimony (v4-10). Then it drops back into trouble: evils without number and his own sins overtake him (v12), and he prays for quick help and for his attackers to be shamed. It closes poor and needy but still naming God as helper and deliverer, asking Him not to delay.

namesIt.text: I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry.

turn.text: May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You; may those who love Your salvation always say, “The LORD be magnified!”

lastLine.text: But I am poor and needy; may the Lord think of me. You are my helper and deliverer; O my God, do not delay.

psalms.hardParts: v12: 'my sins have overtaken me... my heart has failed within me' can land hard on a guilty or depressed reader. v14-15: wishing that those who seek his life be ashamed, confounded and humiliated (mild imprecation). v6-8 is quoted in Hebrews 10 of Christ; not hard, but a reader may be puzzled by 'Sacrifice and offering You did not desire'. Note the order: the rescue comes first and the trouble returns afterwards, so a reader may feel the hope 'wears off'; the ending keeps trust but is still waiting.
psalms.fitNote: Good fit, no numbering error (LXX 39 = English 40). Athanasius gives it to someone enduring hardship under attack who wants to learn what endurance gains, and v1-3 is exactly that: patient waiting answered by rescue and a new song. The second half (v12-17) shows the endurance still going on, which suits the prescription honestly.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Maskil of the sons of Korah.
psalms.movement: It opens with a thirst for God like a deer's for water, tears day and night, and people asking 'Where is your God?' He remembers leading worship in better days, then talks to his own soul: why so downcast? hope in God (v5). The sorrow comes back in waves (v6-10, 'Why have You forgotten me?'), but the same self-address returns as the last line, ending in hope, though not yet in relief.

namesIt.text: Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence.

turn.text: Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence.

lastLine.text: Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God.

psalms.hardParts: No curses or violence. v9 ('Why have You forgotten me?') and v7 ('all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me') say that the flood comes from God, which a hurting reader may find frightening, though it is honest. v3 and v10: the taunt 'Where is your God?' may echo what the reader hears from others or from inside. The hope is spoken to his own soul, not yet felt; the result copy should not promise that the feeling lifts.
psalms.fitNote: Excellent fit for both prescriptions, no numbering error (LXX 41 = English 42). §19: longing for God while enemies taunt (v1-3, v10) and comforting one's soul with hope (v5, v11). §28 quotes the refrain without a number; it stands in 42:5, 42:11 and 43:5. In Hebrew manuscripts Psalms 42 and 43 are generally read as one poem (shared refrain, 43 has no superscription), so the quiz may want to print 43 after 42.

psalms.movement: It opens as a courtroom plea: vindicate me, plead my case, deliver me from deceitful and unjust men, and asks why God seems to have rejected him. At v3 it turns: send Your light and truth to lead me back to Your dwelling, where he will praise God with the harp as his greatest joy. It ends with the same refrain as Psalm 42, telling his downcast soul to hope in God.

namesIt.text: Vindicate me, O God, and plead my case against an ungodly nation; deliver me from deceitful and unjust men.

turn.text: Send out Your light and Your truth; let them lead me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain and to the place where You dwell.

lastLine.text: Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God.

psalms.hardParts: v2: 'Why have You rejected me?' could confirm a reader's fear of rejection by God, though the psalm answers it at once. v1 asks God to judge an 'ungodly nation' and 'deceitful and unjust men'; it is not a curse, but the result must not suggest that the reader's opponents are ungodly. Nothing violent.
psalms.fitNote: Fits both prescriptions, no numbering error (LXX 42 = English 43). §17: the psalm leaves the verdict with God ('Vindicate me... plead my case'), which is exactly Athanasius's point. But Psalm 43 says nothing about 'hands full of blood' or murderous intent; that detail matches Psalm 26:9-10 (bloodthirsty men with wicked schemes in their hands), one of the other psalms §17 lists with it (26, 35, 43). Do not attach the bloodshed wording to 43. §28's refrain is 43:5. Best printed with Psalm 42 as one poem.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. Of the sons of Korah. According to Alamoth. A song.
psalms.movement: It opens by stating that God is refuge and strength, so there is no fear even if the earth gives way and the mountains fall into the sea. It moves to the calm of God's city with its river, where God helps at daybreak while nations rage, with a refrain: the LORD of Hosts is with us. It closes with an invitation to come and see His works, God's own word 'Be still and know that I am God', and the refrain again.

namesIt.text: God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble.

lastLine.text: The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah

psalms.hardParts: v8: 'who brings devastation upon the earth' may jar a reader who has just lived through a disaster. v2-3 and v6 are images of catastrophe and war, heavy for someone in real turmoil but all set inside God's protection. v10 'Be still' is often quoted as 'calm down'; in context it is God ending the war (v9), which should not be turned into advice to stop feeling.
psalms.fitNote: Fair fit, no numbering error (LXX 45 = English 46). Athanasius gives it to one who has been delivered, has taken refuge in God, and wants to thank Him and tell what He did. The refuge (v1, 7, 11) and the 'Come, see the works of the LORD' (v8) fit. But it is a 'we' song about a city and nations under threat, not a personal account of rescue, so 'tell of His mercy to yourself' is only a loose match. The result copy should say 'He was your refuge', not recount a personal story the psalm does not tell.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. When Nathan the prophet came to him after his adultery with Bathsheba.
psalms.movement: It opens with a plea for mercy, grounded in God's loving devotion, and a frank confession: my sin is always before me. From v7 it turns to confident asking (wash me and I will be clean; create in me a clean heart; restore the joy of Your salvation) and to a promise to teach others the way back. It ends with the assurance that God will not despise a broken and contrite heart, then a prayer for Jerusalem and its restored sacrifices.

namesIt.text: Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your loving devotion; according to Your great compassion, blot out my transgressions.

turn.text: Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.

lastLine.text: Then You will delight in righteous sacrifices, in whole burnt offerings; then bulls will be offered on Your altar.

psalms.hardParts: The superscription names adultery with Bathsheba, which may feel accusatory or heavy for readers carrying sexual sin or abuse. v5 ('sinful when my mother conceived me') can feed self-loathing if read without the plea for mercy around it. v4 ('Against You, You only, have I sinned') may seem to set aside the people actually harmed. v8 'the bones You have crushed' and v11 'take not Your Holy Spirit from me' may frighten an anxious conscience. v14 'bloodguilt'. The last line (v18-19, bulls on the altar) is a flat ending for a hurting reader and seems to contradict v16; the result copy should point to v17 as the real resolution.
psalms.fitNote: Exact fit, no numbering error (LXX 50 = English 51). §20 prescribes it for one who has sinned, is ashamed and repenting, and asks mercy; §12 names it as the psalm that stirs repentance when sung as one's own words. The whole psalm is that prayer.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Maskil of David. After Doeg the Edomite went to Saul and told him, “David has gone to the house of Ahimelech.”
psalms.movement: It opens by speaking straight to the boastful slanderer, setting his destructive tongue against God's loving devotion that endures all day long. Verses 2-7 expose the liar and announce that God will uproot him. At verse 8 the singer turns from the enemy to himself, a flourishing olive tree in God's house, and ends waiting on God's name among His saints.

namesIt.text: Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The loving devotion of God endures all day long.

turn.text: But I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God; I trust in the loving devotion of God forever and ever.

lastLine.text: I will praise You forever, because You have done it. I will wait on Your name— for it is good— in the presence of Your saints.

psalms.hardParts: 52:5 God will tear the liar from his tent and uproot him from the land of the living; 52:6-7 the righteous are pictured mocking the fallen evildoer, which can read as gloating.
psalms.fitNote: Honest fit. The superscription is David after Doeg informed on him to Saul, which is exactly being slandered before an evil ruler while the slanderer boasts (verse 1). Letter's 52 = English 52 (LXX 51); no numbering problem.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Mahalath. A Maskil of David.
psalms.movement: It starts with the fool who says there is no God and a sweeping verdict that no one does good. God looks down, and the corrupt who devour His people are suddenly overwhelmed with dread. It ends in a longing prayer that salvation would come from Zion and God's captive people would rejoice.

namesIt.text: The fool says in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt; their ways are vile. There is no one who does good.

turn.text: Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion! When God restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!

lastLine.text: Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion! When God restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!

psalms.hardParts: 53:1 and 53:3 say no one does good, not even one, which a guilt-laden reader may take as a verdict on themselves; 53:5 God scattering the bones of besiegers is violent imagery.
psalms.fitNote: Fits. Athanasius pairs it with Psalm 14 (a near-duplicate) for hearing people deny God's providence; the fool's 'There is no God' is practical denial that God sees or acts, and God looking down (verse 2) answers it. The 'pray, do not join them' part is carried only by the closing longing in verse 6, not by an explicit intercession. English 53 = LXX 52; no numbering problem.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Maskil of David. When the Ziphites went to Saul and said, “Is David not hiding among us?”
psalms.movement: It opens with an urgent plea for God to save and hear, because ruthless strangers are hunting the singer's life. At verse 4 it turns abruptly to confidence that God is his helper and sustainer. It ends in a freewill offering of praise, looking back as if deliverance from every trouble has already come.

namesIt.text: For strangers rise up against me, and ruthless men seek my life— men with no regard for God. Selah

turn.text: Surely God is my helper; the Lord is the sustainer of my soul.

lastLine.text: For He has delivered me from every trouble, and my eyes have looked in triumph on my foes.

psalms.hardParts: 54:5 asks God to destroy the enemies ('In Your faithfulness, destroy them'); 54:7 speaks of looking in triumph on foes.
psalms.fitNote: Exact fit for both uses. The superscription names the Ziphites betraying David's hiding place to Saul, precisely the informers Athanasius cites in §20, and the psalm is sung in the first person by the one hunted (§12). English 54 = LXX 53; no numbering problem.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Maskil of David.
psalms.movement: It starts restless and terrified, pounding heart and terrors of death, wishing for dove's wings to fly away from the city's malice. At its centre it names the deepest wound, that the betrayer is a close friend who once walked with him to God's house, and it turns to calling on God, Who hears morning, noon and night. It ends with the invitation to cast your burden on the LORD, a last word against the deceitful, and a plain 'But I will trust in You.'

namesIt.text: But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend.

turn.text: But I call to God, and the LORD saves me.

lastLine.text: But You, O God, will bring them down to the Pit of destruction; men of bloodshed and deceit will not live out half their days. But I will trust in You.

psalms.hardParts: 55:15 'Let death seize them by surprise; let them go down to Sheol alive' is a curse on the betrayers; 55:23 has God bringing them down to the Pit, so the final verse opens with judgment before its last clause of trust; 55:9 asks God to confound their speech. The turn is not clean: grief and anger recur after verse 16 (verses 20-21).
psalms.fitNote: Strong fit. Verses 12-14 and 20-21 are exactly enemies' insults plus slander from people once thought friends, and verse 22 supplies the comfort Athanasius points to. English 55 = LXX 54; no numbering problem.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “A Dove on Distant Oaks.” A Miktam of David, when the Philistines seized him in Gath.
psalms.movement: It opens hounded all day by attackers, and almost at once (verse 3) decides to trust in fear, a refrain that returns in verses 4 and 10-11. Between the refrains it describes words twisted and steps watched, and asks God to keep every tear in His bottle. It ends in vows and thanksgiving for a soul delivered from death, walking before God in the light of life.

namesIt.text: They conspire, they lurk, they watch my steps while they wait to take my life.

turn.text: When I am afraid, I put my trust in You.

lastLine.text: For You have delivered my soul from death, and my feet from stumbling, that I may walk before God in the light of life.

psalms.hardParts: 56:7 'In Your anger, O God, cast down the nations' asks for judgment on the enemies. Otherwise gentle; 56:8 (tears in God's bottle) is one of the most consoling lines for a hurting reader.
psalms.fitNote: Exact fit. The superscription names the Philistines seizing David in Gath, the 'strangers' Athanasius pairs with the Ziphites, and verses 5-6 describe being watched, twisted and hunted. English 56 = LXX 55; no numbering problem.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A Miktam of David, when he fled from Saul into the cave.
psalms.movement: It opens already taking refuge, sheltering in the shadow of God's wings until the danger passes, while the singer lies among lions whose teeth are spears. Verse 6 admits the soul was despondent before a net and a pit, then sees the hunters fall into it. From verse 7 the heart is steadfast and the psalm rises into dawn-waking praise, ending on God exalted above the heavens.

namesIt.text: Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy, for in You my soul takes refuge. In the shadow of Your wings I will take shelter until the danger has passed.

turn.text: My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast. I will sing and make music.

lastLine.text: Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth.

psalms.hardParts: Little to stumble on: 57:4 (lions, spears, swords) is vivid but not a curse; 57:6 has the enemies falling into their own pit, which is reversal rather than a request for harm.
psalms.fitNote: Exact fit. The superscription is David fleeing from Saul into the cave, the very scene Athanasius cites in §20 (Saul entering the cave unknowing), and the whole psalm is sung by the hunted one in the first person (§12). English 57 = LXX 56; no numbering problem.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A Miktam of David.
psalms.movement: It opens by challenging rulers who sound just but plan injustice in their hearts, then describes them as liars from birth, like a snake that will not listen. The middle is a string of fierce requests that God break their power and make them vanish. It ends with people seeing that there really is a God who judges the earth and rewards the righteous.

namesIt.text: No, in your hearts you devise injustice; with your hands you mete out violence on the earth.

turn.text: Then men will say, “There is surely a reward for the righteous! There is surely a God who judges the earth!”

lastLine.text: Then men will say, “There is surely a reward for the righteous! There is surely a God who judges the earth!”

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 58:6 (shatter their teeth, tear out the fangs); 58:8 (like a slug dissolving, like a stillborn child: may they never see the sun), which could wound anyone who has lost a baby; 58:10 (the righteous wash their feet in the blood of the wicked); 58:3 (the wicked estranged from the womb) can read as fatalism about people. Almost the whole psalm is imprecation; the only hope is the last verse.
psalms.fitNote: Fits. Athanasius (§20) uses it against hypocrites who make a show; the psalm opens on exactly that gap between just-sounding speech and unjust hearts (vv. 1-2). The number is correct (LXX 57 = English 58). The fit is honest but the psalm is one of the harshest in the Psalter, so as a result for a hurting person it needs care: the comfort lies only in v. 11, that God does judge.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A Miktam of David, when Saul sent men to watch David’s house in order to kill him.
psalms.movement: It starts with a cry for rescue from men lying in wait without cause, pictured as dogs prowling the city at night. At v. 8 it turns: God laughs at them, and the singer resolves to keep watch for God, his fortress, even while the prowling refrain returns. It ends in the morning with songs of God's strength and loving devotion.

namesIt.text: But I will sing of Your strength and proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning. For You are my fortress, my refuge in times of trouble.

turn.text: But You, O LORD, laugh at them; You scoff at all the nations.

lastLine.text: To You, O my strength, I sing praises, for You, O God, are my fortress, my God of loving devotion.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 59:5 (show no mercy to the wicked traitors); 59:11-13 (scatter them, bring them down, consume them in wrath till they are no more); 59:6 and 59:14-15 (enemies as snarling, scavenging dogs).
psalms.fitNote: Fits exactly and the number is right (LXX 58 = English 59). The superscription itself names the situation Athanasius gives in §20: Saul had men watch David's house to kill him, and David escaped. The night-to-morning movement (vv. 6, 14 against v. 16) suits his instruction to give thanks and keep it as a memorial of deliverance.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Jeduthun. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It begins already at rest: God alone is rock, salvation and fortress. In the middle it names people who threaten and try to topple the singer like a leaning wall, then answers them by telling his own soul again to rest in God and calling others to pour out their hearts to Him. It ends on what God has spoken: power and loving devotion belong to Him, and He repays each person justly.

namesIt.text: How long will you threaten a man? Will all of you throw him down like a leaning wall or a tottering fence?

lastLine.text: and loving devotion to You, O Lord. For You will repay each man according to his deeds.

psalms.hardParts: Little. Psalm 62:12 (You will repay each man according to his deeds) could unsettle someone already carrying guilt; 62:9 (people are but a vapor) may feel bleak out of context.
psalms.fitNote: Fits well, number right (LXX 61 = English 62). Athanasius (§20) says to meet those who would take your life by submitting all the more to the Lord; the psalm answers the attackers of vv. 3-4 with v. 5's call to rest in God alone. Note that his 'submit' echoes the Greek of v. 1 ('shall not my soul be subject to God?'); the BSB's 'my soul finds rest' carries the same idea as quiet trust rather than submission. It never needs to turn because it starts in trust.

psalms.superscription: A Psalm of David, when he was in the Wilderness of Judah.
psalms.movement: It opens in a dry land with a soul thirsting and seeking God. It moves into memory and satisfaction: God's loving devotion is better than life, and in the night watches the singer clings to Him under the shadow of His wings. It ends with those who seek his life falling and the king rejoicing in God.

namesIt.text: O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You. My body yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water.

lastLine.text: But the king will rejoice in God; all who swear by Him will exult, for the mouths of liars will be shut.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 63:9-10 (those who seek my life go into the depths, fall by the sword, become a portion for foxes).
psalms.fitNote: Fits, number right (LXX 62 = English 63). The superscription places David in the wilderness of Judah, the situation Athanasius names in §20. His 'at daybreak' comes from the Greek of v. 1 ('early will I seek You'); the BSB renders it 'Earnestly I seek You', so the daybreak detail is not visible in this translation. The longing is not lament, so the psalm stays in trust throughout.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It starts with a complaint and a plea to be kept from dread of enemies who sharpen their tongues like swords, ambush the innocent and boast of secret plans no one will see. At v. 7 it turns: God shoots them suddenly, and their own tongues bring them down. It ends with all people pondering God's work and the upright rejoicing and taking refuge in Him.

namesIt.text: Hear, O God, my voice of complaint; preserve my life from dread of the enemy.

turn.text: But God will shoot them with arrows; suddenly they will be wounded.

lastLine.text: Let the righteous rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in Him; let all the upright in heart exult.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 64:7-8 (God shoots them with arrows; their own tongues turned against them). Mild compared with Psalms 58 and 59.
psalms.fitNote: Fits, number right (LXX 63 = English 64): ambush, secret plotting and 'Who will see them?' (vv. 4-6) match the enemies who lie in wait and search things out in §20. But the image Athanasius quotes, their blows being a child's toy arrows, comes from the Greek of v. 7 ('the arrows of babes became their wounds'). The BSB follows the Hebrew and reads 'God will shoot them with arrows', so the children's-arrows line he points to is not in the BSB text; do not claim it is.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. A song.
psalms.movement: It opens with praise waiting for God in Zion, the God who hears prayer and atones for sins that overwhelm. It widens to God's might in forming mountains and stilling the roaring seas and the tumult of the nations. It ends in a harvest scene of watered fields, overflowing pastures and valleys that sing.

namesIt.text: When iniquities prevail against me, You atone for our transgressions.

lastLine.text: The pastures are clothed with flocks, and the valleys are decked with grain. They shout in triumph; indeed, they sing.

psalms.hardParts: None.
psalms.fitNote: Weak fit; flag it. Athanasius lists Psalms 64, 65, 70 and 71 together in §20 for enemies who keep terrifying and hunting you, and the numbering looks consistent (LXX 64 = English 65, his list being LXX 63, 64, 69, 70). But English 65 is a harvest praise psalm with no enemies in it. The only link is v. 3, which in the Greek reads 'the words of the lawless overpowered us' (an outside threat), while the BSB reads 'iniquities prevail against me' (the singer's own sins), plus God stilling 'the tumult of the nations' (v. 7). Do not use Psalm 65 as the result for the fear-of-enemies situation; Psalm 64 carries it honestly.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm. A song.
psalms.movement: It opens by asking God to be gracious and let His face shine on His people. That request widens straight into a call for every nation to praise Him. It ends on a harvest already given and a blessing that reaches the ends of the earth.

namesIt.text: May God be gracious to us and bless us, and cause His face to shine upon us, Selah

lastLine.text: God blesses us, that all the ends of the earth shall fear Him.

psalms.fitNote: Fits. §21 pairs asking for mercy with praising God, and this psalm does both at once: verse 1 asks for grace (the Septuagint opens 'God be merciful to us'), and the rest is praise. The conversion is consistent: LXX 66 = English 67. One caution: it is a prayer for the whole community ('us', 'the nations'), not one person's plea, so a reader carrying a private burden gets a hopeful and generous psalm, not one that names their own pain.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. Of David. To bring remembrance.
psalms.movement: It opens with an urgent plea for God to hurry and help. Next it asks that those who hunt the speaker's life be turned back in shame, and it prays that everyone who seeks God will rejoice. It ends still in need, but naming God as helper and deliverer, so the trust sits inside the plea rather than after it.

namesIt.text: May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded; may those who wish me harm be repelled and humiliated.

turn.text: But I am poor and needy; hurry to me, O God. You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay.

lastLine.text: But I am poor and needy; hurry to me, O God. You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 70:2-3 ask that the speaker's enemies be shamed, humiliated and driven back. It is mild, with no curse of death, but a reader told to love their enemies may hesitate over it. It also ends without resolution ('do not delay'), so someone looking for comfort gets trust held under pressure, not relief.
psalms.fitNote: Fits the part about being hunted: people seeking the speaker's life, gloating 'Aha, aha!' (verse 3). It is short and urgent, not a sustained picture of enemies lying in wait. The 'children's arrows' image in §20 is not in this psalm. It comes from LXX 63 = English Psalm 64:7, which the same sentence also lists. The conversion is consistent (LXX 69 = English 70), so this is not a numbering error. English 70 is almost word for word the same as Psalm 40:13-17.

psalms.movement: It opens by taking refuge in God and asking not to be put to shame, recalling a trust that goes back to birth. In the middle it names enemies who say God has abandoned the speaker, and it pleads not to be discarded in old age. From verse 14 it becomes steadily hopeful, promising praise more and more and trusting God to raise the speaker again from the depths. It ends with a pledge to tell of His righteousness all day long.

namesIt.text: For my enemies speak against me, and those who lie in wait for my life conspire,

turn.text: But I will always hope and will praise You more and more.

lastLine.text: My tongue will indeed proclaim Your righteousness all day long, for those who seek my harm are disgraced and confounded.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 71:11 quotes the enemies saying 'God has forsaken him', which may sting someone who already fears it (the psalm answers it, but the words are there). Psalm 71:13 asks that accusers be 'consumed' and covered with scorn. The last verse, 71:24, closes on the enemies being disgraced, so the final note is partly about their shame. Psalm 71:20 ('You have shown me many troubles') presents hardship as coming from God's hand.
psalms.fitNote: Fits well. Verses 10-11 give exactly the §20 picture of enemies lying in wait and plotting for the speaker's life. The steady refusal to give up, from verse 14 on, matches 'do not give in'. The conversion is consistent (LXX 70 = English 71). As with Psalm 70, the 'children's arrows' image belongs to English Psalm 64:7, not to this psalm. It has no superscription in the Hebrew or the BSB. It is among the best psalms in this set for a hurting reader, because its hope is spelled out and grows to the end.

psalms.superscription: A Psalm of Asaph.
psalms.movement: It opens by saying God is good, then admits the speaker nearly fell away out of envy of the prosperous wicked, and that keeping a pure heart seemed pointless. The turn comes in the sanctuary, where the speaker sees how the wicked end and recognises how bitter and senseless their own thinking had been. It ends in closeness: God holds the speaker's hand, is their portion forever, and it is good to draw near to Him.

namesIt.text: For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.

turn.text: until I entered God’s sanctuary; then I discerned their end.

lastLine.text: But as for me, it is good to draw near to God. I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may proclaim all Your works.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 73:18-20 describes God casting the wicked into ruin and sweeping them away 'by terrors'. Psalm 73:27 says God destroys all who are unfaithful to Him, which an anxious reader may apply to themselves. In Psalm 73:22 the speaker calls himself 'senseless and ignorant' and 'a brute beast', and someone ashamed of their envy could take that as harsh self-contempt. Psalm 73:14 ('punished every morning') can sound like God is punishing the sufferer.
psalms.fitNote: Fits both uses squarely. §21 (the wicked at peace while the righteous suffer) is the whole first half, especially verses 3-14. §28 quotes 'My feet were almost gone', which is this psalm's verse 2 ('my steps had nearly slipped'), so the slip-and-admission use is confirmed by the letter's own quotation. The conversion is consistent (LXX 72 = English 73). This psalm has the clearest and fullest turn of the six (verses 23-26).

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster: To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A Psalm of Asaph. A song.
psalms.movement: It opens in shared thanks because God's Name is near. Then God Himself speaks as the judge who picks the time, holds up the shaking earth and warns the proud not to boast. It ends with the speaker vowing to praise Him forever and God promising to cut down the wicked and raise up the righteous.

namesIt.text: We give thanks to You, O God; we give thanks, for Your Name is near. The people declare Your wondrous works.

lastLine.text: “All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous will be exalted.”

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 75:8 has the cup of foaming wine in the LORD's hand that all the wicked must drink 'to the dregs', an image of God's wrath. Psalm 75:10 ends on God cutting off the horns of the wicked. Most of the psalm is God speaking in judgment, not comfort, so a hurting reader gets reassurance that God judges fairly more than tenderness.
psalms.fitNote: Fits §21 well: the opening verse is thankful public acknowledgement of God and His wondrous works, which is the exomologesis sense. For §15 (thanks after being heard in distress) it fits only halfway: the thanks is there, but the psalm never mentions distress, a cry or an answer. It sits in that list beside English 4 and 116, which do. The conversion looks consistent: LXX 74 = English 75, which opens 'We give thanks to You', and LXX 114 = English 116 in the same list fits exactly. So this is a thin fit, not a numbering error. For a result about being rescued, Psalm 116 (or 4) would carry more of the reader's situation.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Jeduthun. A Psalm of Asaph.
psalms.movement: It opens with a sleepless night of crying out to God, refusing comfort and too troubled to speak. Next it asks the rawest questions in the set: whether God has rejected them for good, forgotten to be gracious, let His promise fail. The turn is a deliberate act of remembering God's past wonders, and the psalm ends retelling the Exodus: God leading His people through the sea like a flock, His footprints unseen.

namesIt.text: In the day of trouble I sought the Lord; through the night my outstretched hands did not grow weary; my soul refused to be comforted.

turn.text: I will remember the works of the LORD; yes, I will remember Your wonders of old.

lastLine.text: You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 77:7-9 asks outright whether the Lord will spurn forever, whether His loving devotion is gone and whether God has forgotten to be gracious.
