That will resonate, but it may unsettle a reader who is not told the psalm moves past it. Psalm 77:4 says God has kept the speaker's eyes from closing. Psalm 77:19 says God's footprints 'were not to be found', which is honest about His hiddenness. The ending is a memory of the Exodus, not a personal rescue, so the hope is 'He has done it before', not 'it is over'. There are no curses or violence against people.
psalms.fitNote: Partial fit. It matches the heart of §21: badly pressed and shaken, praying instead of despairing, with thanks in view. But English 77 never mentions enemies or a refuge taken from the speaker; the trouble is inner and unnamed. The letter's 'when your cry is heard' echoes the Septuagint verse 1 ('He gave heed to me'), but the BSB renders it as a request ('to hear me'), so the psalm as printed does not say the cry was answered. The conversion is consistent: LXX 76 = English 77, and the neighbouring pairings in the same passage (English 76 for 'God is known in Judah', English 79 for the defiled temple) line up. This is not a numbering error, but the enemy framing should not be promised on the result page.

psalms.superscription: A Psalm of Asaph.
psalms.movement: It opens on a ruined sanctuary and unburied dead, then asks how long God's anger will last and pleads for mercy, forgiveness and vengeance on the invaders. Only in the last verse does it turn: once rescued, God's people, His flock, will thank Him forever and pass His praise down the generations.

namesIt.text: They have given the corpses of Your servants as food to the birds of the air, the flesh of Your saints to the beasts of the earth.

turn.text: Then we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture, will thank You forever; from generation to generation we will declare Your praise.

lastLine.text: Then we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture, will thank You forever; from generation to generation we will declare Your praise.

psalms.hardParts: Graphic slaughter and unburied bodies (79:2-3). Prayers for wrath and vengeance on the nations (79:6, 79:10) and for sevenfold payback on the neighbours (79:12). The link between the disaster and 'past sins' (79:8-9) may read as blame to someone whose suffering was not their fault.
psalms.fitNote: A clear, exact fit. Athanasius's picture of a defiled house of God, slain saints and bodies left to the birds is verses 1-3 almost word for word. No sign of a numbering error. For the quiz, note that this is a communal lament over a public atrocity, not a private sorrow; it fits someone grieving for other people's suffering (persecuted Christians, a community struck by violence) better than someone carrying a personal wound.

psalms.superscription: A song. A Psalm of Asaph.
psalms.movement: It opens by begging God not to stay silent, then names a whole coalition of nations plotting to wipe out His people. From verse 9 it recalls God's old victories (Midian, Sisera, Oreb and Zeeb) and asks Him to do it again, and it ends by asking that the enemies be shamed until they know the Lord alone is Most High.

namesIt.text: For with one mind they plot together; they form an alliance against You—

turn.text: Do to them as You did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon,

lastLine.text: May they know that You alone, whose name is the LORD, are Most High over all the earth.

psalms.hardParts: Long imprecation (83:9-17): enemies turned into 'dung on the ground' (83:10), burned like a forest (83:14), 'may they perish in disgrace' (83:17). A list of named nations and a plot to erase 'Israel' (83:4-8) can be heard today as a comment on present-day Middle East politics. Some mercy in it: 83:16 asks for shame so 'that they may seek Your name'.
psalms.fitNote: A good fit: enemies massed on every side (83:5-8) and plotting against God's people (83:3-4). The anchor of hope Athanasius points to sits in the memory of past deliverances (83:9-12) and in the closing confession that the Lord alone is Most High (83:18), not in any stated trust. No numbering error. The hope here is implicit, so the result page may need to point to 83:9 and 83:18 for a hurting reader.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Gittith. A Psalm of the sons of Korah.
psalms.movement: It opens with delight in God's dwelling and a longing that makes the soul faint, even envying the sparrow that nests near His altar. It follows pilgrims who turn a dry valley into springs and go from strength to strength, and it ends by blessing the one who trusts in the Lord, Who withholds no good thing.

namesIt.text: My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD; my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God.

lastLine.text: O LORD of Hosts, how blessed is the man who trusts in You!

psalms.fitNote: An exact fit: longing for God's house and dwelling (84:1-2, 84:10). Athanasius's 'as the Apostle did' points to Paul's longing to depart and be with Christ, which suits a reading of the courts as God's eternal dwelling. No numbering error. It has no dark turn to manage; the ache in it is longing, not pain, and 84:6 (the Valley of Baca becoming springs) speaks gently to anyone longing for God in a hard season.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of the sons of Korah.
psalms.movement: It opens with thanks for mercies already given: captivity reversed, sin forgiven, anger withdrawn. Then it surprisingly turns back to pleading (restore us, will You be angry forever?), and from verse 8 it listens for God's answer, which comes as peace: love and faithfulness meet, righteousness and peace kiss, the land yields its harvest, and righteousness prepares His way.

namesIt.text: You showed favor to Your land, O LORD; You restored Jacob from captivity.

turn.text: I will listen to what God the LORD will say; for He will surely speak peace to His people and His saints; He will not let them return to folly.

lastLine.text: Righteousness will go before Him to prepare the way for His steps.

psalms.hardParts: 85:2-3 ties the restoration to forgiven sin and withdrawn fury, which a reader whose trouble was not their fault might hear as blame. 85:5 ('Will You be angry with us forever?') puts God's anger on the page again after the rescue, which may unsettle someone who has just come through.
psalms.fitNote: A good fit for the opening, where 85:1-3 is thanks after captivity and after anger is spent. The middle (85:4-7) is fresh pleading, so the psalm is not pure thanksgiving; it suits the honest state of 'freed, but not yet whole'. No numbering error; captivity and turned-away anger are exactly Athanasius's words. His 'their anger' may mean the enemies' anger from the preceding sentence, where the psalm speaks of God's; the gap is small.

psalms.superscription: A prayer of David.
psalms.movement: It opens as the plea of someone poor and needy, weaving requests with reasons for trust (God is kind, forgiving, answers when called). In the middle it breaks into praise and a prayer for an undivided heart, then names the threat: ruthless men seeking the speaker's life. It answers that at once with the confession of God's compassion and ends asking for a sign, sure He has already helped and comforted.

namesIt.text: The arrogant rise against me, O God; a band of ruthless men seeks my life; they have no regard for You.

turn.text: But You, O Lord, are a compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.

lastLine.text: Show me a sign of Your goodness, that my enemies may see and be ashamed; for You, O LORD, have helped me and comforted me.

psalms.hardParts: 'Preserve my soul, for I am godly' (86:2) may read as self-righteous, or may shut out a reader who feels far from godly. 86:17 wishes shame on enemies, but mildly. Otherwise gentle.
psalms.fitNote: A clear fit: people rising against the speaker and seeking his life (86:14), with the whole psalm as a prayer to God in distress (86:7). Consistent with LXX 85 = English 86, so no numbering error. One of the best results for a hurting reader: trust runs all through it, and it ends on 'helped me and comforted me'.

psalms.superscription: A song. A Psalm of the sons of Korah. For the choirmaster. According to Mahalath Leannoth. A Maskil of Heman the Ezrahite.
psalms.movement: It opens by calling on the Lord as 'God of my salvation' and crying day and night, then goes down: near death, counted among the dead, laid by God in the lowest pit, friends taken away, shut in with no way out. It asks whether the dead can praise God, cries again in the morning, asks why He hides His face, and ends in darkness, with no word of rescue.

namesIt.text: You have removed my friends from me; You have made me repulsive to them; I am confined and cannot escape.

lastLine.text: You have removed my beloved and my friend; darkness is my closest companion.

psalms.hardParts: The whole psalm. God is named as the source of the suffering (88:6-8, 88:14-18: 'Your wrath has swept over me; Your terrors have destroyed me'). The questions about the dead (88:10-12) can sound like despair of any afterlife. It ends on darkness (88:18) with no turn, which a depressed or suicidal reader could take as confirmation. The only hope is that the speaker keeps praying to 'the God of my salvation' (88:1, 88:9, 88:13); the site would have to point this out gently, without adding a resolution the psalm does not give.
psalms.fitNote: A partial fit. Athanasius prescribes it (with 17, 86 and 140) for praying against enemies who hem you in. Psalm 88 has the hemming in ('I am confined and cannot escape', 88:8; 'they enclose me on every side', 88:17) but NO human enemies: the pressure comes from illness, near death, abandonment by friends and God's own terrors. The numbering is probably not wrong: LXX 87 = English 88, it matches the letter's pattern for 86 and 87, and the neighbouring psalm (English 89) would fit no better. The honest pairing for the quiz is 'shut in, isolated, and hemmed in on every side', not 'opposed by people'. Note that this is the darkest psalm in the Psalter, which bears on whether it should ever be a quiz result without care.

psalms.superscription: A Psalm. A song for the Sabbath day.
psalms.movement: It opens by saying it is good to praise the LORD morning and night, and gives the reason: He has made the singer glad by His deeds. In the middle it sets the wicked, who spring up like grass and are gone, against the LORD, who is exalted forever (v. 8). It ends with the righteous planted in God's house like a palm and a cedar, still bearing fruit in old age and proclaiming that He is upright.

namesIt.text: It is good to praise the LORD, and to sing praises to Your name, O Most High,

lastLine.text: to proclaim, “The LORD is upright; He is my Rock, and in Him there is no unrighteousness.”

psalms.hardParts: Verses 7, 9 and 11 look forward to the destruction of evildoers, and v. 11 takes it personally: the singer's eyes see the enemies fall and his ears hear their wailing. Someone who has been hurt by a particular person may read that as permission to gloat. Verse 10 (a horn like a wild ox, anointed with oil) is obscure imagery that needs a gloss.
psalms.fitNote: Strong fit, with no numbering error. This is Septuagint 91, whose first line in Greek uses the very verb Athanasius has in mind: it is good to give thanks to (openly acknowledge) the Lord. The BSB translates it "praise", so the English hides the word Athanasius was pointing to, but the sense is the same. It is a psalm for someone who already has something to be thankful for. It does not comfort anyone in distress.

psalms.superscription: A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It opens with a song of God's loving devotion and justice, then asks "when will You come to me?" The rest is a king's vows: to walk with integrity at home, keep worthless things from his eyes, and keep slanderers, the proud and liars away from his house. It ends with a vow to purge the wicked from the city of the LORD every morning. It never laments and never turns. It moves from praise to resolve.

namesIt.text: I will sing of Your loving devotion and justice; to You, O LORD, I will sing praises.

lastLine.text: Every morning I will remove all the wicked of the land, that I may cut off every evildoer from the city of the LORD.

psalms.hardParts: Verses 5, 7 and 8 are a ruler's vows to silence slanderers, refuse the proud, and "cut off every evildoer" every morning. Read as personal rules, they sound harsh and like shutting people out. The run of "I will" vows of blamelessness (vv. 2-4) can also feel like a standard of perfection that a struggling reader already knows they fall short of. Verse 3 says "I hate the work of those who fall away", which could sting someone who has drifted from faith.
psalms.fitNote: It fits, with no numbering error (Septuagint 100 = English 101). Verse 1 is exactly the mercy-and-judgment pairing Athanasius names (LXX "mercy and judgment", BSB "loving devotion and justice"), and v. 2's "when will You come to me?" matches the wish to draw near. But this is a psalm of resolve, not consolation: it answers God's mercy with vows of integrity. It will not make a hurting person feel seen. It suits someone who has come through a correction and wants to start again clean.

psalms.superscription: A prayer of one who is afflicted, when he grows faint and pours out his lament before the LORD.
psalms.movement: It opens with a plea not to hide God's face, then a long, bodily description of wasting away: days like smoke, forgetting to eat, lying awake like a lone bird on a housetop. At v. 12 it turns to the LORD enthroned forever, who will rebuild Zion and hear the prisoner's groaning. It slips back once into the singer's broken strength (vv. 23-24), then ends on God, Who remains the same while heaven and earth wear out like a garment, and on the children of His servants living in safety.

namesIt.text: My heart is afflicted, and withered like grass; I even forget to eat my bread.

turn.text: But You, O LORD, sit enthroned forever; Your renown endures to all generations.

lastLine.text: The children of Your servants will dwell securely, and their descendants will be established before You.”

psalms.hardParts: Verse 10 says the suffering comes from God's "indignation and wrath" and that He has "picked me up and cast me aside". A depressed reader could take that as confirmation that God has rejected them. Verse 23 ("He has broken my strength on the way; He has cut short my days") and the plea in v. 24 not to be taken "in the midst of my days" may frighten someone who is ill. Verse 8 has enemies taunting and cursing. The middle section (vv. 13-22) is about Zion and the nations, which may feel far from one person's private exhaustion unless it is explained.
psalms.fitNote: Exact fit, with no numbering error (Septuagint 101 = English 102). The psalm's own superscription describes the state Athanasius names: afflicted, growing faint, pouring out a complaint. Verses 3-11 describe listless weakness better than any other psalm in this batch. It is the best comfort psalm here, and it has a real turn.

psalms.superscription: Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens with the singer ordering his own soul to bless the LORD and not forget His benefits: forgiveness, healing, redemption from the Pit, youth renewed like the eagle's. The middle rests on God's compassion: slow to anger, sins removed as far as east from west, a Father Who knows we are dust. Human life is as short as grass, but His loving devotion lasts forever. It ends by calling angels, hosts and all His works to bless Him, and comes back to "Bless the LORD, O my soul!"

namesIt.text: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds—

lastLine.text: Bless the LORD, all His works in all places of His dominion. Bless the LORD, O my soul!

psalms.hardParts: Verse 3 ("heals all your diseases") can wound someone living with an illness that has not been healed, or grieving someone who was not. Verses 15-16 on how short human life is (like grass, "its place remembers it no more") may land heavily on someone who is grieving. Verses 17-18 limit the promise to "those who fear Him" and "keep His covenant", which an anxious or scrupulous reader may feel shut out of. Verse 9 mentions God's anger, though only to say it will not last.
psalms.fitNote: Exact fit, with no numbering error (Septuagint 102 = English 103). The refrain "Bless the LORD, O my soul" is literally the singer stirring up his own soul to bless God, which is what Athanasius describes. Placed straight after 102, as he places it, it is the natural lift out of weariness. Although it is a praise psalm, much of what it praises (forgiveness, compassion, a Father Who remembers we are dust) is itself comfort.

psalms.movement: It opens with "Bless the LORD, O my soul!" and the LORD robed in light, stretching out the heavens. It then tours creation: the waters bounded, springs in the valleys, bread and wine for people, homes for birds, goats and badgers, moon and sun, lions by night, people at work by day, the teeming sea. Every creature waits on God for food and breath, and He renews the face of the earth. It ends with the singer vowing to sing all his life and closes as it began.

namesIt.text: Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, You are very great; You are clothed with splendor and majesty.

lastLine.text: May sinners vanish from the earth and the wicked be no more. Bless the LORD, O my soul. Hallelujah!

psalms.hardParts: The last verse (v. 35) begins with a wish that sinners vanish from the earth. It arrives abruptly after a gentle hymn, and it is the note the printed result would end on. Verse 29 ("when You take away their breath, they die and return to dust") may land hard on someone who is grieving. The psalm hardly mentions the singer's own situation, so a hurting reader may find it beautiful but impersonal unless the page frames it as lifting the eyes away from oneself.
psalms.fitNote: Good fit, with no numbering error (Septuagint 103 = English 104). It shares the "Bless the LORD, O my soul" frame with 103, and Athanasius pairs the two as the thankful answer to 102. It is praise of God in creation, not thanks for a personal rescue. So it fits the "stir your soul to bless Him in all circumstances" half of his description, not a specific trouble.

psalms.movement: It opens with a call to give thanks to the LORD and make His deeds known among the nations, and to remember His wonders. Then it retells the history: the covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, protection while they were few and strangers, Joseph sold as a slave and then raised to rule, Israel in Egypt, Moses and the plagues, the Exodus, the cloud, the quail, water from the rock. It ends with the people brought out with rejoicing and given the land so that they might keep His laws, and closes with "Hallelujah!"

namesIt.text: Give thanks to the LORD, call upon His name; make known His deeds among the nations.

lastLine.text: that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws. Hallelujah!

psalms.hardParts: Verse 25 says God turned the Egyptians' hearts to hate His people. Verses 28-36 list the plagues, ending in v. 36 with the striking of all the firstborn, which is the death of children. Verse 44 speaks of inheriting "the fruit of others’ labor" in conquered lands. The story is national, not personal. The part most likely to help a hurting reader is Joseph (vv. 17-22): sold, shackled, then proved right and freed. It is worth pointing out on the result page.
psalms.fitNote: Exact fit, with no numbering error (Septuagint 104 = English 105). Its first word in Greek is the same verb Athanasius uses ("Give thanks to / acknowledge the Lord"), and v. 1 adds "make known His deeds among the nations", which is the open, public acknowledgement he means. It suits someone with cause for gratitude, not someone in distress.

psalms.movement: It opens with a call to give thanks and a personal plea to share in God's favour (vv. 1-5), then turns into a long national confession: 'We have sinned like our fathers' (v. 6), followed by a catalogue of Israel's forgetfulness and rebellion from the Red Sea to Canaan and the judgments that followed (vv. 7-43). The hinge is v. 44, where God hears their cry and remembers His covenant anyway; it closes with a plea to be gathered so that they may give thanks, and a doxology (vv. 47-48).

namesIt.text: Hallelujah! Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.

turn.text: Nevertheless He heard their cry; He took note of their distress.

lastLine.text: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Let all the people say, “Amen!” Hallelujah!

psalms.hardParts: Most of the psalm is a record of sin and punishment: a wasting disease sent in answer to craving (v. 15); the earth swallowing Dathan and fire consuming the wicked (vv. 17-18); God swearing to cast them down and scatter them (vv. 26-27); a plague (v. 29); the complaint that they did not destroy the peoples as commanded (v. 34), which reads as endorsing conquest; child sacrifice to demons and the land polluted with blood (vv. 37-38); 'He abhorred His own inheritance' (v. 40). A hurting reader could hear 'your trouble is your punishment' in vv. 40-43 before reaching the mercy of vv. 44-46.
psalms.fitNote: Fits, but only at its frame, not its body. The letter (section 21) lists it among psalms for testifying to or acknowledging God, and in LXX it (LXX 105) opens with the same 'Give thanks / acknowledge the Lord' formula as 107, so the English number 106 is correct here, not a numbering slip. Elsewhere (section 21) the letter also groups it with psalms that recall God's kindness to the fathers and 'how ungrateful are men', which is what the long middle actually is. Someone who wants to thank God will find thanks in vv. 1-2 and 47-48 and a confession of ingratitude in between; exomologesis covers both senses, so it is honest, but it is the least purely 'thankful' of this group and should not be the lead result for a person arriving in gratitude.

psalms.movement: It opens by calling 'the redeemed of the LORD' to give thanks (vv. 1-3), then tells four short stories of people in trouble (lost wanderers, prisoners in darkness, the sick near death, sailors in a storm); each time 'they cried out to the LORD in their trouble' and He delivered them, followed by a refrain to thank Him (vv. 4-32). It widens into a hymn about God reversing fortunes, turning desert to springs and lifting the needy (vv. 33-42), and ends by telling the wise to consider the LORD's loving devotion (v. 43).

namesIt.text: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.

turn.text: Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He delivered them from their distress.

lastLine.text: Let him who is wise pay heed to these things and consider the loving devotion of the LORD.

psalms.hardParts: Two of the four stories tie the suffering to the sufferer's own rebellion or folly: prisoners who 'rebelled against the words of God' (v. 11) and 'Fools, in their rebellious ways' who suffered for their iniquities (v. 17); a reader in illness or depression could take that as blame. God is said to raise the tempest (v. 25) and to turn fruitful land into salt because of wickedness (vv. 33-34), and He 'pours out contempt on the nobles' (v. 40). All mild beside the psalm's repeated rescue.
psalms.fitNote: Fits very well. Listed in section 21 among psalms for thankful acknowledgement of God; in LXX it is 106 and opens with the 'Give thanks' (exomologeisthe) call, and English 107 is the correct conversion. Note that this is the psalm whose refrain 'they cried out to the LORD in their trouble' the online copy elsewhere wrongly attributes to 105, which confirms the known inconsistency but does not affect this pairing. The psalm is thanksgiving from start to finish and is specifically about saying aloud what God has done ('Let the redeemed of the LORD say so', v. 2).

psalms.superscription: A song. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It begins in settled, eager praise: a steadfast heart that will wake the dawn and thank God among the nations (vv. 1-5, the same words as Psalm 57:7-11). It then becomes a prayer for rescue and victory, quoting a divine oracle over the lands of Israel and its neighbours (vv. 6-9, as Psalm 60:5-8), dips into the question 'Have You not rejected us, O God?' (v. 11), and ends in confident trust that with God they will prevail (vv. 12-13).

namesIt.text: I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing Your praises among the peoples.

turn.text: With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies.

lastLine.text: With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies.

psalms.hardParts: The second half is a war prayer: the oracle of vv. 7-9 ('Moab is My washbasin; upon Edom I toss My sandal') is obscure tribal-conquest imagery a modern reader will not follow without a note; v. 11 asks whether God has rejected His people; the last line has God trampling enemies (v. 13).
psalms.fitNote: Half fits. Section 21 lists it among psalms for thankful acknowledgement, and in LXX it is 107, whose v. 3 uses the verb for giving thanks/acknowledging ('I will praise You... among the nations'), so English 108 is the correct conversion, not a slip. But only vv. 1-5 are thanksgiving; vv. 6-13 are a plea for military help. It honestly fits someone who wants to thank God openly, provided the result leans on vv. 1-5; as a whole psalm printed for a grateful reader it is the weakest match of this group.

psalms.movement: It opens with a resolve to give thanks to the LORD with the whole heart, in company with others (v. 1), then lists His works: splendid, remembered, gracious, providing food, keeping covenant, sending redemption (vv. 2-9; in Hebrew an alphabetical acrostic). It ends on a wisdom note: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and His praise endures forever (v. 10). There is no low point; it is thanks from first line to last.

namesIt.text: Hallelujah! I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart in the council of the upright and in the assembly.

lastLine.text: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; all who follow His precepts gain rich understanding. His praise endures forever!

psalms.hardParts: Very little. 'Giving them the inheritance of the nations' (v. 6) alludes to the conquest of Canaan; 'the fear of the LORD' (v. 10) may need a gloss (reverent awe, not terror) for a reader who fears God's anger.
psalms.fitNote: Fits exactly. Section 21 names it (LXX 110, which opens 'I will give thanks/acknowledge You, O Lord, with my whole heart'), and English 111 is the correct conversion. Verse 1 is precisely thankful acknowledgement made openly, 'in the assembly'. This is the cleanest match in the group for a person who simply wants to thank God.

psalms.movement: It opens already on the far side of rescue: 'I love the LORD, for He has heard my voice' (vv. 1-2). It then looks back at the danger, the ropes of death and anguish, and the cry for help (vv. 3-4), names God as gracious and compassionate, the One who saved the helpless (vv. 5-6), and tells the soul to return to its rest. It ends with a promise to walk before the LORD in the land of the living (vv. 7-9).

namesIt.text: I love the LORD, for He has heard my voice— my appeal for mercy.

turn.text: Then I called on the name of the LORD: “O LORD, deliver my soul!”

lastLine.text: I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living.

psalms.hardParts: Verse 3 ('The ropes of death entangled me; the anguish of Sheol overcame me') is vivid near-death language that may hit hard for someone suicidal, grieving or seriously ill. Verse 8 claims deliverance 'from death, my eyes from tears'; a reader still in tears may feel shut out unless the result makes clear this is spoken after being heard.
psalms.fitNote: Fits exactly, with one numbering caution. The letter (section 15, the Psalm 85 passage) says to give thanks in this psalm once the danger has passed and you are free again. Athanasius meant LXX 114, which is English 116:1-9 only; the online copy's bare '116th' hides that, so the split into verses 1-9 is correct and must be kept. The text voices the situation word for word: called on the Lord in distress, was heard, now gives thanks.

psalms.movement: It starts in faith spoken under pressure: 'I believed, therefore I said, I am greatly afflicted', and in alarm, 'All men are liars' (vv. 10-11). It turns at v. 12 to the question of how to repay God's goodness, and answers with worship: lifting the cup of salvation, calling on His name, keeping vows before His people (vv. 13-14, 17-18). It ends as a freed servant ('You have broken my bonds', v. 16) giving thanks in the courts of the LORD's house (v. 19).

namesIt.text: I believed, therefore I said, “I am greatly afflicted.”

turn.text: How can I repay the LORD for all His goodness to me?

lastLine.text: in the courts of the LORD’s house, in your midst, O Jerusalem. Hallelujah!

psalms.hardParts: 'All men are liars!' (v. 11) could sound like permission for bitterness if printed without context (it is said 'in my alarm'). 'Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints' (v. 15) can wound the grieving if read as God being pleased by death; it means their death is weighty and costly to Him, and may need a gentle note. 'The son of Your maidservant' (v. 16) is slave-household language that may puzzle.
psalms.fitNote: Fits, through its first verse. Section 24 says to use this psalm 'from the tenth verse on' when you have faith and believe the prayers you pray; Athanasius meant LXX 115, which begins 'I believed, therefore I spoke' and is exactly English 116:10-19, so the part is correct (Paul quotes the same line in 2 Corinthians 4:13). Verse 10 names the situation directly; the rest shows that faith acting as thanks and kept promises. Note the BSB renders v. 10 'therefore I said', where the Greek Athanasius read has 'therefore I spoke'; the sense is the same.

psalms.movement: It opens with a summons to give thanks because the LORD is good and His loving devotion endures forever, repeated by Israel, the priests and all who fear Him. The middle tells the danger that has already passed (surrounded, swarmed like bees, pushed until falling) and how the LORD helped, then the speaker walks through the gates to give thanks, and the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone. It closes with the same line it opened with, so the whole psalm is a frame of thanks around a remembered rescue.

namesIt.text: The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?

turn.text: In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered and set me free.

lastLine.text: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.

psalms.hardParts: 118:7 "I will look in triumph on those who hate me" and the triple refrain in 118:10-12 "in the name of the LORD I cut them off" (battle against the nations) can read as gloating or violence to a modern reader. 118:18 "The LORD disciplined me severely" may lead a suffering reader to take their pain as punishment. 118:27 (binding the festal sacrifice to the altar's horns) is strange without temple background. The psalm speaks from the far side of rescue, so someone still in the thick of it may feel it runs ahead of them.
psalms.fitNote: Fits both prescriptions honestly. For §21 (thankful acknowledgement): it opens and closes with "Give thanks to the LORD" (the Greek exomologeisthe) and 118:21 is explicit thanks for being answered; it is LXX 117, and the online copy's lists of thanksgiving psalms print "117" in LXX numbering, which is English 118. For §28 (fear): Athanasius quotes "The Lord is my helper, I will not fear what man can do to me", the Septuagint of LXX 117:6; in the BSB that sense is split across 118:6 ("I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?") and 118:7 ("He is my helper"). No numbering error for English 118. If the quiz uses it for thanks, 118:21 names it more directly than 118:6: "I will give You thanks, for You have answered me, and You have become my salvation."

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents.
psalms.movement: It opens by recalling a past answer: in distress the speaker cried to the LORD and He answered. Then it pleads for rescue from lying lips and pronounces the deceitful tongue's end (arrows, burning coals). It closes in weariness at living too long among people who hate peace, still unresolved: the speaker wants peace, they want war.

namesIt.text: Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace.

lastLine.text: I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war.

psalms.hardParts: 120:4 "Sharp arrows will come from the warrior, with burning coals of the broom tree!" is a punitive image against the liar. 120:5 names Meshech and Kedar, remote peoples a modern reader will not know (the sense is 'living far from home among hostile people'). Most importantly it ENDS on conflict with no resolution (120:7); a hurting reader who stops there gets no hope beyond the answered prayer in 120:1, so if printed alone it needs the ascent context (it is the first step, the one that makes you want to leave).
psalms.fitNote: Fits only as a member of the set. Athanasius prescribes the fifteen Gradual Psalms together, one per step of the upward climb, and English 120 is the first of them (LXX 119; the online copy's "119-133" is LXX numbering for English 120-134, so no error in using 120). On its own content, though, it is not a psalm of progress or of straining ahead: it is a complaint about lying tongues and hostile neighbours, the starting point from which the climb begins (the urge to leave behind what 120:5-6 describes). Presenting it alone to someone who feels they are advancing would be a stretch; presenting it as 'the step where you decide to leave' is honest.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents.
psalms.movement: It starts with the traveller looking up at the hills and asking where help comes from, and answers at once: from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth. The voice then shifts to 'you' and piles up assurances of a Keeper who does not slumber, shades by day and night, and guards from all evil. It ends with the LORD watching over every coming and going, now and forevermore.

namesIt.text: He will not allow your foot to slip; your Protector will not slumber.

turn.text: My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.

lastLine.text: The LORD will watch over your coming and going, both now and forevermore.

psalms.hardParts: No curses or violence. The sweeping promises in 121:3 ("He will not allow your foot to slip") and 121:7 ("The LORD will guard you from all evil") can sting a reader whose foot has slipped or who has already suffered harm, and may read as a broken promise if taken as a guarantee of no hardship. 121:6 ("nor the moon by night") reflects an ancient fear that will puzzle some readers.
psalms.fitNote: Fits well. English 121 is the second Song of Ascents (LXX 120), within the fifteen Athanasius sets for the upward climb; its pilgrim imagery (hills ahead, a foot that must not slip on the ascent, coming and going on the road) matches 'one song for each step forward' naturally. No numbering issue.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents. Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens with gladness at the invitation to go up to the house of the LORD and then stands already inside Jerusalem's gates. It admires the city where the tribes go up to give thanks and where the thrones of judgment stand. It ends with a prayer for the city's peace and a resolve to seek its good for the sake of brothers, friends and the house of the LORD.

namesIt.text: I was glad when they said to me, “Let us go to the house of the LORD.”

lastLine.text: For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your prosperity.

psalms.hardParts: No curses or violence. 122:6 "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem" is often read through modern Middle East politics, which may distract or divide. The communal gladness of going up with others (122:1, 122:8) may feel distant to someone isolated or estranged from a church. 122:5 "thrones of judgment" is neutral in context but may unsettle an anxious reader.
psalms.fitNote: Fits. English 122 is the third Song of Ascents (LXX 121), part of Athanasius's set for the upward climb; it is the psalm of arriving and standing in the gates, a natural 'step forward'. It is joyful from start to finish, so it suits a reader who senses progress, not one in distress. No numbering issue.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents.
psalms.movement: It begins with eyes lifted to God enthroned in heaven and compares that gaze to servants watching their master's hand, waiting until He shows mercy. Then it becomes a plea, 'have mercy', because of the contempt endured. It ends on that contempt from the arrogant and proud, with the mercy still awaited.

namesIt.text: I lift up my eyes to You, the One enthroned in heaven.

lastLine.text: We have endured much scorn from the arrogant, much contempt from the proud.

psalms.hardParts: 123:2 compares the believer to servants and a maidservant watching their master's or mistress's hand; the slavery imagery may jar a modern reader. The psalm ends on scorn and contempt with no answer given (123:4), so its hope rests entirely in the waiting gaze of 123:1-2 ("until He shows us mercy"); a hurting reader who reads it as 'the last word' may feel left in the insult.
psalms.fitNote: Fits as a member of the set, loosely on its own. It is the fourth Song of Ascents (English 123 = LXX 122), within the fifteen Athanasius prescribes for the upward climb, and the upward look in 123:1 suits 'climbing' well. But its content is patient waiting under contempt, not a sense of moving forward; it honestly speaks to someone pressing on while scorned. No numbering issue.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents. Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens with a call for Israel to say what would have happened if the LORD had not been on their side: swallowed alive, engulfed by floods, swept away by raging waters. Then it blesses the LORD for not giving them up as prey, and pictures the escape as a bird slipping from a torn snare. It ends by placing all help in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.

namesIt.text: We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler; the net is torn, and we have slipped away.

turn.text: Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth.

lastLine.text: Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.

psalms.hardParts: Vivid images of being eaten or drowned (124:3 "they would have swallowed us alive", 124:6 "prey to their teeth"). The premise "If the LORD had not been on our side" (124:1-2) may wound a reader who was not rescued, implying God was not on theirs. No curses on enemies.
psalms.fitNote: Fits as a member of the set. It is the fifth Song of Ascents (English 124 = LXX 123), within the fifteen Athanasius gives for the upward climb, and the torn net and escaping bird (124:7) suit 'forgetting what is behind'. Its content is thanks for a narrow escape rather than steady progress, so it best serves someone who feels they have just got free of something. No numbering issue.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents.
psalms.movement: It opens already standing firm: those who trust the LORD are as immovable as Mount Zion, and He surrounds His people as the mountains ring Jerusalem. It then promises that the wicked will not rule the land of the righteous, asks God to do good to the upright, and closes by separating the crooked from His people with a blessing of peace. There is no lament to climb out of; it is a steady song for someone already on the way.

namesIt.text: Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion. It cannot be moved; it abides forever.

lastLine.text: But those who turn to crooked ways the LORD will banish with the evildoers. Peace be upon Israel.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 125:4-5 can read as conditional: God does good 'to those who are good', and those who 'turn to crooked ways' are banished with the evildoers. Someone who feels they have slipped may read themselves into verse 5 rather than into the blessing. Verse 3 ('the scepter of the wicked') is mild.
psalms.fitNote: Fits as a member of the set. Athanasius (§24) gives the fifteen Gradual Psalms as a whole, one for each step of advance; he does not single this one out. Its superscription marks it a song of ascents and English 125 lies inside English 120-134 (the letter's online copy prints the range in LXX numbers, 119-133). Its content is steadiness while climbing more than straining forward, which suits a step on the way. No numbering error. (A separate genre list in the online copy puts '125' among psalms of thanksgiving and jubilation; English 125 is not really jubilant, so that list likely uses LXX numbering there, meaning English 126. That does not affect the §24 pairing.)

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents.
psalms.movement: It begins with remembered rescue: when the LORD brought the captives home it felt like a dream, mouths full of laughter, even the nations saying He had done great things. Then it turns to a present plea for restoration again, like dry streambeds in the Negev filling. It ends on a promise: those who sow in tears will reap with joy, and the one who goes out weeping will come home carrying sheaves.

namesIt.text: The LORD has done great things for us; we are filled with joy.

turn.text: Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy.

lastLine.text: He who goes out weeping, bearing a trail of seed, will surely return with shouts of joy, carrying sheaves of grain.

psalms.hardParts: Little to trip on. Verses 1-3 are exuberant about a past rescue, which a person still in the middle of loss may not feel yet; verse 4 shows the psalm itself is still asking. Verses 5-6 promise a harvest but not its timing; do not present them as a quick fix.
psalms.fitNote: §24: fits, as one of the fifteen songs of ascents (superscription confirms; English 126 is inside 120-134). §22: FLAG. In the letter's own sentence about the time when their anger has abated and you are free again, the psalms named are the 85th and the 116th (C.S.M.V. copy, the sentence after the 84th; Greek LXX 84 and 115 = English 85 and 116:10-19). Psalm 126 is not in that sentence. The letter does mention Psalm 126 elsewhere (§5) as telling the story of the return under Ezra, quoting its first line, but that is historical description, not a prescription. The content of 126 fits 'captivity over, give thanks' very well, which is probably how the pairing crept in, but as a §22 prescription it is not one Athanasius made. Recommend re-checking §22 and replacing 126 with English 85 (and 116:10-19) there, keeping 126 only under §24.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents. Of Solomon.
psalms.movement: It opens with a warning: unless the LORD builds the house and guards the city, all the labour and all the watching are wasted. It then gently undoes anxious overwork (rising early and staying up late is vain, for He gives sleep to His beloved). It ends by calling children a heritage and a reward from the LORD, like arrows in a warrior's hand.

namesIt.text: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain; unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain.

lastLine.text: Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. He will not be put to shame when he confronts the enemies at the gate.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 127:3-5 (children as God's reward; 'Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them') can wound the infertile, the childless, the single, or parents who have lost a child, and it is the psalm's last word. Verse 2 ('In vain you rise early and stay up late') can sting someone who has no choice but to work long hours; it is a word against anxious self-reliance, not against work.
psalms.fitNote: Fits as one of the fifteen songs of ascents in §24 (superscription confirms). It is not an obvious 'straining forward' psalm on its own; its lesson for the climber is that the climb is God's building, not ours. No numbering error. Note: the letter also names 'the 127th' of the Gradual Psalms, with the 30th, for when you dedicate your home (your soul as the house where you receive the Lord); English 127 ('Unless the LORD builds the house') fits that pairing well, so it is a second, stronger real pairing for this psalm.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents.
psalms.movement: It opens by calling blessed everyone who fears the LORD and walks in His ways. It then pictures that blessing in an ordinary home: eating the fruit of your own work, a fruitful household, children around the table. It closes as a benediction from Zion: may you see Jerusalem prosper, see your grandchildren, and peace be upon Israel.

namesIt.text: Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways!

lastLine.text: that you may see your children’s children. Peace be upon Israel!

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 128:2-4 and 6 tie blessing to prosperity, a wife and sons, and grandchildren. A single, childless, widowed, divorced or poor reader may feel excluded, or may hear that their lack means they do not fear the LORD. The psalm is addressed to a man and his household (verse 3, 'Your wife'), which some modern readers will notice.
psalms.fitNote: Fits as one of the fifteen songs of ascents in §24 (superscription confirms); Athanasius gives the set, not this psalm singly, and 'walk in His ways' suits a step forward. No numbering error. The letter also lists '128' among psalms to use when you want to call someone blessed, which English 128 fits exactly.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents.
psalms.movement: It starts by looking back over a lifetime of being attacked from youth, 'but they have not prevailed against me', with the image of ploughmen cutting long furrows on the speaker's back. It turns on one line: the LORD is righteous and has cut the cords of the wicked. It ends with a prayer that those who hate Zion wither like grass on a roof and never receive a blessing.

namesIt.text: many a time they have persecuted me from my youth, but they have not prevailed against me.

turn.text: The LORD is righteous; He has cut me from the cords of the wicked.

lastLine.text: May none who pass by say to them, “The blessing of the LORD be on you; we bless you in the name of the LORD.”

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 129:3 ('The plowmen plowed over my back; they made their furrows long') is an image of scourging that could be hard for survivors of abuse or violence. Psalm 129:5-8 is an imprecation: may haters of Zion be shamed, wither like rooftop grass, and never be blessed; the psalm ends on that withheld blessing, not on hope, so the result page should point back to verse 4.
psalms.fitNote: Fits as one of the fifteen songs of ascents in §24 (superscription confirms). Of the six it best matches 'forgetting what is behind': it looks back on long suffering and declares it did not win. But its ending is a curse, not a step forward, so it is an awkward single result for a hurting reader unless verse 4 is foregrounded. No numbering error.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents.
psalms.movement: It begins at the bottom, crying to the LORD out of the depths and begging Him to listen. It faces the fear that no one could stand if He kept a record of sins, and turns at once: with Him there is forgiveness. It then waits for Him more than night watchmen wait for morning, and ends by calling all Israel to hope, because He will redeem from all iniquity.

namesIt.text: I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope.

turn.text: But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared.

lastLine.text: And He will redeem Israel from all iniquity.

psalms.hardParts: Nothing violent and no curses. Psalm 130:3 ('If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities...') may stir guilt in a scrupulous reader, but verse 4 answers it at once. Someone in deep depression may find 'the depths' (verse 1) very close to home; the psalm stays with them there before it hopes.
psalms.fitNote: Fits as one of the fifteen songs of ascents in §24 (superscription confirms; English 130 is inside 120-134). As a single psalm it is more a cry from the bottom than a sense of climbing upward; its place in the ascent is the step of waiting and hoping. For a hurting reader it is the strongest of these six, with a clear turn and a hopeful last line. No numbering error.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents. Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens by setting ambition down: the singer is not proud and does not reach for things too high. It settles into a picture of a soul made quiet, like a weaned child resting against its mother. It ends by turning outward and telling all Israel to hope in the LORD now and forever.

namesIt.text: Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.

lastLine.text: O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore.

psalms.fitNote: Fits, but only as part of a series. Athanasius (§24) gives the fifteen Gradual Psalms as a set, one for each step of the climb, for someone who feels they are pressing on and leaving the past behind (Phil 3:13-14). He does not give each psalm its own occasion. English 131 is LXX 130, one of the Gradual Psalms either way, and its superscription says so, so the numbering is right. On its own terms it speaks of growth as becoming humbler and quieter, not of striving. That is an honest fit for a step on the way up, but a result page should say it comes from the ascent series and was not singled out by him.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents.
psalms.movement: It begins by asking the LORD to remember David's hardships and his vow not to rest until he had found God a dwelling. The pilgrims then set out to worship at His footstool and pray for His priests, His saints and His anointed. At verse 11 the plea gives way to God's own oath, and the psalm ends with God speaking: Zion is His home forever, and He promises to feed the poor, clothe the priests with salvation and make the crown gleam.

namesIt.text: Let us go to His dwelling place; let us worship at His footstool.

turn.text: The LORD swore an oath to David, a promise He will not revoke: “One of your descendants I will place on your throne.

lastLine.text: I will clothe his enemies with shame, but the crown upon him will gleam.”

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 132:18 promises shame for the king's enemies (mild). Psalm 132:12 makes the throne depend on the sons keeping the covenant, which an anxious reader could take as God's favour being conditional. Most of the psalm is about David, the ark and Zion's priests, so a modern reader may find it distant from their own life; it needs a sentence on why a psalm about a king's vow fits a personal climb.
psalms.fitNote: Fits only through the series. Athanasius (§24) prescribes the fifteen Gradual Psalms as a whole for someone pressing forward, one for each step; English 132 (LXX 131) is one of them, and its superscription confirms it, so there is no numbering error. On its own the content is royal and about Zion, a vow not to rest until God has a dwelling and God's answering promise. That can be read as the resolve of someone going up, but it is the weakest personal fit of the four. If the quiz gives single results, this one is better used as a step inside the set than as a stand-alone answer.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents. Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens with delight at how good it is when brothers live together in harmony. Two pictures follow: oil running down Aaron's beard and dew falling from Hermon onto Zion's mountains. It ends by naming Zion as the place where the LORD has given the blessing of life forever.

namesIt.text: Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!

lastLine.text: It is like the dew of Hermon falling on the mountains of Zion. For there the LORD has bestowed the blessing of life forevermore.

psalms.fitNote: Fits as one of the fifteen Gradual Psalms that Athanasius (§24) gives together for someone pressing forward, one for each step. English 133 is LXX 132, and its superscription names it a song of ascents, so the numbering is right. Its own subject is harmony among believers, not personal progress, so it does not describe the climbing feeling. It fits as a step near the top of the ascent, where the pilgrims arrive together, and the result should say it belongs to the series.

psalms.superscription: A song of ascents.
psalms.movement: It calls the LORD's servants who stand in His house by night to bless Him. They are told to lift their hands toward the sanctuary. It ends with a blessing handed back to them from the Maker of heaven and earth, out of Zion.

namesIt.text: Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD who serve by night in the house of the LORD!

lastLine.text: May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion.

psalms.fitNote: Fits as the last of the fifteen Gradual Psalms, which Athanasius (§24) gives as a set for someone pressing forward, one for each step of the advance. English 134 is LXX 133, the last number in his range (LXX 119-133 = English 120-134), and its superscription confirms it. As the final step it pictures the climb finished: the pilgrim is inside the house, blessing God and blessed by Him. That is an honest fit for the end of the ascent. It does not speak to the effort of climbing, so it should not be the result for someone who is only starting out.

psalms.movement: It opens with a call to give thanks to the LORD because He is good, and every line carries the same refrain: His loving devotion endures forever. It moves through creation and the exodus, the wilderness and the land given to Israel. Near the end it turns personal ('He remembered us in our low estate') and closes with a final call to thank the God of heaven.

namesIt.text: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good. His loving devotion endures forever.

lastLine.text: Give thanks to the God of heaven! His loving devotion endures forever.

psalms.hardParts: Violence praised inside the refrain: Psalm 136:10 (the firstborn of Egypt struck down), Psalm 136:15 (Pharaoh's army swept into the sea), Psalm 136:17-20 (kings struck down and slaughtered, named). A hurting reader may stumble over God's love being sung alongside killing, and a grieving parent may stop at verse 10. Verses 23-25 are where it comes closest to the reader's own life.
psalms.fitNote: Fits closely. In §21 Athanasius lists psalms for thankful acknowledgement of God (exomologesis). The list in the online copy is in English numbering (9, 75, 92, 105-107, 111, 118, 136, 138...), and those are the psalms whose Greek opening is a call to 'give thanks' or 'confess' the Lord. English 136 is LXX 135, which opens with exactly that call and repeats it. The copy's '136' is therefore right in English numbering and should not be read as LXX 136 (English 137, By the rivers of Babylon), which would not fit at all. Worth keeping that ambiguity in mind when building the data.

psalms.movement: It opens with the exiles sitting and weeping by Babylon's rivers, harps hung on the willows, refusing to sing the LORD's song for their captors. In the middle the singer takes an oath never to forget Jerusalem, which is the psalm's only step toward home. It ends in raw anger: a plea that God remember Edom, and a blessing on whoever pays Babylon back, down to its infants.

namesIt.text: By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion.

lastLine.text: Blessed is he who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rocks.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 137:8-9 blesses whoever repays Babylon and dashes its infants against the rocks; this is the last line, so printing the whole psalm leaves the reader on it. Psalm 137:7 asks God to remember Edom's cruelty against them. Psalm 137:5-6 is a self-curse (right hand withered, tongue stuck) if the singer forgets Jerusalem, which a scrupulous or anxious reader may take literally. Other Fathers read verse 9 allegorically, as sinful thoughts dashed against the rock that is Christ (Augustine's commentary on this psalm, numbered 136 in his Bible). That is a real patristic reading, but the Letter to Marcellinus does not make it, so it must not be credited to Athanasius.
psalms.fitNote: Fits clearly, and the numbering is right. In §25 Athanasius says that when you realise you have been led astray, you should stop, sit down and weep as they did by Babylon's waters, which is verse 1 almost word for word. The online copy's '137' is English 137 (LXX 136). His use is figurative: the exile's captivity stands for a mind carried off by other people's arguments or alien thoughts. In the psalm itself the exiles are grieving, not repenting of their own sin. The hope Athanasius sees is in stopping and remembering home (verses 5-6). The psalm has no turn toward trust and ends in a curse, so the result page has to name that hope itself and handle verses 8-9 plainly, or a hurting reader is left on the harshest line in the Psalter.

psalms.superscription: Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens in wholehearted thanks spoken out loud, and grounds that thanks in one remembered fact: on the day David called, God answered and gave him strength (v3). It widens to the kings of the earth joining the song, then comes back to the one singing, trusting that God will keep him in the middle of future trouble. It ends in quiet confidence that God will finish what He began, with a last plea not to be let go.

namesIt.text: I give You thanks with all my heart; before the gods I sing Your praises.

lastLine.text: The LORD will fulfill His purpose for me. O LORD, Your loving devotion endures forever— do not abandon the works of Your hands.

psalms.hardParts: Little that would wound. "Before the gods" (138:1) may puzzle a modern reader; it means praising openly before every rival power. "The proud He knows from afar" (138:6) is a gentle warning, not a curse. "The anger of my foes" (138:7) is named but not cursed.
psalms.fitNote: Honest, strong fit. Athanasius's LXX 137 is English 138, and the online copy's number is right here. It is thanks said openly, which is exactly the thankful acknowledgement §21 means (not confession of sin), and v3 gives the reason for the thanks: God answered when he called. No numbering problem.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It opens in wonder that God knows the singer completely: every thought, every road, even the dark and the womb, with nowhere he can go that God is not already holding him (v1-18). It then breaks suddenly into anger at God's enemies (v19-22). It ends by turning that searching gaze inward, freely asking God to test his heart and lead him on the everlasting way.

namesIt.text: Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my concerns.

lastLine.text: See if there is any offensive way in me; lead me in the way everlasting.

psalms.hardParts: 139:19-22: "O God, that You would slay the wicked" and "I hate them with perfect hatred; I count them as my enemies." This is sharp, and a hurting reader could take it as licence for hatred; the psalm answers it straight away by asking God to search the singer's own heart (v23-24). Also 139:7 ("Where can I flee from Your presence?") and 139:11-12 can feel like being watched to someone who feels guilty or exposed, but the psalm means them as being held (v10). 139:13-16 (the womb, days written in God's book) can be tender ground for readers who have lost a pregnancy or a child.
psalms.fitNote: Good fit on testing, looser on thanks. Athanasius's LXX 138 is English 139, and the online copy's number is right. The heart of it is "test me" (v23), a free surrender to God's testing, which suits §25's point that testing proves a person. The thanks after the trial has passed shows up only as praise and wonder (v14, v17), not as thanks for a particular rescue. No numbering problem.

psalms.superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It opens with an urgent cry to be rescued from violent, scheming men whose words sting like snake venom and who set snares along the path (v1-5). Halfway through, the singer holds on to God by name, "You are my God", and to God as the One who shields his head in battle (v6-7), then asks for the schemers' plans to come down on their own heads (v8-11). It ends in settled certainty that God defends the poor and that the upright will live in His presence.

namesIt.text: Rescue me, O LORD, from evil men. Protect me from men of violence,

turn.text: I know that the LORD upholds justice for the poor and defends the cause of the needy.

lastLine.text: Surely the righteous will praise Your name; the upright will dwell in Your presence.

psalms.hardParts: 140:9-11 are curses: "May burning coals fall on them; may they be thrown into the fire, into the miry pits, never to rise again" and "may calamity hunt down the man of violence." A reader could take this as permission to wish harm on someone; it is best read as handing judgement to God rather than taking it. 140:3 and 140:5 (venomous tongues, hidden snares) may bring back real abuse or slander.
psalms.fitNote: Exact fit. Athanasius's LXX 139 is English 140, and the online copy's number in §25 is right. It is a plea for rescue from enemies who "surround" the singer (v9), which is §25's case exactly. Warning: the online copy's "140" in §17 is a different psalm (LXX 140 = English 141); do not mix the two up.

psalms.superscription: A Psalm of David.
psalms.movement: It opens as an evening prayer rising like incense, asking God to come quickly (v1-2). It then asks God to guard the singer's own mouth and heart from being pulled into the wrongdoing and pleasures of the wicked, and welcomes correction from the righteous (v3-7). At v8 it turns: his eyes are fixed on God, his refuge, and it ends asking to walk through their snares unharmed.

namesIt.text: Keep me from the snares they have laid for me, and from the lures of evildoers.

turn.text: But my eyes are fixed on You, O GOD the Lord. In You I seek refuge; do not leave my soul defenseless.

lastLine.text: Let the wicked fall into their own nets, while I pass by in safety.

psalms.hardParts: 141:6 ("When their rulers are thrown down from the cliffs") is violent. 141:7 ("our bones have been scattered at the mouth of Sheol") is a grim picture that can weigh on a despairing reader. 141:5 ("Let the righteous man strike me") means welcoming honest rebuke, and must never be read as telling someone to put up with abuse. 141:10 wishes the wicked caught in their own traps, a mild imprecation.
psalms.fitNote: Fair fit, with a numbering flag. The online copy prints "140" in §17, which is Athanasius's LXX number left unconverted (it converted the neighbouring 17, 86 and 88); in English Bibles it is 141. Eng 141 is truly a prayer made because of opponents who set snares (v9-10), but most of it is about keeping the singer's own heart from being drawn in (v3-5), not about being surrounded. English 140, which Athanasius gives for enemies closing in again (§25), fits "hemming in" more closely, but by the numbering §17 means 141.

psalms.superscription: A Maskil of David, when he was in the cave. A prayer.
psalms.movement: It opens with a cry out loud for mercy, the singer pouring out his trouble, faint in spirit, snares on his path, and no one at his right hand who cares whether he lives (v1-4). At v5 he says to God, "You are my refuge", his portion among the living. It ends still asking, low and outmatched, yet already seeing himself freed and the righteous gathering round him because of God's goodness.

namesIt.text: Listen to my cry, for I am brought quite low. Rescue me from my pursuers, for they are too strong for me.

turn.text: I cry to You, O LORD: “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.”

lastLine.text: Free my soul from prison, that I may praise Your name. The righteous will gather around me because of Your goodness to me.

psalms.hardParts: No curses. 142:4 ("no one attends to me... no one cares for my soul") puts isolation very bluntly; for a lonely or suicidal reader it is validating, but the result should not leave them there, and v5 and v7 answer it. The rescue is not yet done when the psalm ends: it closes in hope and petition, not in deliverance already received.
psalms.fitNote: Excellent fit for both uses. The online copy's "142" is right (LXX 141 = English 142). The psalm's own superscription places it in the cave, which is exactly §20's picture of the pursuer entering the cave where David hid (1 Samuel 24). Its first-person cry against pursuers "too strong for me" (v6) is exactly §12's point about singing as the one who suffers.

psalms.superscription: Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens in blessing and confidence: God is David's rock, his fortress and shield, the One who trains his hands for battle (v1-2). It pauses on how small and brief a man is (v3-4), then calls God down in storm and lightning to rescue him from deceitful foreigners, promising a new song to the God who saved David from the deadly sword (v5-11). It ends in a picture of peace, with thriving children, full barns, no breach in the walls, and no cry in the streets, blessing the people whose God is the LORD.

namesIt.text: to Him who gives victory to kings, who frees His servant David from the deadly sword.

lastLine.text: Blessed are the people of whom this is so; blessed are the people whose God is the LORD.

psalms.hardParts: 144:1 ("who trains my hands for war, my fingers for battle") and 144:6 ("shoot Your arrows and rout them") are battle language that can read as glorifying war. 144:7 and 144:11 ("the grasp of foreigners") could be misread as hostility to foreigners; in context they are hostile invaders known for lying. 144:12-14 (sons, daughters, full barns, flocks) may sting a reader who is childless, grieving or poor. 144:4 ("Man is like a breath") is humbling rather than harmful.
psalms.fitNote: Strong fit. The online copy's "144" is right (LXX 143 = English 144). In the Septuagint this psalm's title adds that it was sung against Goliath; the BSB superscription says only "Of David.", so the Goliath link comes from Athanasius's Greek text, not the English heading. The psalm itself backs it up: David rescued from the deadly sword (v10), God training his hands for battle (v1), and a people kept safe (v12-15), which suits §25's enemy rising against God's people and the singer together. The trust David shows here is in God, not his own strength (v3-4).

psalms.superscription: A Psalm of praise. Of David.
psalms.movement: It opens with one person's vow to bless God's name every day and forever, then widens outward: generation telling generation, and a portrait of the LORD as gracious, compassionate and good to all He has made. From verse 13 it grows tender and specific (He holds up those who fall, feeds every creature, is near to all who call on Him in truth), and it closes by returning to the singer's own mouth and calling every creature to bless His holy name forever.

namesIt.text: The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made.

lastLine.text: My mouth will declare the praise of the LORD; let every creature bless His holy name forever and ever.

psalms.hardParts: Psalm 145:20 ends with "but all the wicked He will destroy", a jolt of judgment in an otherwise gentle psalm. Psalm 145:19 ("He fulfills the desires of those who fear Him") and 145:18-19 generally can sting a reader whose prayers feel unanswered, if read as a guarantee rather than praise. Otherwise nothing harsh: no lament and no curse.
psalms.fitNote: Fits honestly and well. Athanasius (§25) prescribes it for marvelling at God's kindness to all and remembering His goodness to yourself, then praising Him; verses 8-9 and 14-16 say exactly that ("good to all", compassion on all He has made, lifting all who are bowed down), and verses 1-2 are the singer's own vow to bless Him. NUMBERING FLAG: the online C.S.M.V. copy at this spot prints "Psalm 105", which does not match (English 105 recounts God's dealings with Abraham, Joseph and the Exodus). The surrounding sequence (Goliath psalm printed as 144, i.e. LXX 143 = English 144) and the Greek original point to LXX 144, which is English Psalm 145, the psalm analysed here. The "105" in the online copy appears to be a conversion or typesetting error; worth confirming against the Greek (PG 27) before publishing.

critic.verdict: The pairing list is complete and its numbers hold up. I re-read the whole English copy and then checked every numbered recommendation in §§12, 15–26, 28 and 33 against the TLG Greek (scratchpad/greek/marc-greek2.txt, lines 216–219 and 265–382). I checked the §17 and §28 disputes against the Migne OCR (pg27.txt). I checked §§15–26 against the modern Greek EPE translation (scratchpad/gd.txt). No pairing in the letter is missing from the list, and none on the list is invented. Every English number matches the Greek, allowing for the LXX splits and merges (9-10, 114-115, 116:1-9 and 116:10-19, 147). The pass rightly caught every error in the English copy: 27→13, 19→84, 105→145, 95→48, 116→126, the added 71 and 126 in the thanks list, the added 113 and 117 in the praise list, the added 141, 142 and 146 in the prayer list, the dropped Sabbath 92, and 3→2 in §26. Its claims to have read the Greek are backed by the files: the Latin "16, 85, 87 et 140" is on pg27.txt line 1891, Migne prints ιζ' and πζ', Migne's κη' and κθ' bracket the sadness, slip and fear lines, and ἑκατοστῷ ἕκτῳ appears in §4. The weaknesses are elsewhere. Four entries filed as "teaching" are addressed to the reader's own soul in the Greek: 37, 91, 20 and the §33 verses of Psalm 119. None of them has a shape analysis, and they are the entries that would answer the top modern needs (fear and protection, envy, praying for someone). One variant reading, one word choice and one reading of a disputed word are not recorded. The "four witnesses" are not independent. The modern-needs table's coverage column contradicts the pairings in places, and its strength ratings rest on autocomplete order, not search volume.

gaps.what: Psalm 91 is filed as 'teaching', but the Greek says παραθαρσῦναι θέλων σεαυτὸν καὶ τοὺς ἑτέρους: encourage yourself and others, and show that hope in God makes the soul fearless (ἄφοβον). The EPE agrees ('τον εαυτό σου'). So it is a first-person soul situation, and the letter's most direct answer to fear. It has NO shape analysis. The modern-needs table rates fear and protection 'strong' and protection only 'loosely' covered, and ignores 91, the psalm most searched for protection.

Psalm 37 is filed as 'teaching', but the Greek says λέγε καὶ σαυτῷ καὶ τοῖς ἑτέροις: say it to yourself and to others, so as not to envy the wicked. It is the only pairing about envying the wicked besides 73. It has no shape analysis, although the modern need 'Injustice; the wicked prospering; envy' is marked as covered.

The modern need 'Someone you love is going through something' is rated strong and marked 'covers'. The only pairings behind that are §17 Psalm 20 (comfort the afflicted and pray over them) and §33 Psalm 119:16, 54, 92 (whoever cares for sufferers should say these words, and God grants full healing, τελείαν τὴν θεραπείαν). Both are filed as 'teaching' and NEITHER has a shape analysis. §33 is also the letter's only hook for the 'sickness/healing' need, which the table marks 'none'.

A variant reading is not recorded, although UNSETTLED is empty. In the thanks (ἐξομολόγησις) list, the EPE modern Greek reads 115 where the TLG and the Migne OCR read ριζ' (117). The list keeps English 118 (LXX 117), which is right: the identical list in the §14 catalogue (line 243) also has ριζ', and every psalm in the list opens with ἐξομολογ-, which LXX 117 does and LXX 115 does not. But the dispute should be recorded, since the pass says it used the EPE as a witness.
gaps.where: §21, list of 'when you need to give thanks' (line 324; gd.txt)

gaps.what: The reading of exomologesis as thankful acknowledgement is defensible, since every psalm in the list opens with ἐξομολογήσομαι/ἐξομολογεῖσθε. But the EPE translates it as 'when you need to confess' (εξομολογηθείς), and the C.S.M.V. has 'testify concerning God'. The same word means confession two sections earlier (§20, Psalm 51: τοὺς τῆς ἐξομολογήσεως καὶ μετανοίας λόγους). Record the split so the result copy does not state one reading as settled.

The Psalm 52 situation reads 'seeing the devil gloat'. The Greek is τὸν διάβολον κατακαυχώμενον, right after διεβλήθης ('you were slandered'). Both the EPE ('ο συκοφάντης') and the C.S.M.V. ('the slanderer') take it as the human slanderer (Doeg). Printing 'the devil' on a result would put a contested gloss in Athanasius's mouth.

The witnesses are over-counted. The TLG 2035.059 is a digitisation of the Migne PG 27 text, the Migne Latin is a translation printed with that text, and the EPE follows the same edition. So 'four witnesses' against the TLG on §17 are really one edition checked against its own mistyped digital copy. The conclusions (ιζ' = 18, πζ' = 88) stand because the Migne scan outranks the TLG transcription, but there is no manuscript or critical-edition check. Gregg (Paulist 1980) and any critical text were not consulted. This matters most for §12, where the C.S.M.V. read 10 and 11 and may have followed a different text.
gaps.where: GREEK SOURCE CLAIMED, disputes (1)-(2); §12 Psalms 12 and 17

gaps.what: The coverage column contradicts the pairings in several places. 'Guidance/feeling lost' is marked 'none', but §17 Psalm 23 is glossed on the list itself as 'shepherded and guided on your way' (εὐοδούμενον). 'Loneliness' is marked 'loosely', but §20 Psalm 63 says outright 'do not fear as though you were alone there, God is with you' (μὴ φοβηθῇς ὡς μόνος ὢν). 'Temptation' is marked 'loosely', but §25 Psalm 139 (temptations as testing) and Psalm 137 (captive to alien thoughts) are direct. 'Anger' is marked 'loosely' and misses that Athanasius himself quotes 'Cease from anger and forsake wrath' (LXX 36:8 = English Psalm 37:8, marc-greek2.txt line 157) as a law the Psalter lays down.

The strength ratings (strong/moderate/weak) rest on Google autocomplete presence and position, which do not measure search volume. Two claims are cut off and their sources cannot be checked: 'American Bible Society publi…' under Betrayal and 'Bible Gateway's historical top key…' under Joy. Each needs a URL. There is also nothing to show the autocomplete was queried from the US as stated. The owner is waiting on Bing Keyword Research numbers for exactly this kind of claim.
gaps.where: MODERN NEEDS table, strength and source columns

gaps.what: 'Joy, wanting to praise' is marked 'covers', but it rests on entries filed as 'other' or 'occasion' that have no shape analysis: 33 (sing together), 93 and 98 (sing to the Lord), 135 and 146–150 (how to praise). Only 65, 105 and 107 have shapes. The letter's own joy line, 'Is any among you cheerful? Let him sing' (James 5:13, §28), names no psalm.

Other entries outside 'soul' that could honestly serve as results also have no shape analysis. Psalm 143 (§25, 'prayer and supplication', paired with 5, which has one). Psalm 90 (§17, how Moses prayed). Psalm 74 (§21, consolation when God is angry with His people). Psalm 41 (§19, mercy to the poor).

Leaving out the §14 genre catalogue is defensible. But it has one label that answers a modern need: προτρεπτικὸς εἰς ἀνδρίαν (hortatory to courage), LXX 80 = English 81 (line 254). The English copy's version of the catalogue is badly abridged and renumbered, so a reader who used only that copy would miss this label. Record it as a secondary, genre-level support for the 'Strength and courage' need, not as a pairing.

The Greek praise list names LXX 146 AND LXX 147 separately (ρμς', ρμζ'). Both are parts of English Psalm 147 (147:1-11 and 147:12-20). The list prints '147' once, without the split, although it handles 116:1-9 and 116:10-19 that way. Minor, but keep it consistent if verse ranges are ever printed.

Psalm 151 cannot be printed from the BSB. The list already notes this. The result flow still needs a decision: drop it, or print it from a public-domain LXX translation such as Brenton. Otherwise Athanasius's leadership pairing has no text.

greekCat.greekSource: FOUND AND READ. Primary: the TLG text of Athanasius, Epistula ad Marcellinum (TLG 2035.059, from Migne PG 27.12-45), posted with TLG permission by Documenta Catholica Omnia: http://www.documentacatholicaomnia.eu/02g/0295-0373,_Athanasius,_Epistula_ad_Marcellinum_de_interpretatione_Psalmorum,_MGR.pdf. I extracted it with pdftotext and read every Greek numeral in the letter myself. Working copies: C:/Users/Light/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-Light-Desktop-claude-theology-compass/5d5b7ea0-870f-4d9b-a8bd-900bab31fcb0/scratchpad/greek/marc-greek2.txt, one sentence per line, split numerals rejoined. One problem with this text: it prints both stigma (6) and koppa (90) as 'ς'. I told them apart by their place in the numeral (ϙα = 91, ϙϛ = 96, κϛ = 26) and by what the psalm says. Second witness: the archive.org scan of Migne PG 27 (https://archive.org/details/patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_027), whose OCR text I saved as greek/pg27.txt. Its Greek column is readable, and in its Latin column the Arabic psalm numbers survive, e.g. 'psalle 16, 85, 87 et 140'. It also gave the section numbers (Migne's §15-§28 and §33 markers). I checked every catalogue numeral against the Migne Greek, and against the Latin wherever its digits could be read. They disagree in two places. The TLG text reads ιϛ (16) for being rescued from enemies and πϛ (86) in the prayer-against-opponents list. Migne's Greek and Latin read ιζ (17) and πζ (87), which also fit the psalms' content and superscriptions, so I followed Migne. The First1KGreek corpus on GitHub has only six Athanasius works (tlg002, 003, 117, 130-132) and does not include this letter.

entries.situation: Singing a psalm while thinking about your own troubles, so its words feel like your own
entries.greek: τὸν τρίτον ψάλλει τις εἰς τὰς ἰδίας θλίψεις συνορῶν
entries.evidence: Greek ordinal τρίτον; Migne scan agrees; Eng 3 superscription: when David fled from Absalom

entries.situation: Putting your own trust in God and your own prayer into words
entries.greek: τὸν ιαʹ καὶ τὸν ιςʹ ὡς εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν πεποίθησιν καὶ προσευχήν
entries.evidence: ιαʹ and ιϛʹ in TLG and in the Migne scan (OCR 'τα’ καὶ τὸν ις’'). The English copy's 11 is wrong and 17 is missing. Eng 17 superscription: 'A prayer of David'

entries.situation: Being struck by conscience and wanting words of your own for repentance
entries.greek: τὸν μὲν νʹ ψαλμὸν ὡς αὐτός ἐστι τὰ ἴδια τῆς μετανοίας ἑαυτοῦ λέγων ῥήματα
entries.evidence: νʹ in both witnesses. The English copy attaches 51 to the earlier conscience clause, which in the Greek names no psalm. Eng 51 superscription: Nathan after Bathsheba

entries.situation: Being persecuted and singing these psalms as the one who is suffering, not as if about someone else
entries.greek: τὸν δὲ νγʹ, καὶ τὸν νεʹ, καὶ τὸν νςʹ, καὶ τὸν ρμαʹ ... ὡς ὢν ὁ πάσχων
entries.evidence: Greek numerals agree in TLG and Migne. The Eng superscriptions are all flight and persecution scenes: Ziphites, Gath, and the cave twice

entries.situation: Wanting to call someone blessed: how to do it, on what grounds, and what to say
